chapters.title: Chapter 1 — An Essay Concerning the True Original, Extent and End of Civil Government
paragraphs: In the previous discourse I have shown:
(1). That Adam did not have — either by a natural right of fatherhood or by a positive gift from God — any such authority over his children, or dominion over the world, as is claimed:
(2). That even if he had, his heirs still had no right to it:

(3). That if his heirs had, there is no law of nature or positive law of God that decides who the rightful heir is in every case that may arise; so the right of succession, and with it the right to rule, could not have been settled with any certainty:

(4). That even if that had been settled, all knowledge of which is the eldest line of Adam’s descendants has been lost so completely and for so long that, among the races of mankind and the families of the world, no one has the slightest claim over another to be the eldest house and to hold the right of inheritance:

Since all these premises have, I think, been clearly established, it is impossible for the rulers now on earth to gain any benefit, or to draw even the faintest shadow of authority, from what is held to be the source of all power: Adam’s private dominion and paternal jurisdiction. Anyone, then, who does not want to give good reason for thinking that all government in the world is simply the product of force and violence, and that men live together by no other rule than that of beasts, where the strongest wins — and so lay a foundation for endless disorder and harm, tumult, sedition and rebellion (the very things the followers of that hypothesis protest against so loudly) — must necessarily find another origin for government, another source of political power, and another way of designating and knowing the persons who hold it, than the one Sir Robert Filmer has taught us.

For this purpose, I think it will not be out of place to set down what I take political power to be, so that the power of a MAGISTRATE over a subject can be distinguished from that of a FATHER over his children, a MASTER over his servant, a HUSBAND over his wife, and a LORD over his slave. All these distinct powers sometimes come together in the same man; and if we consider him in each of these different relations, it may help us to tell these powers apart from one another, and to show the difference between a ruler of a commonwealth, a father of a family, and a captain of a galley.

POLITICAL POWER, then, I take to be a RIGHT to make laws with penalties of death, and therefore with all lesser penalties, for regulating and preserving property; and to use the force of the community in executing such laws and in defending the commonwealth from foreign injury; and all this only for the public good.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 — Of the State of Nature
paragraphs: TO understand political power correctly, and to trace it back to its origin, we must consider what state all men are naturally in. It is a state of perfect freedom to order their actions and to dispose of their possessions and persons as they think fit, within the bounds of the law of nature, without asking anyone’s permission or depending on the will of any other man.

It is also a state of equality, in which all power and jurisdiction is mutual, and no one has more than another. For nothing is more evident than this: creatures of the same species and rank, all born without distinction to the same advantages of nature and to the use of the same faculties, should also be equal to one another, without subordination or subjection — unless the lord and master of them all should, by some clear declaration of his will, set one above another, and by an evident and plain appointment give him an unquestionable right to dominion and sovereignty.

The judicious Hooker regards this natural equality of men as so evident in itself, and so far beyond all question, that he makes it the foundation of men’s obligation to love one another. On that obligation he builds the duties they owe one another, and from it he derives the great maxims of justice and charity. His words are:

“The same natural motive has led men to recognize that it is no less their duty to love others than to love themselves. For since things that are equal must all be measured by one and the same standard, if I cannot help wishing to receive good — as much good from every man’s hands as any man can wish for his own soul — how could I expect any part of this desire of mine to be satisfied unless I take care to satisfy the same desire, which is undoubtedly in other men too, since they are of one and the same nature? To have anything offered to them that goes against this desire must in every respect grieve them as much as it would grieve me. So if I do harm, I must expect to suffer harm, since there is no reason why others should show me a greater measure of love than I have shown them. My desire, therefore, to be loved by my equals in nature as much as possible places on me a natural duty to bear them fully the same affection in return. And everyone knows the many rules and principles that natural reason has drawn, for the direction of life, from this relation of equality between ourselves and those who are as ourselves.” Hooker, Ecclesiastical Polity, book I.

But although this is a state of liberty, it is not a state of licence. A man in that state has an uncontrollable liberty to dispose of his person or possessions, yet he does not have the liberty to destroy himself, or even any creature in his possession, except where some nobler use than its mere preservation calls for it. The state of nature has a law of nature to govern it, which binds everyone. And reason, which is that law, teaches all mankind who will only consult it that, since all are equal and independent, no one ought to harm another in his life, health, liberty, or possessions. For all men are the workmanship of one omnipotent and infinitely wise maker, all the servants of one sovereign master, sent into the world by his order and on his business. So they are his property, since they are his workmanship, made to last as long as he pleases, not as long as another man pleases. And since we are furnished with the same faculties and all share in one community of nature, no such subordination can be supposed among us as would authorize us to destroy one another, as if we were made for one another’s use, the way the lower ranks of creatures are made for ours. Everyone is bound to preserve himself and not to abandon his post wilfully; and for the same reason, when his own preservation is not at stake, he ought as far as he can to preserve the rest of mankind. And unless it is to do justice on an offender, he may not take away or impair another’s life, or anything that serves to preserve another’s life, liberty, health, limb, or goods.

And so that all men may be restrained from invading the rights of others and from hurting one another, and so that the law of nature, which wills the peace and preservation of all mankind, may be observed, the execution of the law of nature is, in that state, placed in every man’s hands. This gives everyone a right to punish those who break that law, to whatever degree may prevent its violation. For the law of nature, like all other laws that concern men in this world, would be pointless if no one in the state of nature had the power to enforce it, and in that way to protect the innocent and restrain offenders. And if anyone in the state of nature may punish another for any wrong he has done, then everyone may. For in that state of perfect equality, where by nature no one has superiority or jurisdiction over another, whatever one person may do in enforcing that law, everyone must necessarily have a right to do.

This, then, is how one man in the state of nature comes to have a power over another. But it is not an absolute or arbitrary power to treat a criminal, once he has him in his hands, according to the heat of passion or the boundless excesses of his own will. It is only a power to pay him back, as far as calm reason and conscience direct, with what is proportionate to his offence — that is, as much as may serve for reparation and restraint. For these two are the only reasons why one man may lawfully do harm to another, which is what we call punishment. By breaking the law of nature, the offender declares that he lives by some other rule than reason and common equity, which is the measure God has set for men’s actions for their mutual security. So he becomes dangerous to mankind, because he has slighted and broken the bond meant to protect them from injury and violence. This is a trespass against the whole species, and against the peace and safety the law of nature provides for it. On this account, therefore, every man, by the right he has to preserve mankind in general, may restrain, or where necessary destroy, whatever is harmful to them. And so he may bring on anyone who has broken that law such evil as may make him regret doing it, and in that way deter him, and others by his example, from doing the same harm. In this case, and on this ground, EVERY MAN HAS A RIGHT TO PUNISH THE OFFENDER, AND BE EXECUTIONER OF THE LAW OF NATURE.

I have no doubt that this will seem a very strange doctrine to some men. But before they condemn it, I ask them to explain to me by what right any prince or state can put to death or punish a foreigner for a crime he commits in their country. Their laws certainly do not reach a stranger by virtue of any sanction they receive from the published will of the legislative. They do not speak to him, and even if they did, he would not be bound to listen to them. The legislative authority that makes them binding on the subjects of that commonwealth has no power over him. To an Indian, those who have the supreme power of making laws in England, France or Holland are, like the rest of the world, only men without authority. So if every man does not have a power, by the law of nature, to punish offences against it as he soberly judges the case requires, I do not see how the magistrates of any community can punish a foreigner from another country, since in relation to him they can have no more power than every man naturally may have over another.

Besides the crime, which consists in violating the law and departing from the right rule of reason — by which a man so far becomes degenerate, and declares that he is abandoning the principles of human nature and is a harmful creature — there is commonly an injury done to some person or other, and some other man suffers damage by his offence. In that case the one who has suffered the damage has, in addition to the right of punishment he shares with other men, a particular right to seek reparation from the one who caused it. And any other person who thinks it just may also join the injured party and help him recover from the offender as much as will make good the harm he has suffered.

From these two distinct rights — the right to punish the crime for the sake of restraint and to prevent similar offences, which belongs to everyone, and the right to take reparation, which belongs only to the injured party — it follows that the magistrate, who by being magistrate has the common right of punishing placed in his hands, can often, by his own authority, remit the punishment of criminal offences where the public good does not require the law to be executed. But he cannot remit the satisfaction owed to any private man for the damage he has received. The person who suffered the damage has a right to demand that in his own name, and only he can remit it. The injured person has this power of taking for himself the goods or service of the offender by the right of self-preservation, just as every man has a power to punish the crime to prevent its being committed again, by the right he has to preserve all mankind and to do everything reasonable he can toward that end. This is why every man in the state of nature has a power to kill a murderer. He does it both to deter others from the same injury, which no reparation can make good, by the example of the punishment that everyone inflicts for it, and also to protect men from the attempts of a criminal who has renounced reason, the common rule and measure God has given to mankind. By the unjust violence and slaughter he has committed on one man, such a criminal has declared war against all mankind, and therefore he may be destroyed like a lion or a tiger, one of those wild, savage beasts with which men can have neither society nor security. And on this is grounded that great law of nature, “Whoso sheddeth man’s blood, by man shall his blood be shed.” And Cain was so fully convinced that everyone had a right to destroy such a criminal that, after murdering his brother, he cried out, “Every one that findeth me, shall slay me” — so plainly was it written in the hearts of all mankind.

For the same reason a man in the state of nature may punish the lesser breaches of that law. Someone may ask: with death? I answer that each offence may be punished to the degree, and with as much severity, as will be enough to make it a bad bargain for the offender, give him cause to repent, and frighten others away from doing the same. Every offence that can be committed in the state of nature may also be punished in the state of nature, equally, and as far as it may be in a commonwealth. It would be beside my present purpose to go here into the details of the law of nature, or of its scale of punishments. Yet it is certain that there is such a law, and that it is as intelligible and plain to a rational creature who studies it as the positive laws of commonwealths are — perhaps even plainer, by as much as reason is easier to understand than the fancies and intricate schemes of men, who put contrary and hidden interests into words. For that is truly what a great part of the municipal laws of countries are. They are right only so far as they are founded on the law of nature, by which they are to be regulated and interpreted.

Against this strange doctrine — namely, that in the state of nature everyone has the executive power of the law of nature — I have no doubt it will be objected that it is unreasonable for men to be judges in their own cases; that self-love will make men partial to themselves and their friends; and that, on the other side, ill nature, passion and revenge will carry them too far in punishing others. From this, the objection says, nothing but confusion and disorder will follow, and so God has certainly appointed government to restrain men’s partiality and violence. I readily grant that civil government is the proper remedy for the inconveniences of the state of nature, which must certainly be great where men may be judges in their own case. It is easy to imagine that a man unjust enough to do his brother an injury will hardly be just enough to condemn himself for it. But I would ask those who make this objection to remember that absolute monarchs are only men. If government is to be the remedy for the evils that necessarily follow from men being judges in their own cases, and if the state of nature is therefore not to be endured, I would like to know what kind of government that is, and how much better it is than the state of nature, where one man commanding a multitude has the liberty to be judge in his own case and may do whatever he pleases to all his subjects, without anyone having the slightest liberty to question or check those who carry out his will? And where whatever he does, whether he is led by reason, mistake or passion, must be submitted to? Things are much better in the state of nature, where men are not bound to submit to the unjust will of another. And if the one who judges judges wrongly, in his own case or any other, he is answerable for it to the rest of mankind.

It is often asked, as if it were a powerful objection: where are there, or where were there ever, any men in such a state of nature? For now it may be enough to answer that, since all princes and rulers of independent governments throughout the world are in a state of nature, it is plain that the world never was, and never will be, without numbers of men in that state. I have named all governors of independent communities, whether or not they are in league with others. For it is not every compact that ends the state of nature between men, but only this one: agreeing together mutually to enter into one community and make one body politic. Men may make other promises and compacts with one another and still be in the state of nature. The promises and bargains for trade and the like between the two men on the desert island mentioned by Garcilasso de la Vega in his history of Peru, or between a Swiss and an Indian in the woods of America, are binding on them, even though they are completely in a state of nature in relation to one another. For truthfulness and keeping faith belong to men as men, and not as members of society.

To those who say that there were never any men in the state of nature, I will not only set against them the authority of the judicious Hooker (Ecclesiastical Polity, book I, section 10), where he says:

“The laws we have mentioned so far — that is, the laws of nature — bind men absolutely, simply as men, even though they have never had any settled fellowship, and never any solemn agreement among themselves about what to do or not to do. But since we are not able by ourselves to provide an adequate supply of the things needed for the kind of life our nature desires, a life fit for the dignity of man, we are naturally led to seek communion and fellowship with others, in order to make up for the defects and imperfections that are in us when we live alone and entirely by ourselves. This was the cause of men first uniting themselves in political societies.”

But I further affirm that all men are naturally in that state, and remain in it until, by their own consent, they make themselves members of some political society. And I have no doubt that in the rest of this discourse I shall make this very clear.

chapters.title: Chapter 3 — Of the State of War
paragraphs: THE state of war is a state of enmity and destruction. So if a man declares, by word or action, a settled and calm design on another man’s life — not a passionate and hasty one — he puts himself in a state of war with the man against whom he has declared that intention. He has thereby exposed his own life to the other’s power, to be taken away by him, or by anyone who joins him in his defence and takes up his quarrel. For it is reasonable and just that I should have a right to destroy what threatens me with destruction. By the fundamental law of nature, man is to be preserved as far as possible, and when not all can be preserved, the safety of the innocent is to be preferred. So a man may destroy someone who makes war on him, or who has revealed hostility to his very existence, for the same reason that he may kill a wolf or a lion. Such men are not bound by the ties of the common law of reason; they have no other rule than force and violence, and so they may be treated as beasts of prey — those dangerous and harmful creatures that will certainly destroy him whenever he falls into their power.

This is why anyone who tries to get another man into his absolute power thereby puts himself into a state of war with him; for that must be understood as declaring a design on his life. I have reason to conclude that someone who wants to get me into his power without my consent would treat me as he pleased once he had me there, and would destroy me too if he took a fancy to. For nobody can want to have me in his absolute power except to force me into something against my right to freedom — that is, to make me a slave. Being free from such force is the only security for my preservation, and reason tells me to regard as an enemy to my preservation anyone who would take away the freedom that protects it. So whoever attempts to enslave me thereby puts himself into a state of war with me. Anyone who, in the state of nature, would take away the freedom that belongs to someone in that state must necessarily be supposed to intend to take away everything else, since freedom is the foundation of all the rest. In the same way, anyone who, in the state of society, would take away the freedom belonging to the members of that society or commonwealth must be supposed to intend to take everything else from them too, and so must be regarded as being in a state of war.

This makes it lawful for a man to kill a thief who has not hurt him in the least, and has not declared any design on his life beyond using force to get him into his power so as to take his money, or whatever else he likes, from him. When someone uses force, where he has no right, to get me into his power, whatever his pretext may be, I have no reason to suppose that a man who would take away my liberty would not take away everything else once he had me in his power. It is therefore lawful for me to treat him as someone who has put himself into a state of war with me — that is, to kill him if I can. For whoever brings about a state of war and is the aggressor in it justly exposes himself to that risk.

And here we have the plain difference between the state of nature and the state of war. Some men have confused them, but they are as far apart as a state of peace, good will, mutual help and preservation is from a state of enmity, malice, violence and mutual destruction. Men living together according to reason, without a common superior on earth with authority to judge between them, is properly the state of nature. But force, or a declared design of force, against the person of another, where there is no common superior on earth to appeal to for relief, is the state of war. And it is the lack of such an appeal that gives a man the right of war even against an aggressor, though that aggressor is in society and a fellow subject. So a thief who has stolen everything I own I may not harm except by appealing to the law; yet I may kill him when he attacks me to rob me of no more than my horse or my coat. The reason is that the law, which was made for my preservation, permits me to defend myself, and gives me the right of war — a liberty to kill the aggressor — wherever it cannot step in to protect my life from immediate force; for a life, once lost, can never be repaired. The law allows this because the aggressor leaves no time to appeal to our common judge, or for the law to decide, in a case where the harm may be irreparable. The lack of a common judge with authority puts all men in a state of nature; force without right against a man’s person creates a state of war, both where there is a common judge and where there is not.

But once the actual force is over, the state of war ends between those who live in society and are equally subject, on both sides, to the fair judgment of the law. For then the remedy of appeal is open, both for the past injury and to prevent future harm. But where there is no such appeal — as in the state of nature, where there are no positive laws and no judges with authority to appeal to — the state of war, once begun, continues. The innocent party has a right to destroy the other whenever he can, until the aggressor offers peace and seeks reconciliation on terms that may repair whatever wrongs he has already done and secure the innocent for the future. Indeed, even where an appeal to the law and to established judges is open, if the remedy is refused by an obvious perversion of justice, and the laws are shamelessly twisted to protect the violence or injuries of some men, or some party of men, or to shield them from penalty, it is hard to see this as anything but a state of war. For wherever violence is used and injury done, it is still violence and injury, even if it is done by the hands appointed to administer justice, and however much it is dressed up with the name, pretexts or forms of law. The purpose of law is to protect and redress the innocent by applying it impartially to everyone under it. Wherever that is not done in good faith, war is made on those who suffer; and since they have no appeal on earth to set things right, they are left with the only remedy in such cases: an appeal to heaven.

Avoiding this state of war — in which there is no appeal but to heaven, and into which even the smallest disagreement tends to lead where there is no authority to decide between the parties — is one great reason why men put themselves into society and leave the state of nature. For where there is an authority, a power on earth from which relief can be had by appeal, the state of war cannot continue, and the dispute is decided by that power. If there had been any such court, any higher jurisdiction on earth, to decide the right between Jephthah and the Ammonites, they would never have come to a state of war. But we see that he was forced to appeal to heaven: “The Lord the Judge,” he says, “be judge this day between the children of Israel and the children of Ammon” (Judg. xi. 27). Then, pursuing and relying on his appeal, he leads his army out to battle. So in such disputes, when the question is asked, who shall be judge? it cannot mean who shall decide the dispute. Everyone knows what Jephthah tells us here: that the Lord the Judge shall judge. Where there is no judge on earth, the appeal lies to God in heaven. So the question cannot mean: who shall judge whether another has put himself in a state of war with me, and whether I may, as Jephthah did, appeal to heaven about it? Of that I alone can be judge, in my own conscience, as I will answer for it on the great day to the supreme judge of all men.

chapters.title: Chapter 4 — Of Slavery
paragraphs: THE natural liberty of man is to be free from any superior power on earth, and not to be under the will or legislative authority of any man, but to have only the law of nature as his rule. The liberty of man in society is to be under no legislative power except the one established by consent in the commonwealth, and under the dominion of no will and the restraint of no law except what that legislative enacts in accordance with the trust placed in it. Freedom, then, is not what Sir Robert Filmer tells us it is (Observations, A. 55): “a liberty for every one to do what he likes, to live as he pleases, and not to be tied by any laws.” The freedom of men under government is to have a fixed rule to live by, common to everyone in that society and made by the legislative power set up in it. It is a liberty to follow my own will in everything where that rule is silent, and not to be subject to the changeable, uncertain, unknown, arbitrary will of another man. In the same way, freedom of nature is to be under no restraint other than the law of nature.

This freedom from absolute, arbitrary power is so necessary to a man’s preservation, and so closely bound up with it, that he cannot give it up except by something that forfeits his preservation and his life together. For since a man does not have power over his own life, he cannot, by compact or by his own consent, make himself anyone’s slave, or put himself under another’s absolute, arbitrary power to take his life whenever that other pleases. Nobody can give more power than he has himself, and a man who cannot take his own life cannot give anyone else power over it. It is true that if a man has, through his own fault, forfeited his life by some act that deserves death, the person to whom he has forfeited it may, once he has him in his power, put off taking it and make use of him for his own service; and this does him no injury. For whenever the slave finds that the hardship of his slavery outweighs the value of his life, it is in his power to bring on himself the death he wants by resisting his master’s will.

This is the complete condition of slavery, which is nothing other than the state of war continued between a lawful conqueror and a captive. For if they once enter into a compact, agreeing on limited power on one side and obedience on the other, the state of war and slavery ends for as long as the compact lasts. As has already been said, no man can by agreement hand over to another what he does not have himself: a power over his own life.

I admit that we find, among the Jews as well as other nations, that men did sell themselves. But plainly this was only into hard service, not into slavery. It is clear that the person sold was not under an absolute, arbitrary, despotic power, because the master could not have had the power to kill, at any time, a man whom he was obliged to release from his service at a fixed time. The master of such a servant was so far from having arbitrary power over his life that he could not even maim him at will: the loss of an eye or a tooth set the servant free (Exod. xxi.).

chapters.title: Chapter 5 — Of Property
paragraphs: We may consider natural reason, which tells us that men, once born, have a right to their preservation, and so to food and drink and whatever else nature provides for their subsistence. Or we may consider revelation, which gives us an account of the grants God made of the world to Adam, and to Noah and his sons. Either way it is very clear that God, as King David says (Psal. cxv. 16), “has given the earth to the children of men” — given it to mankind in common. But once this is assumed, some people find it very hard to see how anyone could ever come to have a property in anything. I will not be content with answering that, if it is hard to explain property on the assumption that God gave the world to Adam and his descendants in common, it is impossible for any man except one universal monarch to have any property on the assumption that God gave the world to Adam and his heirs in succession, to the exclusion of all the rest of his descendants. Instead I shall try to show how men might come to have a property in separate parts of what God gave to mankind in common, and that without any express agreement of all the commoners.

God, who has given the world to men in common, has also given them reason to make use of it to the best advantage of life and convenience. The earth and everything in it is given to men for the support and comfort of their existence. All the fruits it naturally produces, and the beasts it feeds, belong to mankind in common, since they are produced by the spontaneous hand of nature; and no one originally has a private dominion over any of them, excluding the rest of mankind, while they remain in this natural state. Yet since they are given for men to use, there must necessarily be some means of appropriating them in one way or another before they can be of any use, or any benefit at all, to a particular man. The fruit or venison that feeds the wild Indian, who knows no enclosure and is still a tenant in common, must be his — and so much his, that is, so much a part of him, that no one else can any longer have any right to it — before it can do him any good in sustaining his life.

Though the earth and all lower creatures are common to all men, every man has a property in his own person. Nobody has any right to this but himself. The labour of his body and the work of his hands, we may say, are properly his. So whatever he removes from the state that nature has provided and left it in, he has mixed his labour with, and joined to it something that is his own, and in this way he makes it his property. Since he has removed it from the common state nature placed it in, his labour has attached something to it that excludes the common right of other men. For this labour is unquestionably the labourer’s property, so no one but he can have a right to what it has once been joined to — at least where there is enough, and as good, left in common for others.

A man who lives on the acorns he picked up under an oak, or the apples he gathered from the trees in the wood, has certainly appropriated them to himself. Nobody can deny that the nourishment is his. So I ask: when did they begin to be his? When he digested them? When he ate them? When he boiled them? When he brought them home? Or when he picked them up? It is plain that if the first gathering did not make them his, nothing else could. That labour marked them off from what was common. It added something to them beyond what nature, the common mother of all, had done, and so they became his private right. Will anyone say he had no right to the acorns or apples he appropriated in this way because he did not have the consent of all mankind to make them his? Was it robbery to take for himself what belonged to everyone in common? If consent like that were necessary, man would have starved, despite all the plenty God had given him. We see in commons that remain common by agreement that it is the taking of any part of what is common, and removing it from the state nature leaves it in, that begins property; without that, the common is of no use. And taking this part or that does not depend on the express consent of all the commoners. So the grass my horse has eaten, the turf my servant has cut, and the ore I have dug in any place where I have a right to them in common with others become my property, without anyone else assigning them to me or consenting to it. The labour that was mine, in removing them from the common state they were in, has fixed my property in them.

If the explicit consent of every commoner were required before anyone could appropriate any part of what is given in common, children or servants could not cut up the meat their father or master had provided for them in common without first assigning each person his own portion. The water running in the fountain is everyone’s, yet who can doubt that the water in the pitcher belongs only to the man who drew it out? His labour has taken it out of the hands of nature, where it was common and belonged equally to all her children, and in doing so has appropriated it to him.

So this law of reason makes the deer belong to the Indian who has killed it. It is accepted as the goods of the man who has spent his labour on it, even though before it was everyone’s common right. And among those counted the civilized part of mankind, who have made and multiplied positive laws to determine property, this original law of nature for the beginning of property in what was previously common still applies. By virtue of it, any fish a man catches in the ocean — that great common of mankind which still remains — or any ambergris he picks up here, becomes the property of the one who took the trouble over it, through the labour that removes it from the common state nature left it in. Even among us, the hare that someone is hunting is considered to belong to the man who pursues her during the chase. For since she is an animal still regarded as common, and no man’s private possession, whoever has spent enough labour on any animal of that kind to find and pursue her has thereby removed her from the state of nature, in which she was common, and has begun a property.

It may perhaps be objected that if gathering acorns or other fruits of the earth gives a right to them, then anyone may hoard up as much as he likes. I answer: not so. The same law of nature that gives us property in this way also sets limits to that property. “God has given us all things richly” (1 Tim. vi. 12) is the voice of reason confirmed by inspiration. But how far has he given them to us? To enjoy. As much as anyone can make use of to any advantage of life before it spoils, so much he may fix a property in by his labour. Whatever goes beyond this is more than his share and belongs to others. Nothing was made by God for man to spoil or destroy. So, considering how plentiful natural provisions were for a long time in the world, how few people there were to consume them, and how small a part of that provision one man’s industry could reach and hoard up to the harm of others — especially if he kept within the limits reason sets on what might serve his use — there could then be little room for quarrels or disputes about property established in this way.

But the chief matter of property now is not the fruits of the earth and the beasts that live on it, but the earth itself, since that takes in and carries with it all the rest. I think it is plain that property in land, too, is acquired in the same way as the former. As much land as a man tills, plants, improves and cultivates, and can use the produce of, is his property. By his labour he, as it were, encloses it from the common. Nor will it undermine his right to say that everyone else has an equal title to it, so that he cannot appropriate or enclose it without the consent of all his fellow commoners, that is, all mankind. When God gave the world in common to all mankind, he also commanded man to labour, and the poverty of man’s condition required it of him. God and his reason commanded him to subdue the earth — that is, to improve it for the benefit of life — and in doing so to invest in it something that was his own: his labour. Whoever, in obedience to this command of God, subdued, tilled and sowed any part of it thereby attached to it something that was his property, to which no one else had any title, and which no one could take from him without injury.

Nor did this appropriation of any plot of land by improving it harm any other man, since there was still enough, and as good, left — more than those not yet provided for could use. In effect, then, there was never any less left for others because he had enclosed some for himself. For a man who leaves as much as another can make use of does as well as if he took nothing at all. Nobody could think himself injured by another man’s drinking, even if he took a long drink, when he himself had a whole river of the same water left to quench his thirst. And the case of land and water, where there is enough of both, is exactly the same.

God gave the world to men in common. But since he gave it to them for their benefit, and for the greatest conveniences of life they could draw from it, we cannot suppose he meant it always to stay common and uncultivated. He gave it for the use of the industrious and rational (and labour was to be their title to it), not to the whims or greed of the quarrelsome and contentious. A man who had as good land left for him to improve as what was already taken had no need to complain, and ought not to interfere with what had already been improved by another’s labour. If he did, it is plain that what he wanted was the benefit of another’s efforts, to which he had no right, and not the ground God had given him in common with others to work on — ground of which there was as good left as what was already occupied, and more than he knew what to do with, or than his industry could reach.

It is true that in land that is common in England, or in any other country where there are plenty of people living under government who have money and commerce, no one can enclose or appropriate any part without the consent of all his fellow commoners. That is because it is left common by compact, that is, by the law of the land, which must not be violated. And though such land is common with respect to some men, it is not common to all mankind; it is the joint property of this country, or this parish. Besides, what remained after such an enclosure would not be as good for the rest of the commoners as the whole was when they could all use the whole. But in the beginning, when the great common of the world was first being peopled, it was quite otherwise. The law man lived under then was rather in favour of appropriating. God commanded him to labour, and his needs forced him to. Wherever he had fixed his labour, that was his property, which could not be taken from him. And so we see that subduing or cultivating the earth and having dominion over it are joined together; the one gave title to the other. So God, by commanding man to subdue the earth, gave him authority to appropriate to that extent. And the condition of human life, which requires labour and materials to work on, necessarily brings in private possessions.

Nature has set the measure of property well, by the extent of men’s labour and the conveniences of life. No man’s labour could subdue or appropriate everything, and no man’s enjoyment could consume more than a small part. So it was impossible for any man in this way to encroach on another’s right, or to acquire a property to the harm of his neighbour, who would still have room for as good and as large a possession (after the other had taken his) as there was before the appropriation. In the first ages of the world, this measure kept every man’s possession to a very modest size — such as he could appropriate without injuring anybody — for then men were more in danger of getting lost by wandering away from their company in what was then the vast wilderness of the earth than of being short of room to plant. And the same measure may still be allowed without harm to anyone, full as the world seems. For suppose a man, or a family, in the condition men were in when the world was first peopled by the children of Adam or Noah, and let him plant in some vacant inland part of America. We shall find that the possessions he could make for himself, by the measures we have given, would not be very large, and even today would not harm the rest of mankind, or give them reason to complain or think themselves injured by this man’s encroachment — even though the human race has now spread to every corner of the world and vastly exceeds the small number there was at the beginning. Indeed, land in itself is worth so little without labour that I have heard it claimed that even in Spain a man may be allowed to plough, sow and reap without being disturbed on land he has no other title to than the fact that he is using it. On the contrary, the inhabitants think themselves indebted to a man who, by his industry on neglected and therefore waste land, has increased the stock of corn they lacked. But however that may be — I lay no weight on it — this I dare boldly affirm: the same rule of property, namely that every man should have as much as he could make use of, would still hold in the world without leaving anyone short, since there is land enough in the world for twice the number of its inhabitants, if the invention of money, and men’s tacit agreement to put a value on it, had not introduced (by consent) larger possessions and a right to them. How it has done this I shall shortly show at greater length.

This much is certain. In the beginning, before the desire to have more than man needed had altered the intrinsic value of things, which depends only on their usefulness to human life, or before men had agreed that a little piece of yellow metal, which would keep without wasting or decaying, should be worth a large piece of meat or a whole heap of corn, men did have a right to appropriate by their labour, each for himself, as much of the things of nature as he could use. Yet this could not be much, nor could it harm others, where the same plenty was still left to those who would put in the same industry. Let me add that a man who appropriates land to himself by his labour does not reduce the common stock of mankind but increases it. For the provisions that support human life produced by one acre of enclosed and cultivated land are (to put it very conservatively) ten times more than those yielded by an acre of equally rich land lying waste in common. So a man who encloses land, and gets a greater plenty of the conveniences of life from ten acres than he could have from a hundred left to nature, may truly be said to give ninety acres to mankind. For his labour now supplies him from ten acres with provisions that used to be the produce of a hundred lying in common. I have rated the improved land very low here, making its yield only ten to one, when it is much nearer a hundred to one. For I ask whether, in the wild woods and uncultivated waste of America, left to nature without any improvement, tillage or husbandry, a thousand acres yield their needy and wretched inhabitants as many conveniences of life as ten acres of equally fertile land do in Devonshire, where they are well cultivated?

Before land was appropriated, whoever gathered as much wild fruit, or killed, caught or tamed as many beasts, as he could — whoever spent his efforts on any of the spontaneous products of nature in such a way as to alter them from the state nature had put them in, by applying some of his labour to them — thereby acquired a property in them. But if they perished in his possession without being properly used — if the fruit rotted or the venison went bad before he could consume it — he offended against the common law of nature and was liable to be punished. He had invaded his neighbour’s share, because he had no right to any of them beyond what his use required and what might serve to provide him with the conveniences of life.

The same measures governed the possession of land as well. Whatever he tilled and harvested, stored and used before it spoiled, was his own particular right. Whatever land he enclosed, and could graze and make use of, the cattle and the produce were also his. But if the grass in his enclosure rotted on the ground, or the fruit of his planting perished without being gathered and stored, this part of the earth, despite his enclosure, was still to be regarded as waste, and might become the possession of anyone else. So at the beginning Cain might take as much ground as he could till and make it his own land, and still leave enough for Abel’s sheep to graze on; a few acres would serve for both their possessions. But as families grew, and industry increased their stocks, their possessions grew with their need of them. Even so, this was usually without any fixed property in the ground they used, until they formed communities, settled together and built cities. Then, by consent, they came in time to mark out the bounds of their separate territories, agree on boundaries between themselves and their neighbours, and settle by their own laws the properties of the members of the same society. For we see that in the part of the world first inhabited, and therefore likely to be the most populous, even as late as Abraham’s time people wandered freely up and down with their flocks and herds, which were their wealth; and Abraham did this in a country where he was a stranger. From this it is plain that at least a large part of the land lay in common, and that the inhabitants did not value it or claim property in any more than they used. But when there was not enough room in the same place for their herds to graze together, they separated by consent, as Abraham and Lot did (Gen. xiii. 5), and extended their pasture wherever it suited them best. And for the same reason Esau left his father and his brother and settled in Mount Seir (Gen. xxxvi. 6).

And so, without supposing that Adam had any private dominion and property over the whole world, excluding all other men — which cannot be proved in any way, nor can anyone’s property be derived from it — but supposing that the world was given, as it was, to the children of men in common, we see how labour could give men distinct titles to separate plots of it for their private uses. In this there could be no doubt about right, and no room for quarrels.

Nor is it as strange as it may perhaps seem before we think about it that the property of labour should be able to outweigh the community of land. For it is labour, indeed, that makes the difference in value in everything. Let anyone consider the difference between an acre of land planted with tobacco or sugar, or sown with wheat or barley, and an acre of the same land lying in common without any cultivation on it, and he will find that the improvement made by labour accounts for by far the greater part of the value. I think it would be a very modest estimate to say that, of the products of the earth useful to human life, nine tenths are the effects of labour. Indeed, if we value things correctly as they come to our use, and add up the various costs spent on them — what in them is purely owing to nature and what to labour — we shall find that in most of them ninety-nine hundredths must be wholly put down to labour.

There could be no clearer proof of this than various nations of the Americans. They are rich in land and poor in all the comforts of life. Nature has supplied them as generously as any other people with the materials of plenty — that is, a fruitful soil, able to produce in abundance whatever might serve for food, clothing and pleasure. Yet because they do not improve it by labour, they do not have a hundredth part of the conveniences we enjoy; and the king of a large and fruitful territory there is fed, housed and clothed worse than a day labourer in England.

To make this a little clearer, let us just trace some of the ordinary provisions of life through their various stages before they come to our use, and see how much of their value they receive from human industry. Bread, wine and cloth are things in daily use and great plenty. Yet if labour did not supply us with these more useful commodities, acorns, water and leaves or skins would have to be our bread, drink and clothing. For whatever bread is worth more than acorns, wine more than water, and cloth or silk more than leaves, skins or moss, is owed entirely to labour and industry. The one set is the food and clothing that unaided nature provides for us; the other is the provisions that our industry and effort prepare for us. When anyone has calculated how much the latter exceed the former in value, he will see how much labour makes up by far the greatest part of the value of the things we enjoy in this world. The ground that produces the materials is hardly to be counted in at all, or at most only as a very small part — so small that even among us, land left wholly to nature, with no improvement by pasture, tillage or planting, is called waste, as indeed it is; and we shall find its benefit amounts to little more than nothing.

This shows how much a large population is to be preferred to large territories, and that the increase of lands and the right use of them is the great art of government. And a prince who is so wise and godlike as to secure, by established laws of liberty, protection and encouragement for the honest industry of mankind against the oppression of power and the narrowness of party will soon be too strong for his neighbours. But this is by the way.
To return to the argument at hand.

An acre of land here that bears twenty bushels of wheat, and another in America that would do the same with the same husbandry, undoubtedly have the same natural, intrinsic value. Yet the benefit mankind receives from the one in a year is worth £5, and from the other possibly not worth a penny, if all the profit an Indian got from it were valued and sold here; at least, I can truly say, not a thousandth part as much. It is labour, then, that puts the greatest part of the value on land, without which it would hardly be worth anything. It is to labour that we owe the greatest part of all its useful products. For everything by which the straw, bran and bread from that acre of wheat are worth more than the produce of an acre of equally good land lying waste is entirely the effect of labour. It is not merely the ploughman’s effort, the reaper’s and thresher’s toil and the baker’s sweat that must be counted into the bread we eat. The labour of those who broke in the oxen, who dug and worked the iron and stones, who felled and shaped the timber used for the plough, the mill, the oven or any of the other tools — and they are a vast number — needed for this corn, from its being seed to be sown to its being made into bread, must all be charged to the account of labour and recognized as its effect. Nature and the earth supplied only the materials, which in themselves are almost worthless. If we could trace them, it would be a strange list of the things that industry provided and used for every loaf of bread before it came to our use: iron, wood, leather, bark, timber, stone, bricks, coal, lime, cloth, dyes, pitch, tar, masts, ropes, and all the materials used in the ship that brought any of the commodities used by any of the workmen in any part of the work. It would be almost impossible, or at least too long, to list them all.

From all this it is evident that, although the things of nature are given in common, man, by being master of himself and owner of his own person and of its actions or labour, still had within himself the great foundation of property. And what made up the greater part of what he used for the support or comfort of his existence, once invention and the arts had improved the conveniences of life, was entirely his own and did not belong in common to others.

So in the beginning labour gave a right of property wherever anyone chose to apply it to what was common; and what was common remained for a long time by far the greater part, and is still more than mankind makes use of. At first men were for the most part content with what unaided nature offered for their needs. Later, in some parts of the world, where the growth of population and stock, together with the use of money, had made land scarce and so of some value, the various communities settled the bounds of their separate territories, and by their own laws regulated the properties of the private men of their society; and so, by compact and agreement, they settled the property that labour and industry had begun. And the leagues made between various states and kingdoms, expressly or tacitly disowning all claim and right to the land in the other’s possession, have by common consent given up their claims to the natural common right they originally had to those countries, and so have settled by positive agreement a property among themselves in distinct parts and parcels of the earth. Yet even so, there are still great tracts of land to be found which lie waste (their inhabitants not having joined the rest of mankind in consenting to the use of their common money). These lands are more than the people who live on them do or can make use of, and so they still lie in common — though this can hardly happen among the part of mankind that has consented to the use of money.

Most of the things really useful to human life — the things the need to survive made the first commoners of the world look for, as it does the Americans now — are generally things that do not last long; if they are not used up, they decay and perish of themselves. Gold, silver and diamonds are things whose value comes from fancy or agreement rather than from real use and the necessary support of life. Now, of the good things nature has provided in common, everyone had a right (as has been said) to as much as he could use, and a property in everything he could bring about with his labour: everything his industry could reach, to alter it from the state nature had put it in, was his. A man who gathered a hundred bushels of acorns or apples thereby had a property in them; they were his goods as soon as they were gathered. He had only to make sure that he used them before they spoiled; otherwise he took more than his share and robbed others. And indeed it was foolish, as well as dishonest, to hoard more than he could use. If he gave part of them away to someone else, so that they did not perish uselessly in his possession, this too was making use of them. And if he traded plums that would have rotted in a week for nuts that would stay good to eat for a whole year, he did no injury. He did not waste the common stock, or destroy any part of the share of goods that belonged to others, as long as nothing perished uselessly in his hands. Again, if he chose to give his nuts for a piece of metal because he liked its colour, or to exchange his sheep for shells, or his wool for a sparkling pebble or a diamond, and to keep these by him all his life, he did not invade the right of others. He might pile up as much of these durable things as he pleased, since going beyond the bounds of his just property lay not in the size of his possessions but in letting anything perish uselessly in them.

And this is how money came into use: some durable thing that men could keep without its spoiling, and that by mutual consent they would accept in exchange for the truly useful but perishable necessities of life.

And just as different degrees of industry tended to give men possessions in different proportions, so this invention of money gave them the opportunity to keep and enlarge them. For suppose there were an island, cut off from all possible trade with the rest of the world, with only a hundred families on it. Suppose it had sheep, horses and cows, and other useful animals, wholesome fruits, and enough land for corn for a hundred thousand times as many people, but nothing on the island fit to serve as money, because everything there was either too common or too perishable. What reason could anyone there have to enlarge his possessions beyond what his family could use, and a plentiful supply for its consumption — whether from what their own industry produced, or from what they could get by bartering with others for similarly perishable, useful goods? Where there is not something that is both lasting and scarce, and so valuable enough to be hoarded, men will not tend to enlarge their holdings of land, however rich it may be and however free they are to take it. For I ask: what value would a man put on ten thousand, or a hundred thousand, acres of excellent land, already cultivated and well stocked with cattle, in the middle of the inland parts of America, where he had no hope of trade with other parts of the world to bring him money by selling the produce? It would not be worth enclosing, and we would see him give back to the wild common of nature whatever was more than would supply him and his family with the conveniences of life available there.

So in the beginning all the world was America, and more so than America is now, for no such thing as money was known anywhere. Find something that has the use and value of money among his neighbours, and you will see the same man at once begin to enlarge his possessions.

But gold and silver are of little use to human life compared with food, clothing and transport, and get their value only from men’s consent, though labour still largely sets the measure of it. So it is plain that men have agreed to an unequal and disproportionate possession of the earth. By a tacit and voluntary consent they have found a way in which a man may fairly possess more land than he himself can use the produce of: he receives gold and silver in exchange for the surplus, and these can be hoarded without injury to anyone, since these metals do not spoil or decay in the hands of the person who has them. Men have made this division of things into unequal private possessions workable outside the bounds of society, and without compact, simply by putting a value on gold and silver and tacitly agreeing to use money. For under governments, the laws regulate the right of property, and the possession of land is determined by positive constitutions.

And so, I think, it is very easy to see, without any difficulty, how labour could at first begin a title of property in the common things of nature, and how spending it on our uses set limits to that title. So there could then be no reason to quarrel over title, nor any doubt about how large a possession it gave. Right and convenience went together. For as a man had a right to everything he could apply his labour to, so he had no temptation to labour for more than he could make use of. This left no room for disputes about title, nor for encroaching on the rights of others. The portion a man cut out for himself was easy to see, and it was pointless, as well as dishonest, to cut out too much for himself, or take more than he needed.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 — Of Paternal Power
paragraphs: It may perhaps be criticized as an irrelevant quibble, in a discourse of this kind, to find fault with words and names that have become established in the world. And yet it may not be a bad idea to offer new ones when the old ones tend to lead men into mistakes, as this term “paternal power” has probably done. It seems to place the power of parents over their children wholly in the father, as if the mother had no share in it; whereas, if we consult reason or revelation, we shall find that she has an equal title. This may give one reason to ask whether it would not be more properly called “parental power.” For whatever obligation nature and the right of generation lays on children, it must certainly bind them equally to both of the joint causes of it. And accordingly we see that the positive law of God everywhere joins them together, without distinction, when it commands the obedience of children: “Honour thy father and thy mother,” Exod. xx. 12; “Whosoever curseth his father or his mother,” Lev. xx. 9; “Ye shall fear every man his mother and his father,” Lev. xix. 3; “Children, obey your parents,” etc., Eph. vi. 1. That is the language of both the Old and the New Testament.

If this one thing alone had been well considered, without looking any deeper into the matter, it might perhaps have kept men from running into the gross mistakes they have made about this power of parents. Under the title of “paternal power” it seemed to belong to the father alone, and so it could bear the name of absolute dominion and regal authority without sounding very harsh. But it would have sounded strange, and the very name would have shown the absurdity, if this supposed absolute power over children had been called “parental,” because that name would have revealed that it belonged to the mother too. For it hardly serves the purpose of those men who argue so hard for the absolute power and authority of “the fatherhood,” as they call it, that the mother should have any share in it. And it would have given poor support to the monarchy they argue for, if the very name had shown that the fundamental authority from which they want to derive the government of a single person alone was placed not in one person but in two jointly. But let this matter of names pass.

Although I said above, in Chapter II, “That all men by nature are equal,” I cannot be supposed to mean every sort of equality. Age or virtue may give men a just precedence. Excellence of abilities and merit may place others above the common level. Birth may oblige some, and alliance or benefits others, to show respect to those to whom nature, gratitude or other considerations may have made it due. And yet all this is consistent with the equality that all men share with respect to jurisdiction or dominion over one another. That was the equality I spoke of there, as the one relevant to the business at hand: the equal right that every man has to his natural freedom, without being subjected to the will or authority of any other man.

Children, I admit, are not born in this full state of equality, though they are born to it. Their parents have a sort of rule and jurisdiction over them when they come into the world, and for some time afterwards; but it is only a temporary one. The bonds of this subjection are like the swaddling clothes they are wrapped in and supported by in the weakness of their infancy. Age and reason loosen them as the children grow up, until at last they drop off entirely and leave a man at his own free disposal.

Adam was created a perfect man, his body and mind in full possession of their strength and reason. So he was able, from the first instant of his existence, to provide for his own support and preservation, and to govern his actions according to the dictates of the law of reason that God had implanted in him. From him the world has been peopled with his descendants, who are all born infants, weak and helpless, without knowledge or understanding. But to make up for the defects of this imperfect state until growth and age have removed them, Adam and Eve, and all parents after them, were under an obligation by the law of nature to preserve, nourish and educate the children they had begotten — not as their own workmanship, but as the workmanship of their own maker, the Almighty, to whom they were to be accountable for them.

The law that was to govern Adam was the same law that was to govern all his posterity: the law of reason. But his offspring came into the world by a different way from him — by a natural birth, which produced them ignorant and without the use of reason — and so they were not immediately under that law. For nobody can be under a law that has not been promulgated to him; and since this law is promulgated, or made known, by reason alone, someone who has not come to the use of his reason cannot be said to be under it. Adam’s children, then, were not under this law of reason as soon as they were born, and so they were not immediately free. For law, properly understood, is not so much the limitation as the direction of a free and intelligent agent to his proper interest, and it prescribes no further than is for the general good of those under that law. If they could be happier without it, the law would vanish of itself as a useless thing; and something that fences us in only from bogs and cliffs hardly deserves the name of confinement. So, however it may be misunderstood, the end of law is not to abolish or restrain freedom but to preserve and enlarge it. For in all the states of created beings capable of laws, where there is no law there is no freedom. Liberty means being free from restraint and violence from others, and that cannot be where there is no law. But freedom is not, as we are told, a liberty for every man to do whatever he likes (for who could be free when every other man’s whims might domineer over him?). It is a liberty to dispose of and order as he likes his person, actions, possessions and his whole property, within what is allowed by the laws he is under, and in all this not to be subject to the arbitrary will of another, but freely to follow his own.

The power that parents have over their children, then, arises from the duty that lies on them to take care of their offspring during the imperfect state of childhood. What the children need, and what the parents are bound to provide, is to inform their minds and govern the actions of their still-ignorant minority until reason takes its place and relieves the parents of that trouble. For God, having given man an understanding to direct his actions, has allowed him a freedom of will and a liberty of acting as properly belonging to it, within the bounds of the law he is under. But while he is in a condition in which he has no understanding of his own to direct his will, he is not to have any will of his own to follow. The one who understands for him must also will for him; he must prescribe to his will and regulate his actions. But when the son reaches the condition that made his father a free man, the son is a free man too.

This holds for all the laws a man is under, whether natural or civil. Is a man under the law of nature? What made him free of that law? What gave him the free disposal of his property according to his own will, within the scope of that law? I answer: a state of maturity in which he might be supposed capable of knowing that law, so that he could keep his actions within its bounds. When he has reached that state, he is presumed to know how far that law is to be his guide and how far he may make use of his freedom, and so he comes to have it. Until then, somebody else must guide him, someone who is presumed to know how far the law allows liberty. If such a state of reason, such an age of discretion, made him free, the same will make his son free too. Is a man under the law of England? What made him free of that law — that is, free to dispose of his actions and possessions according to his own will, within what that law permits? A capacity to know that law, which that law supposes to come at the age of twenty-one, and in some cases sooner. If this made the father free, it will make the son free too. Until then, we see, the law allows the son no will of his own; he is to be guided by the will of his father or guardian, who is to understand for him. And if the father dies without appointing a deputy in his trust — if he has not provided a tutor to govern his son during his minority, while he lacks understanding — the law takes care of it. Someone else must govern him and be a will to him until he has reached a state of freedom and his understanding is fit to take over the government of his will. But after that, father and son are equally free, just as tutor and pupil are once the pupil’s minority is over. They are equally subjects of the same law together, with no dominion left in the father over the life, liberty or estate of his son, whether they are only in the state of nature and under the law of nature, or under the positive laws of an established government.

But if, through defects that may occur outside the ordinary course of nature, someone does not reach the degree of reason at which he might be supposed capable of knowing the law and so of living within its rules, he is never capable of being a free man. He is never let loose to dispose of his own will, because he knows no limits to it and lacks understanding, its proper guide. Instead he remains under the guardianship and government of others for as long as his own understanding is incapable of that charge. And so lunatics and idiots are never set free from the government of their parents:

“Children, who have not yet come to those years at which they may have the use of reason; and innocents, who are excluded by a natural defect from ever having it; and, thirdly, madmen, who for the present cannot possibly have the use of right reason to guide themselves — these have for their guide the reason that guides other men, who are tutors over them, to seek and secure their good for them,” says Hooker, Ecclesiastical Polity, book I, section 7. All of this seems to be no more than the duty that God and nature have laid on man, as on other creatures, to preserve their offspring until they are able to fend for themselves; and it hardly amounts to an example or proof of the regal authority of parents.

Thus we are born free, just as we are born rational — not that we actually have the exercise of either. Age, which brings the one, brings the other with it too. And so we see how natural freedom and subjection to parents can exist together, and how both are founded on the same principle. A child is free by his father’s title, by his father’s understanding, which is to govern him until he has an understanding of his own. The freedom of a man at the age of discretion and the subjection of a child to his parents while he is still short of that age are so consistent, and so easy to tell apart, that even the most blinkered champions of monarchy “by right of fatherhood” cannot miss the difference, and the most obstinate must admit that the two are consistent. For suppose their doctrine were entirely true. Suppose the right heir of Adam were now known, and by that title settled as a monarch on his throne, invested with all the absolute, unlimited power Sir Robert Filmer talks of. If he died as soon as his heir was born, would the child not have to be in subjection to his mother and nurse, to tutors and governors, however free and however sovereign he was, until age and education brought him the reason and ability to govern himself and others? The necessities of his life, the health of his body and the instruction of his mind would require him to be directed by the will of others and not by his own. And yet would anyone think that this restraint and subjection was inconsistent with the liberty or sovereignty he had a right to, or robbed him of it, or handed over his empire to those who governed him during his minority? This government over him only prepared him better and sooner for it. If anybody should ask me when my son is of age to be free, I shall answer: just when his monarch is of age to govern. “But at what time,” says the judicious Hooker, Ecclesiastical Polity, book I, section 6, “a man may be said to have attained so far the use of reason as suffices to make him capable of those laws by which he is then bound to guide his actions — this is a great deal easier for sense to discern than for anyone to determine by skill and learning.”

Commonwealths themselves recognize and allow that there is a time when men are to begin to act as free men. Therefore, until that time, they do not require oaths of fealty or allegiance, or any other public acknowledgment of, or submission to, the government of their countries.

The freedom of man, then, and his liberty of acting according to his own will, is grounded on his having reason, which is able to instruct him in the law he is to govern himself by, and to make him know how far he is left to the freedom of his own will. To turn him loose to unrestrained liberty before he has reason to guide him is not to allow him the privilege of his nature to be free. It is to thrust him out among the beasts, and to abandon him to a state as wretched, and as far beneath that of a man, as theirs. This is what puts authority into the parents’ hands to govern their children during their minority. God has made it their business to devote this care to their offspring, and has placed in them suitable inclinations of tenderness and concern to temper this power and to apply it, as his wisdom designed, to the children’s good for as long as they need to be under it.

But what reason can turn this care that parents owe their offspring into an absolute, arbitrary dominion of the father? His power reaches no further than this: by whatever discipline he finds most effective, to give their bodies such strength and health, and their minds such vigour and uprightness, as may best fit his children to be most useful to themselves and others; and, if his circumstances make it necessary, to make them work for their own living when they are able. But in this power the mother too has her share with the father.

Indeed, this power belongs to the father so little by any special right of nature, and only as the guardian of his children, that when he gives up his care of them he loses his power over them. That power goes along with their nourishment and education, to which it is inseparably attached, and it belongs as much to the foster-father of an abandoned child as to the natural father of another. So little power does the bare act of begetting give a man over his offspring, if all his care ends there and this is his only title to the name and authority of a father. And what will become of this paternal power in that part of the world where one woman has more than one husband at a time? Or in those parts of America where, when husband and wife separate (which happens frequently), the children are all left to the mother, go with her, and are wholly under her care and provision? If the father dies while the children are young, do they not naturally, everywhere, owe the same obedience to their mother during their minority as they would to their father if he were alive? And will anyone say that the mother has a legislative power over her children — that she can make standing rules of perpetual obligation, by which they ought to regulate all the concerns of their property and limit their liberty for the whole course of their lives? Or can she enforce the observance of those rules with capital punishment? For this is the proper power of the magistrate, of which the father has not even the shadow. His command over his children is only temporary, and does not reach their life or property. It is only a help to the weakness and imperfection of their minority, a discipline necessary to their education. And though a father may dispose of his own possessions as he pleases once his children are out of danger of perishing from want, his power does not extend to the lives or goods that either their own industry or another’s generosity has made theirs; nor to their liberty either, once they have reached the enfranchisement of the age of discretion. The father’s empire then ceases, and from then on he can no more dispose of his son’s liberty than of any other man’s. And it must be far from an absolute or perpetual jurisdiction if a man may withdraw himself from it, having permission from divine authority to “leave father and mother, and cleave to his wife.”

But there comes a time when a child is as free from subjection to the will and command of his father as the father himself is free from subjection to the will of anybody else, and when each of them is under no restraint except what is common to them both, whether that is the law of nature or the municipal law of their country. Even so, this freedom does not exempt a son from the honour he ought, by the law of God and nature, to pay his parents. God made parents the instruments of his great design of continuing the human race, and the means of life to their children. And just as he has laid on them an obligation to nourish, preserve and bring up their offspring, so he has laid on the children a perpetual obligation to honour their parents. This obligation contains an inward esteem and reverence, to be shown by every outward expression. It restrains the child from anything that might ever injure or insult, disturb or endanger, the happiness or life of those from whom he received his own. And it commits him to every act of defence, relief, assistance and comfort toward those through whom he came into being and was made capable of any of life’s enjoyments. No state and no freedom can release children from this obligation. But this is very far from giving parents a power of command over their children, or an authority to make laws for them and dispose of their lives or liberties as they please. It is one thing to owe honour, respect, gratitude and assistance; it is another to require absolute obedience and submission. A monarch on his throne owes his mother the honour due to parents; and yet this does not lessen his authority or subject him to her government.

The subjection of a minor places in the father a temporary government, which ends with the child’s minority. The honour a child owes places in the parents a perpetual right to respect, reverence, support and compliance too — more or less, according as the father’s care, expense and kindness in his education have been more or less. This does not end with minority but holds in every part and condition of a man’s life. The failure to distinguish these two powers — namely, the one the father has by the right of tuition during minority, and the right of honour all his life — may perhaps have caused a great part of the mistakes about this matter. For, properly speaking, the first of these is rather the privilege of children and the duty of parents than any prerogative of paternal power. The nourishment and education of their children is a charge laid so firmly on parents, for their children’s good, that nothing can release them from taking care of it. And though the power of commanding and punishing them goes along with it, God has woven into the principles of human nature such tenderness for their offspring that there is little fear parents will use their power too harshly. The excess is seldom on the severe side, since the strong bias of nature pulls the other way.
