And therefore, when God Almighty wanted to express his gentle dealing with the Israelites, he told them that though he chastened them, “he chastened them as a man chastens his son,” Deut. viii. 5 — that is, with tenderness and affection, keeping them under no severer discipline than was absolutely best for them — discipline that it would have been less kind to relax. This is the power to which children are commanded to be obedient, so that their parents’ pains and care may not be increased or poorly rewarded.

On the other side, honour and support — everything that gratitude requires in return for the benefits received by and from them — is the indispensable duty of the child and the proper privilege of the parents. This is intended for the parents’ advantage, as the other is for the child’s. Yet education, the parents’ duty, seems to carry the most power, because the ignorance and weaknesses of childhood need restraint and correction, which is a visible exercise of rule and a kind of dominion. And the duty contained in the word “honour” requires less obedience, though the obligation is stronger on grown children than on younger ones. For who can think that the command “Children obey your parents” requires of a man who has children of his own the same submission to his father as it requires of his own still-young children to him? Or that by this precept he would be bound to obey all his father’s commands, if his father, out of a conceited sense of authority, were indiscreet enough to go on treating him as a boy?

The first part of paternal power, then — or rather duty — which is education, belongs to the father in such a way that it ends at a certain time. When the business of education is over it ceases of itself, and it can also be transferred before then. For a man may put his son’s tuition into other hands; and someone who has apprenticed his son to another has released him, for that period, from a great part of his obedience both to himself and to his mother. But the whole duty of honour, the other part, remains fully intact for them both; nothing can cancel it. It is so inseparable from them both that the father’s authority cannot deprive the mother of this right, nor can any man release his son from honouring her who bore him. But both of these are very far from a power to make laws and to enforce them with penalties that may reach estate, liberty, limbs and life. The power of commanding ends with minority. And though, after that, honour and respect, support and defence, and whatever gratitude can oblige a man to for the highest benefits he is naturally capable of, are always due from a son to his parents, all this puts no sceptre into the father’s hand, no sovereign power of commanding. He has no dominion over his son’s property or actions, nor any right that his will should dictate to his son’s in all things — however fitting it may be for his son to defer to it in many things that are not very inconvenient to him and his family.

A man may owe honour and respect to an elderly or wise man, defence to his child or friend, relief and support to the distressed, and gratitude to a benefactor — to such a degree that everything he has and everything he can do cannot sufficiently repay it. But none of this gives anyone authority, or any right to make laws over the person from whom it is owed. And it is plain that all this is due not merely to the bare title of father. That is not only because, as has been said, it is owed to the mother too; it is also because these obligations to parents, and the degree of what is required of children, may vary with the different care and kindness, trouble and expense, that is often spent on one child more than another.

This shows why parents in societies where they themselves are subjects keep a power over their children, and have as much right to their subjection as those who are in the state of nature. That could not possibly be so if all political power were only paternal, and the two were truly one and the same thing. For then, since all paternal power would be in the prince, the subject could naturally have none of it. But these two powers, political and paternal, are so completely distinct and separate, are built on such different foundations and given for such different ends, that every subject who is a father has as much paternal power over his children as the prince has over his. And every prince who has parents owes them as much filial duty and obedience as the lowest of his subjects owes to theirs. Paternal power, therefore, cannot contain any part or degree of the kind of dominion that a prince or magistrate has over his subject.

The parents’ obligation to bring up their children, and the children’s obligation to honour their parents, contain all the power on the one side and all the submission on the other that belong to this relationship. Yet there is another power ordinarily held by the father, by which he has a hold on the obedience of his children. He shares it with other men; but the occasions for exercising it arise almost constantly for fathers in their private families, while examples of it elsewhere are rare and less noticed, and so it passes in the world for a part of paternal jurisdiction. This is the power men generally have to bestow their estates on those who please them best. The father’s possessions are what his children expect and inherit, ordinarily in certain proportions according to the law and custom of each country. Yet it is commonly in the father’s power to bestow them with a more sparing or a more generous hand, according to how far the behaviour of this or that child has suited his will and temper.

This is no small hold on the obedience of children. And since the enjoyment of land always carries with it submission to the government of the country of which that land is a part, it has commonly been supposed that a father could bind his posterity to the government of which he himself was a subject, and that his compact held them. But this is only a necessary condition attached to the land, and the inheritance of an estate under that government reaches only those who will take it on that condition. So it is no natural tie or engagement, but a voluntary submission. For every man’s children are by nature as free as he himself or any of his ancestors ever were, and while they are in that freedom they may choose what society they will join and what commonwealth they will put themselves under. But if they want to enjoy the inheritance of their ancestors, they must take it on the same terms their ancestors had it, and submit to all the conditions attached to such a possession. By this power, indeed, fathers oblige their children to obey them even after they are past their minority, and very commonly they also subject them to this or that political power. But neither of these is by any special right of fatherhood; it is by the reward they hold in their hands to enforce and repay such compliance. It is no more power than a Frenchman has over an Englishman who, in the hope of an estate the Frenchman will leave him, will certainly be strongly tied to obey him. And if the Englishman wants to enjoy the estate once it is left to him, he must certainly take it on the conditions attached to the possession of land in the country where it lies, whether that is France or England.

To conclude, then: the father’s power of commanding extends no further than his children’s minority, and only to a degree fit for the discipline and government of that age. The honour and respect, and all that the Latins called piety, which children are bound to owe their parents all their lives and in every condition, together with all the support and defence due to them, give the father no power of governing — that is, of making laws and imposing penalties on his children. By all this he has no dominion over his son’s property or actions. And yet it is easy to see how, in the first ages of the world, and still in places where the thinness of the population lets families separate into unoccupied areas and gives them room to move or settle in still-vacant lands, the father of the family could easily become its prince.* He had been a ruler from the beginning of his children’s infancy. And since it would be hard for them to live together without some government, it was most likely to rest, by the express or tacit consent of the children once they were grown, in the father, where it seemed simply to continue without any change. In fact, nothing more was required for it than allowing the father to exercise alone, in his family, the executive power of the law of nature that every free man naturally has, and by that permission handing over to him a monarchical power while they remained in the family. But that this was not by any paternal right, but only by the consent of his children, is evident from this: nobody doubts that if a stranger, whom chance or business had brought to his family, had killed any of his children there, or committed any other crime, the father might condemn him and put him to death, or otherwise punish him, just as he could any of his children. He could not possibly do this by virtue of any paternal authority over someone who was not his child; he did it by virtue of the executive power of the law of nature, to which he had a right as a man. And he alone could punish him in his family, because the respect of his children had set aside their own exercise of such a power, to give way to the dignity and authority they were willing to leave in him, above the rest of his family.

(*“It is therefore no improbable opinion, which the arch-philosopher held, that the chief person in every household was always, as it were, a king. So when numbers of households joined together in civil societies, kings were the first kind of governors among them. This also seems to be the reason why the name of fathers still remained with those who, from being fathers, were made rulers; and the ancient custom of governors to do as Melchizedec did, and, being kings, to exercise the office of priests, which fathers did at first, perhaps grew up on the same occasion. However, this is not the only kind of government that has been accepted in the world. The inconveniences of one kind have caused various others to be devised. So, in a word, all public government, of whatever kind, seems evidently to have arisen from deliberate advice, consultation and agreement between men, who judged it convenient and beneficial; for there is no impossibility in nature, considered by itself, that man might have lived without any public government.” Hooker, Ecclesiastical Polity, book I, section 10.)

So it was easy, and almost natural, for children, by a tacit and hardly avoidable consent, to make way for the father’s authority and government. In childhood they had been used to following his direction and to referring their little disputes to him; and when they were men, who was fitter to rule them? Their small properties and smaller greed seldom produced bigger disputes; and when any did arise, where could they find a fitter umpire than the man by whose care every one of them had been sustained and brought up, and who had a tenderness for them all? It is no wonder that they made no distinction between minority and full age, or looked out for twenty-one or any other age that might make them the free disposers of themselves and their fortunes, when they could have no desire to leave their pupilage. The government they had been under during it continued to be more their protection than their restraint; and nowhere could they find greater security for their peace, liberties and fortunes than in the rule of a father.

Thus the natural fathers of families, by an imperceptible change, became their political monarchs too. And as they happened to live long and leave able and worthy heirs for several successive generations, or otherwise, so they laid the foundations of hereditary or elective kingdoms, under various constitutions and customs, as chance, design or circumstances happened to shape them. But suppose princes hold their titles by their fathers’ right, and suppose it is sufficient proof of the natural right of fathers to political authority that they were commonly the ones in whose hands we find, de facto, the exercise of government. I say, if this argument is good, it will just as strongly prove that all princes — indeed, princes only — ought to be priests, since it is as certain that in the beginning the father of the family was priest as that he was ruler in his own household.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 — Of Political or Civil Society
paragraphs: God made man such a creature that, in his own judgment, it was not good for him to be alone. So he put him under strong obligations of necessity, convenience and inclination to drive him into society, and he also equipped him with understanding and language to continue and enjoy it. The first society was between man and wife, which gave rise to the society between parents and children; and in time the society between master and servant was added to these. And though all of these might meet together, and commonly did, to make up a single family, in which the master or mistress had some sort of rule proper to a family, each of them, or all of them together, fell short of political society. We shall see this if we consider the different ends, ties and limits of each.

Conjugal society is made by a voluntary compact between man and woman. And although it consists chiefly in such a communion of, and right in, one another’s bodies as is necessary to its chief end, procreation, it also brings with it mutual support and assistance, and a shared interest too. This is necessary not only to unite their care and affection, but also for their common offspring, who have a right to be nourished and maintained by them until they are able to provide for themselves.

For the end of the union between male and female is not merely procreation but the continuation of the species. So this union between male and female ought to last, even after procreation, as long as is necessary for the nourishment and support of the young, who are to be sustained by those who produced them until they are able to fend and provide for themselves. We find the lower creatures steadily obeying this rule, which the infinitely wise maker has set for the works of his hands. In those viviparous animals that feed on grass, the union between male and female lasts no longer than the act of copulation itself. This is because the mother’s teat is enough to nourish the young until they can feed on grass, so the male only begets them and does not concern himself with the female or the young, to whose sustenance he can contribute nothing. But in beasts of prey the union lasts longer. The mother is not well able to subsist herself and nourish her numerous offspring by her own prey alone — a more laborious, as well as more dangerous, way of living than feeding on grass — and so the male’s assistance is necessary to maintain their common family, which cannot survive until the young are able to hunt for themselves, except by the joint care of male and female. The same is to be observed in all birds (except some domestic ones, where plenty of food excuses the cock from feeding and taking care of the young brood): because their young need food in the nest, the cock and hen stay mates until the young are able to use their wings and provide for themselves.

And in this, I think, lies the chief reason, if not the only one, why male and female in mankind are tied to a longer union than other creatures. It is because the female is capable of conceiving, and in fact is commonly pregnant again and gives birth to a new child, long before the previous one has stopped depending on his parents’ help for support, is able to fend for himself, and has received all the assistance due to him from his parents. So the father, who is bound to take care of those he has begotten, is under an obligation to continue in conjugal society with the same woman longer than other creatures do. With them, the young are able to subsist on their own before the time of procreation comes round again, so the conjugal bond dissolves of itself, and they are at liberty until Hymen, at his usual yearly season, summons them again to choose new mates. Here one cannot help admiring the wisdom of the great Creator. Having given man foresight, and an ability to store up for the future as well as to supply present needs, he has made it necessary that the society of man and wife should last longer than that of male and female among other creatures. In this way their industry might be encouraged and their interests better united, to make provision and store up goods for their common offspring — which uncertain mixing, or easy and frequent dissolutions of conjugal society, would greatly disturb.

But although these are ties on mankind which make the conjugal bond firmer and more lasting in man than in the other species of animals, they would still give one reason to ask why this compact — where procreation and education are secured and inheritance provided for — may not be made terminable, either by consent, or at a certain time, or on certain conditions, just like any other voluntary compact. For there is no necessity, either in the nature of the thing or in its ends, that it should always be for life. I mean, for those who are under no restraint of any positive law that ordains all such contracts to be perpetual.

But husband and wife, though they have only one common concern, still have different understandings, and so will unavoidably sometimes have different wills too. It is therefore necessary that the final decision — that is, the rule — should be placed somewhere, and it naturally falls to the man’s share, as the abler and the stronger. But this extends only to matters of their common interest and property. It leaves the wife in full and free possession of what is her own particular right by contract, and gives the husband no more power over her life than she has over his. The husband’s power is so far from that of an absolute monarch that the wife has, in many cases, a liberty to separate from him where natural right or their contract allows it — whether that contract was made by themselves in the state of nature or by the customs or laws of the country they live in. And on such a separation the children fall to the father’s or the mother’s lot, as that contract determines.

For since all the ends of marriage are to be achieved under political government as well as in the state of nature, the civil magistrate does not curtail the right or power of either party that is naturally necessary to those ends — namely, procreation and mutual support and assistance while they are together. He only decides any dispute that may arise between man and wife about them. If it were otherwise, and absolute sovereignty and power of life and death naturally belonged to the husband and were necessary to the society between man and wife, there could be no marriage in any of those countries where the husband is allowed no such absolute authority. But since the ends of marriage require no such power in the husband, the condition of conjugal society did not place it in him, because it is not at all necessary to that state. Conjugal society could exist and attain its ends without it. Indeed, community of goods and the power over them, mutual assistance and maintenance, and other things belonging to conjugal society, might be varied and regulated by the contract that unites man and wife in that society, as far as is consistent with procreation and bringing up the children until they can fend for themselves. For nothing is necessary to any society that is not necessary to the ends for which it is made.

The society between parents and children, and the distinct rights and powers belonging to each of them, I have discussed at such length in the previous chapter that I need not say anything about it here. And I think it is plain that it is very different from a political society.

Master and servant are names as old as history, but they are given to people in very different conditions. For a free man makes himself a servant to another by selling him, for a certain time, the service he undertakes to do, in exchange for wages he is to receive. And though this commonly places him in his master’s household and under its ordinary discipline, it gives the master only a temporary power over him, and no greater than what is contained in the contract between them. But there is another sort of servant, whom we call by a special name, slaves. Being captives taken in a just war, they are by the right of nature subjected to the absolute dominion and arbitrary power of their masters. These men have, as I say, forfeited their lives, and with them their liberties, and lost their estates; and being in the state of slavery, they are not capable of any property. So in that state they cannot be considered any part of civil society, the chief end of which is the preservation of property.

Let us therefore consider the master of a family with all these subordinate relations of wife, children, servants and slaves, united under the domestic rule of a family. Whatever resemblance it may have to a little commonwealth in its order, its offices, and even its numbers, it is still very far from being one, in its constitution, power and end. Or if it must be thought a monarchy, with the paterfamilias as its absolute monarch, then absolute monarchy will have only a very fragmented and short-lived power. For it is plain, from what has been said already, that the master of the family has a very distinct and differently limited power, both in time and in extent, over the different persons in it. Except for the slave (and the family is just as much a family, and his power as paterfamilias just as great, whether or not there are any slaves in it), he has no legislative power of life and death over any of them, and no power either that the mistress of a family may not have as well as he. And he certainly cannot have absolute power over the whole family when he has only a very limited power over every individual in it. But how a family, or any other society of men, differs from what is properly political society we shall best see by considering what political society itself consists in.

Man is born, as has been proved, with a title to perfect freedom and to an uncontrolled enjoyment of all the rights and privileges of the law of nature, equally with any other man or number of men in the world. So he has by nature a power not only to preserve his property — that is, his life, liberty and estate — against the injuries and attempts of other men, but also to judge and punish breaches of that law by others as he is persuaded the offence deserves, even with death itself, in crimes where, in his opinion, the heinousness of the deed requires it. But no political society can exist or survive without having in itself the power to preserve property, and, for that purpose, to punish the offences of all those in that society. So there, and there only, is political society where every one of the members has given up this natural power and resigned it into the hands of the community, in all cases that do not exclude him from appealing for protection to the law established by it. In this way all private judgment of every individual member is excluded, and the community becomes the umpire, by settled standing rules that are impartial and the same for all parties. Through men who have authority from the community to execute those rules, it decides all the disputes that may arise between any members of that society concerning any matter of right, and it punishes the offences any member has committed against the society with such penalties as the law has established. By this it is easy to see who are, and who are not, in political society together. Those who are united into one body, and have a common established law and judiciary to appeal to, with authority to decide disputes between them and punish offenders, are in civil society with one another. But those who have no such common appeal — I mean on earth — are still in the state of nature, each being, where there is no other, judge and executioner for himself. And that, as I have shown before, is the perfect state of nature.

And so the commonwealth acquires a power to set down what punishment shall belong to the various offences, committed among the members of that society, which they think deserve it (which is the power of making laws), as well as the power to punish any injury done to any of its members by anyone who does not belong to it (which is the power of war and peace); and all this for the preservation of the property of all the members of that society, as far as possible. Every man who has entered into civil society and become a member of any commonwealth has thereby given up his power to punish offences against the law of nature according to his own private judgment. Yet along with the judgment of offences, which he has handed over to the legislative in all cases where he can appeal to the magistrate, he has given the commonwealth a right to employ his force to carry out the judgments of the commonwealth whenever he is called on to do so. And these are in fact his own judgments, since they are made by himself or his representative. Here we have the origin of the legislative and executive power of civil society. That power is to judge by standing laws how far offences committed within the commonwealth are to be punished; and also to determine, by occasional judgments based on the present circumstances of the case, how far injuries from outside are to be avenged; and in both of these to employ all the force of all the members when there is need.

Wherever, therefore, any number of men are united into one society in such a way that each of them gives up his executive power of the law of nature and resigns it to the public, there and there only is a political, or civil, society. And this happens wherever any number of men in the state of nature enter into society to make one people, one body politic, under one supreme government; or else when anyone joins himself to, and becomes incorporated with, any government already formed. For by doing so he authorizes the society, or, what amounts to the same thing, its legislative, to make laws for him as the public good of the society requires; and his own assistance is due for carrying them out, as it would be for his own decrees. And this takes men out of a state of nature into that of a commonwealth, by setting up a judge on earth with authority to settle all disputes and redress the injuries that may happen to any member of the commonwealth; and that judge is the legislative, or the magistrates appointed by it. And wherever there are any number of men, however associated, who have no such decisive power to appeal to, they are still in the state of nature.

Hence it is evident that absolute monarchy, which some men count the only government in the world, is in fact inconsistent with civil society, and so can be no form of civil government at all. For the end of civil society is to avoid and remedy those inconveniences of the state of nature which necessarily follow from every man’s being judge in his own case. It does this by setting up a known authority to which every member of that society may appeal for any injury received or any dispute that may arise, and which every member of the society ought to obey.* Wherever there are any persons who do not have such an authority to appeal to for deciding any difference between them, those persons are still in the state of nature. And so is every absolute prince in relation to those who are under his dominion.

(*“The public power of all society is above every soul contained in that same society; and the principal use of that power is to give laws to all who are under it. We must obey such laws in such cases, unless there is reason shown which may necessarily compel the conclusion that the law of reason, or of God, commands the contrary.” Hooker, Ecclesiastical Polity, book I, section 16.)

For since he is supposed to have all power, both legislative and executive, in himself alone, there is no judge to be found, and no appeal open to anyone, who may fairly, impartially and with authority decide, and from whose decision relief and redress may be expected for any injury or inconvenience suffered from the prince or by his order. So such a man, whatever his title — Czar, or Grand Seignior, or whatever you please — is as much in the state of nature with all under his dominion as he is with the rest of mankind. For wherever any two men have no standing rule and no common judge on earth to appeal to for deciding disputes of right between them, they are still in the state of* nature and under all its inconveniences. There is only this miserable difference for the subject, or rather the slave, of an absolute prince. In the ordinary state of nature he has a liberty to judge of his right and to maintain it as well as he is able. Now, whenever his property is invaded by the will and order of his monarch, he not only has no appeal, as those in society ought to have, but — as if he were degraded from the common state of rational creatures — he is denied the liberty to judge of, or to defend, his right. And so he is exposed to all the misery and inconveniences that a man can fear from someone who is in the unrestrained state of nature and is yet corrupted by flattery and armed with power.

(*“To remove all such mutual grievances, injuries and wrongs” — that is, such as attend men in the state of nature — “there was no way except by coming to an arrangement and agreement among themselves: by ordaining some kind of public government, and by making themselves subject to it, so that those to whom they granted authority to rule and govern might secure the peace, tranquillity and happy condition of the rest. Men always knew that where force and injury were offered, they might defend themselves. They knew that, however men may seek their own advantage, if this were done with injury to others it was not to be tolerated, but was to be resisted by all men and by all good means. Finally, they knew that no man might reasonably take it on himself to determine his own right and, according to his own determination, proceed to maintain it, because every man is partial towards himself and those he greatly cares for. They knew, therefore, that strife and troubles would be endless unless they all gave their common consent to be ordered by some persons they should agree on. Without that consent there would be no reason why one man should take it on himself to be lord or judge over another.” Hooker, Ecclesiastical Polity, book I, section 10.)

For anyone who thinks that absolute power purifies men’s blood and corrects the baseness of human nature need only read the history of this or any other age to be convinced of the contrary. A man who would have been insolent and harmful in the woods of America would probably not be much better on a throne, where perhaps learning and religion will be found to justify everything he does to his subjects, and the sword will immediately silence all who dare question it. For what the protection of absolute monarchy amounts to, what kind of fathers of their countries it makes princes, and to what degree of happiness and security it brings civil society where this sort of government has been brought to perfection — anyone who looks into the recent account of Ceylon may easily see.

In absolute monarchies, it is true, as in other governments of the world, the subjects have an appeal to the law, and judges to decide any disputes and restrain any violence that may occur among the subjects themselves. Everyone thinks this necessary, and believes that anyone who tried to take it away would deserve to be thought a declared enemy of society and mankind. But whether this comes from a true love of mankind and society, and the kind of charity we all owe one another, there is reason to doubt. For this is no more than what every man who loves his own power, profit or greatness may, and naturally must, do: keep those animals that labour and drudge only for his pleasure and advantage from hurting or destroying one another. And so they are taken care of, not out of any love the master has for them, but out of love of himself and the profit they bring him. For if it is asked what security, what protection, there is in such a state against the violence and oppression of this absolute ruler, the very question can hardly be tolerated. They are ready to tell you that merely asking about safety deserves death. Between subject and subject, they will grant, there must be measures, laws and judges for their mutual peace and security. But as for the ruler, he ought to be absolute and is above all such considerations; because he has the power to do more hurt and wrong, it is right when he does it. To ask how you may be protected from harm or injury on the side where the strongest hand is able to do it is at once called the voice of faction and rebellion. It is as if, when men left the state of nature and entered into society, they agreed that all of them but one should be under the restraint of laws, but that he should still keep all the liberty of the state of nature, increased with power and made licentious by impunity. This is to think that men are so foolish that they take care to avoid what harm may be done to them by polecats or foxes, but are content — indeed, think it safety — to be devoured by lions.

But whatever flatterers may say to beguile people’s understanding, it does not stop men from feeling. And when they perceive that any man, whatever his station, is outside the bounds of the civil society they belong to, and that they have no appeal on earth against any harm they may receive from him, they are apt to think themselves in the state of nature with respect to him. They are apt, too, to take care, as soon as they can, to have the safety and security in civil society for which it was first instituted, and for which alone they entered into it. And so, although perhaps at first (as will be shown more fully later in this discourse) some one good and excellent man gained pre-eminence over the rest, and such deference was paid to his goodness and virtue, as to a kind of natural authority, that the chief rule, with the arbitration of their differences, passed into his hands by tacit consent, without any other safeguard than the assurance they had of his uprightness and wisdom — yet in the end time did its work. It gave authority and (as some men would persuade us) sacredness to customs that the careless and unforeseeing innocence of the first ages had begun, and it brought in successors of another kind. When that happened, the people found their properties not secure under the government as it then was (whereas government has no other end but the preservation of* property), and so they could never be safe or at rest, nor think themselves in civil society, until the legislature was placed in collective bodies of men — call them senate, parliament, or what you please. By this means every single person became subject, equally with the lowest men, to those laws which he himself, as part of the legislative, had established. Nor could anyone, by his own authority, avoid the force of the law once it was made, or plead exemption by any claim of superiority so as to license his own misconduct or that of any of his dependants.** No man in civil society can be exempted from its laws. For if any man may do what he thinks fit, and there is no appeal on earth for redress or security against any harm he does, I ask whether he is not still completely in the state of nature, and so can be no part or member of that civil society — unless someone will say that the state of nature and civil society are one and the same thing, which I have never yet found anyone so great a patron of anarchy as to affirm.

(*“At first, when some particular kind of government had once been appointed, it may be that nothing further was then thought about the manner of governing, but everything was left to the wisdom and discretion of those who were to rule. Then, by experience, they found this very inconvenient for all parties, so that the thing they had devised as a remedy in fact only increased the sore it should have cured. They saw that living by one man’s will became the cause of all men’s misery. This compelled them to turn to laws, in which all men might see their duty beforehand and know the penalties for transgressing them.” Hooker, Ecclesiastical Polity, book I, section 10.)
(**“Civil law, being the act of the whole body politic, therefore overrules each separate part of that same body.” Hooker, Ecclesiastical Polity, book I, section 10.)

chapters.title: Chapter 8 — Of the Beginning of Political Societies
paragraphs: Men are by nature all free, equal and independent, as has been said. So no one can be put out of this condition and subjected to the political power of another without his own consent. The only way anyone gives up his natural liberty and puts on the bonds of civil society is by agreeing with other men to join and unite into a community. They do this so that they can live comfortably, safely and peaceably with one another, in secure enjoyment of their properties, and with greater security against anyone who is not part of it. Any number of men may do this, because it does no injury to the freedom of the rest: they are left as they were, in the liberty of the state of nature. When any number of men have consented in this way to make one community or government, they are by that very act incorporated at once and make one body politic, in which the majority have a right to act and to bind the rest.

For when any number of men have made a community by the consent of every individual, they have by that act made the community one body, with a power to act as one body — and that can only be by the will and decision of the majority. The reason is this. What moves any community to act is only the consent of the individuals in it; and whatever is one body must move one way. So the body must move in the direction the greater force carries it, and that force is the consent of the majority. Otherwise it cannot possibly act or continue as one body, one community — which is what every individual who united into it agreed it should do. And so everyone is bound by that consent to be bound by the majority. That is why we see that in assemblies empowered to act by positive laws, where the positive law that empowers them sets no number, the act of the majority passes for the act of the whole. As a matter of course it decides the question, since by the law of nature and reason it has the power of the whole.

And so every man, by consenting with others to make one body politic under one government, puts himself under an obligation to everyone in that society to submit to the decision of the majority and to be bound by it. Otherwise this original compact, by which he and others incorporate into one society, would mean nothing. It would be no compact at all if he were left free, and under no other ties than he was under before in the state of nature. For what appearance of a compact would there be? What new engagement would there be, if he were bound by the decrees of the society no further than he himself thought fit and actually consented to? That would still leave him as great a liberty as he had before his compact, or as anyone else has in the state of nature, who may submit himself and consent to any of its acts if he thinks fit.

For if the consent of the majority is not, in reason, to be accepted as the act of the whole and to bind every individual, then nothing but the consent of every individual can make anything the act of the whole. But such consent is almost impossible ever to obtain. Consider ill health and the demands of business, which in any number of people — even one much smaller than a commonwealth — will necessarily keep many away from the public assembly. Add to that the variety of opinions and the conflict of interests that unavoidably arise in every gathering of men, and coming into society on such terms would be just like Cato’s coming into the theatre, only to go out again. A constitution like this would make the mighty Leviathan shorter-lived than the feeblest creatures, and would not let it outlast the day it was born. That cannot be supposed until we can believe that rational creatures would desire and set up societies only for them to be dissolved. For where the majority cannot bind the rest, the society cannot act as one body, and so it will immediately be dissolved again.

Whoever, therefore, unite into a community out of a state of nature must be understood to give up to the majority of the community all the power necessary to the ends for which they unite into society — unless they have expressly agreed on some number greater than the majority. And this is done simply by agreeing to unite into one political society, which is the whole compact there is, or needs to be, between the individuals who enter into or make up a commonwealth. So what begins and actually constitutes any political society is nothing but the consent of any number of free men capable of a majority to unite and incorporate into such a society. And this, and this alone, is what did or could give a beginning to any lawful government in the world.

To this I find two objections made. First, that no instances can be found in history of a company of men, independent and equal among themselves, who met together and in this way began and set up a government.
Secondly, that it is impossible for men to do so by right, because all men are born under government, and so they must submit to it and are not at liberty to begin a new one.

To the first objection I answer this. It is not at all surprising that history gives us only a very small account of men who lived together in the state of nature. The inconveniences of that condition, and men’s love of society and need for it, no sooner brought any number of them together than they immediately united and incorporated, if they intended to stay together. And if we may not suppose that men were ever in the state of nature because we do not hear much of them in that state, we may just as well suppose that the armies of Salmanasser or Xerxes were never children, because we hear little of them until they were men and formed into armies. Everywhere, government comes before records. Writing seldom arrives among a people until civil society has lasted a long time and, through other more necessary arts, has provided for their safety, ease and plenty. Only then do they begin to look into the history of their founders and search out their origins, when they have outlived the memory of them. For it is with commonwealths as with individual persons: they are commonly ignorant of their own births and infancies. And if they know anything of their origins, they owe it to the chance records that others have kept. And the accounts we do have of the beginning of any political communities in the world — except that of the Jews, where God himself directly intervened, and which does not favour paternal dominion at all — are all either plain instances of the kind of beginning I have described, or at least show clear traces of it.

Anyone who will not allow that Rome and Venice began by the uniting together of a number of men who were free and independent of one another, with no natural superiority or subjection among them, must show a strange inclination to deny plain matters of fact when they do not agree with his hypothesis. And if Josephus Acosta’s word may be taken, he tells us that in many parts of America there was no government at all.

“There are great and evident grounds for conjecture,” he says, speaking of the people of Peru, “that these men for a long time had neither kings nor commonwealths, but lived in bands, as they do to this day in Florida — the Cheriquanas, those of Brazil, and many other nations, which have no fixed kings, but, as occasion arises in peace or war, choose their captains as they please.” Book I, chapter 25.

It may be said that every man there was born subject to his father, or to the head of his family. But I have already proved that the subjection a child owes to a father did not take away his freedom to unite into whatever political society he thought fit. Be that as it may, these men were evidently free in fact. Whatever superiority some political writers would now place in any of them, they themselves did not claim it; by consent they were all equal, until by the same consent they set rulers over themselves. So their political societies all began from a voluntary union, and from the mutual agreement of men acting freely in the choice of their governors and of their forms of government.

And I hope those who went away from Sparta with Palantus, mentioned by Justin (book III, chapter 4), will be allowed to have been free men, independent of one another, who set up a government over themselves by their own consent. So I have given several examples from history of people who were free and in the state of nature, and who met together, incorporated and began a commonwealth. And if the lack of such instances is an argument to prove that government was not, and could not be, begun in this way, I suppose the champions of paternal empire had better leave it alone than urge it against natural liberty. For if they can give as many instances from history of governments begun on paternal right, I think one might yield them the case without much danger — though at best an argument from what has been to what ought by right to be has no great force. But if I might advise them on the matter, they would do well not to search too far into the origins of governments as they have begun de facto. Otherwise they may find, at the foundation of most of them, something very little favourable to the design they promote, and to the kind of power they contend for.

But to conclude: reason is plainly on our side that men are naturally free, and the examples of history show that the governments of the world which began in peace had their beginning laid on that foundation, and were made by the consent of the people. So there can be little room for doubt, either about where the right lies, or about what the opinion or practice of mankind has been concerning the first setting up of governments.

I will not deny that if we look back as far as history will guide us towards the origin of commonwealths, we shall generally find them under the government and administration of one man. I am also inclined to believe that where a family was large enough to support itself, and stayed together as a whole without mixing with others — as often happens where there is much land and few people — the government commonly began with the father. For the father had, by the law of nature, the same power as every other man to punish any offences against that law as he thought fit. So he could punish his children when they transgressed, even when they were grown men and no longer under his tutelage. And they were very likely to submit to his punishment, and all in their turn to join with him against the offender. In this way they gave him power to carry out his sentence against any transgression, and so in effect made him the lawmaker and governor over all who remained together with his family. He was the one best fitted to be trusted. Paternal affection secured their property and interests under his care, and the habit of obeying him in their childhood made it easier to submit to him than to anyone else. If, then, they had to have someone to rule them — and government is hardly to be avoided among men who live together — who was so likely to be the man as he who was their common father? Unless, that is, negligence, cruelty, or some other defect of mind or body made him unfit for it. But when the father died and left an heir less fit to rule, for lack of age, wisdom, courage or some other quality, or where several families met and agreed to stay together, there can be no doubt that they used their natural freedom to set up the man they judged the ablest and the most likely to rule them well. In keeping with this, we find that the peoples of America — who lived beyond the reach of the conquering swords and spreading domination of the two great empires of Peru and Mexico — enjoyed their own natural freedom. Caeteris paribus, they commonly prefer the heir of their dead king; yet if they find him in any way weak or incapable, they pass him over and set up the boldest and bravest man as their ruler.

So, looking back as far as records give us any account of the peopling of the world and the history of nations, we commonly find government in one man’s hands. Yet this does not overturn what I affirm, namely that the beginning of political society depends on the consent of individuals to join and make one society; and when they are incorporated in this way, they might set up whatever form of government they thought fit. But since this has led men into the mistake of thinking that government was by nature monarchical and belonged to the father, it may not be out of place to consider here why people at the beginning generally settled on this form. Perhaps, in the first founding of some commonwealths, the father’s pre-eminence gave rise to it and placed power in one hand at the beginning. Even so, it is plain that what kept the form of government in a single person was not any regard or respect for paternal authority. For all petty monarchies — that is, almost all monarchies near their origins — have commonly been elective, at least on occasion.

First, then, in the beginning of things, the father’s government of his children during their childhood had accustomed them to the rule of one man. It had taught them that where this rule was exercised with care and skill, with affection and love for those under it, it was enough to obtain and preserve for men all the political happiness they looked for in society. It was no wonder, then, that they should settle on, and naturally fall into, the form of government they had all been used to from infancy, and which they had found by experience to be both easy and safe. Add to this that monarchy is simple and the most obvious form to men who had not been taught by experience about forms of government, nor by the ambition or insolence of empire to beware of the encroachments of prerogative or the inconveniences of absolute power, which a monarchy passed down by succession was apt to lay claim to and bring upon them. So it was not at all strange that they did not trouble themselves much to think of ways of restraining any excesses of those to whom they had given authority over them, or of balancing the power of government by placing separate parts of it in different hands. They had not felt the oppression of tyrannical dominion. Nor did the fashion of the age, or their possessions, or their way of living (which offered little to feed covetousness or ambition) give them any reason to fear it or to guard against it. And so it is no wonder that they put themselves under a frame of government which was not only, as I said, the most obvious and simple, but also the best suited to their present state and condition — which needed defence against foreign invasions and injuries more than it needed a multitude of laws. The equality of a simple, poor way of living, which kept each man’s desires within the narrow bounds of his own small property, produced few disputes. So there was no need of many laws to settle them, or of a variety of officers to oversee proceedings or look after the execution of justice, where there were only few trespasses and few offenders. Now, those who like one another well enough to join into society must be supposed to have some acquaintance and friendship with each other, and some trust in one another. So they could not help fearing others more than they feared one another. Their first care and thought, therefore, must be supposed to have been how to secure themselves against foreign force. It was natural for them to put themselves under a frame of government that would best serve that end, and to choose the wisest and bravest man to lead them in their wars and against their enemies, and in this chiefly to be their ruler.

So we see that the kings of the Indians in America (which is still a pattern of the first ages in Asia and Europe), while the inhabitants are too few for the country, and the lack of people and money gives men no temptation to enlarge their holdings of land or to fight over wider territory, are little more than generals of their armies. Though these kings command absolutely in war, at home and in time of peace they exercise very little dominion and have only a very moderate sovereignty; decisions of peace and war ordinarily lie either with the people or with a council. War itself, however, does not allow a plurality of commanders, and so it naturally places the command in the king’s sole authority.

And so in Israel itself, the chief business of their judges and first kings seems to have been to be captains in war and leaders of their armies. Besides what is meant by “going out and in before the people” — which meant marching out to war and home again at the head of their forces — this appears plainly in the story of Jephthah. When the Ammonites made war on Israel, the Gileadites in fear sent to Jephthah, a bastard of their family whom they had cast off, and agreed with him that if he would help them against the Ammonites, they would make him their ruler. This they do in these words: “And the people made him head and captain over them,” Judg. xi. 11 — which, it seems, was the same thing as being judge. “And he judged Israel,” Judg. xii. 7; that is, he was their captain-general for six years. So when Jotham reproaches the Shechemites with the debt they owed to Gideon, who had been their judge and ruler, he tells them, “He fought for you, and adventured his life far, and delivered you out of the hands of Midian,” Judg. ix. 17. Nothing is mentioned of him except what he did as a general; and indeed that is all that is found in his history, or in that of any of the other judges. And Abimelech in particular is called king, though at most he was only their general. And when the children of Israel, weary of the bad conduct of Samuel’s sons, wanted a king “like all the nations, to judge them, and to go out before them, and to fight their battles,” 1 Sam. viii. 20, God granted their desire and said to Samuel, “I will send thee a man, and thou shalt anoint him to be captain over my people Israel, that he may save my people out of the hands of the Philistines,” ix. 16. It is as if the only business of a king had been to lead out their armies and fight in their defence. Accordingly, at Saul’s inauguration, when a vial of oil was poured on him, God declares to Saul that the Lord had anointed him to be captain over his inheritance, x. 1. And so those who were unwilling to have Saul as their king, after he had been solemnly chosen and hailed as king by the tribes at Mispah, made no other objection than this: “How shall this man save us?” v. 27 — as if they had said, “This man is unfit to be our king; he does not have enough skill and leadership in war to be able to defend us.” And when God resolved to transfer the government to David, it is in these words: “But now thy kingdom shall not continue: the Lord hath sought him a man after his own heart, and the Lord hath commanded him to be captain over his people,” xiii. 14. It is as if the whole of kingly authority were nothing else than being their general. And so the tribes who had stuck to Saul’s family and opposed David’s reign, when they came to Hebron with terms of submission to him, told him, among the other arguments they had for submitting to him as their king, that he had in effect been their king in Saul’s time, and so they had every reason to receive him as their king now. “Also,” they say, “in time past, when Saul was king over us, thou wast he that reddest out and broughtest in Israel, and the Lord said unto thee, Thou shalt feed my people Israel, and thou shalt be a captain over Israel.”

So it may have been that a family grew up by degrees into a commonwealth. The fatherly authority was continued on to the elder son; everyone in his turn grew up under it and tacitly submitted to it; and since its ease and equality offended no one, everyone went along with it, until time seemed to have confirmed it and settled a right of succession by prescription. Or it may have been that several families, or the descendants of several families, whom chance, neighbourhood or business brought together, united into society. In that case the need for a general whose leadership might defend them against their enemies in war, together with the great confidence in one another that the innocence and sincerity of that poor but virtuous age gave men (and such are almost all the ages that begin governments which ever come to last in the world), made the first founders of commonwealths generally put the rule into one man’s hands, without any other express limitation or restraint than what the nature of the thing and the end of government required. Whichever of these it was that first put the rule into the hands of a single person, it is certain that nobody was entrusted with it except for the public good and safety, and that in the infancy of commonwealths those who held it commonly used it for those ends. And unless they had done so, young societies could not have survived. Without such nursing fathers, tender and careful of the public welfare, all governments would have sunk under the weakness and infirmities of their infancy, and the prince and the people would soon have perished together.

It is true that the golden age came before vain ambition, and amor sceleratus habendi — evil craving for possession — had corrupted men’s minds into a mistaken idea of true power and honour. That age had more virtue, and so better governors as well as less vicious subjects. There was then no stretching of prerogative on the one side to oppress the people, and so, on the other side, no dispute about privilege to lessen or restrain the power of the magistrate; and so there was no contest between rulers and people about governors or government. But in later ages* ambition and luxury wanted to keep and increase that power without doing the business for which it was given, and, aided by flattery, taught princes to have interests distinct and separate from those of their people. Then men found it necessary to examine more carefully the origin and rights of government, and to find ways to restrain the excesses and prevent the abuses of that power which they had entrusted to another’s hands only for their own good, and which they found was being used to hurt them.

(*“At first, when some particular kind of government was once approved, it may be that nothing further was then thought of concerning the manner of governing, but everything was left to the wisdom and discretion of those who were to rule. Then by experience they found this very inconvenient in every respect, so that the thing they had devised as a remedy in fact only increased the sore it should have cured. They saw that to live by one man’s will became the cause of all men’s misery. This forced them to come to laws, in which all men might see their duty beforehand and know the penalties for breaking them.” Hooker, Ecclesiastical Polity, book I, section 10.)

So we may see how probable it is that people who were naturally free, and who by their own consent either submitted to the government of their father or united together out of different families to make a government, should generally put the rule into one man’s hands and choose to be under the leadership of a single person. They did this without even limiting or regulating his power by express conditions, since they thought it safe enough in his honesty and prudence. Yet they never dreamed of monarchy being jure divino, which we never heard of among mankind until it was revealed to us by the theology of this last age. Nor did they ever allow paternal power to have a right to dominion, or to be the foundation of all government. And this may be enough to show that, as far as we have any light from history, we have reason to conclude that all peaceful beginnings of government have been laid in the consent of the people. I say peaceful, because I shall have occasion in another place to speak of conquest, which some regard as a way in which governments begin.
The other objection I find urged against the beginning of political societies in the way I have described is this, namely:

That since all men are born under some government or other, it is impossible that any of them should ever be free and at liberty to unite together and begin a new one, or ever be able to set up a lawful government.

If this argument is good, I ask: how did so many lawful monarchies come into the world? For if anyone, on this supposition, can show me a single man in any age of the world free to begin a lawful monarchy, I will undertake to show him ten other free men at liberty, at the same time, to unite and begin a new government under a regal or any other form. It is a demonstration: if anyone born under the dominion of another may be so free as to have a right to command others in a new and distinct empire, then everyone born under the dominion of another may be just as free, and may become a ruler, or a subject, of a distinct and separate government. So by this principle of their own, either all men, however they are born, are free, or else there is only one lawful prince, one lawful government, in the world. And then they have nothing to do but simply show us which that is. When they have done that, I do not doubt that all mankind will readily agree to obey him.

It would be a sufficient answer to their objection to show that it involves them in the same difficulties as it does those they use it against. Still, I shall try to expose the weakness of this argument a little further. All men, they say, are born under government, and therefore they cannot be at liberty to begin a new one. Everyone is born a subject to his father or his prince, and is therefore under the perpetual tie of subjection and allegiance. But it is plain that mankind never acknowledged or took account of any such natural subjection that they were born into, to the one or to the other, which bound them, without their own consent, to be subject to them and their heirs.

For there are no examples so frequent in history, both sacred and secular, as those of men withdrawing themselves and their obedience from the jurisdiction they were born under, and from the family or community they were brought up in, and setting up new governments in other places. From this sprang all those many petty commonwealths in the beginning of the ages. They kept multiplying as long as there was room enough, until the stronger or more fortunate swallowed up the weaker; and those great ones in turn broke to pieces and dissolved into smaller dominions. All this is so much testimony against paternal sovereignty. It plainly proves that it was not the natural right of the father, descending to his heirs, that made governments in the beginning. On that basis there could not possibly have been so many little kingdoms. There would have been nothing but one universal monarchy, if men had not been at liberty to separate themselves from their families, and from whatever government was set up in them, and to go and make distinct commonwealths and other governments as they thought fit.

This has been the practice of the world from its very beginning to this day. Nor is it now any more a hindrance to the freedom of mankind that they are born under constituted and ancient states, which have established laws and settled forms of government, than if they were born in the woods, among the unconfined inhabitants who run loose there. Those who would persuade us that by being born under any government we are naturally its subjects, and no longer have any title or claim to the freedom of the state of nature, have no other reason to offer for it (apart from paternal power, which we have already answered) than this: that our fathers or ancestors gave away their natural liberty, and so bound themselves and their descendants to perpetual subjection to the government they themselves submitted to. It is true that whatever engagements or promises anyone has made for himself, he is under the obligation of them. But he cannot, by any compact whatever, bind his children or descendants. For his son, when he is a man, is altogether as free as the father, and no act of the father can give away the son’s liberty any more than it can anyone else’s. The father may indeed attach such conditions to the land he enjoyed as a subject of a commonwealth as may oblige his son to be of that community, if the son wants to enjoy the possessions that were his father’s. For since that estate is the father’s property, he may dispose of it or settle it as he pleases.

And this has generally been what led people into mistakes on this matter. Commonwealths do not allow any part of their dominions to be broken off, or to be enjoyed by anyone but members of their community. So the son cannot ordinarily enjoy his father’s possessions except on the same terms as his father did, by becoming a member of the society. By doing so he immediately puts himself under the government he finds established there, as much as any other subject of that commonwealth. And so the consent of free men born under government, which alone makes them members of it, is given separately, each in his turn as he comes of age, and not by a multitude together. People therefore take no notice of it; and thinking that it is not done at all, or is not necessary, they conclude that they are subjects by nature, just as they are men.

But it is plain that governments themselves understand it otherwise. They claim no power over the son because of the power they had over the father, and they do not regard children as their subjects just because their fathers are. If a subject of England has a child by an English woman in France, whose subject is he? Not the king of England’s, for he must have permission to be admitted to its privileges. Nor the king of France’s, for in that case how does his father have the liberty to bring him away and raise him as he pleases? And who was ever judged a traitor or deserter for leaving, or making war against, a country merely because he was born in it of parents who were foreigners there? It is plain, then, both from the practice of governments themselves and from the law of right reason, that a child is born a subject of no country or government. He is under his father’s care and authority until he reaches the age of discretion; and then he is a free man, at liberty to choose what government he will put himself under, and what body politic he will unite himself to. For if an Englishman’s son born in France is at liberty to do so, it is evident that no tie is laid on him by his father’s being a subject of this kingdom, and that he is not bound by any compact of his ancestors. Why, then, should his son not have the same liberty for the same reason, though he is born somewhere else? For the power a father naturally has over his children is the same wherever they are born, and the ties of natural obligation are not bounded by the positive limits of kingdoms and commonwealths.

Every man, as has been shown, is naturally free, and nothing can put him into subjection to any earthly power except his own consent. So we must consider what is to be understood as a sufficient declaration of a man’s consent to make him subject to the laws of any government. There is a common distinction between an express and a tacit consent, which bears on our present case. Nobody doubts that the express consent of any man entering into a society makes him a full member of that society and a subject of that government. The difficulty is what ought to count as a tacit consent, and how far it binds — that is, how far anyone is to be regarded as having consented, and so submitted to any government, where he has given no expression of it at all. And to this I say that every man who has any possessions in, or enjoyment of, any part of the dominions of any government gives his tacit consent by doing so. To that extent he is as much obliged to obey the laws of that government, for as long as that enjoyment lasts, as anyone under it. This holds whether his possession is of land, to him and his heirs for ever, or a lodging only for a week, or whether it is simply travelling freely on the highway. In effect it reaches as far as the mere presence of anyone within the territories of that government.

To understand this better, we should consider that every man, when he first incorporates himself into any commonwealth, by uniting himself to it also annexes and submits to the community whatever possessions he has or shall acquire that do not already belong to some other government. For it would be a direct contradiction for anyone to enter into society with others for the securing and regulating of property, and yet to suppose that his land, whose property is to be regulated by the laws of the society, should be exempt from the jurisdiction of the government to which he himself, the owner of the land, is a subject. By the same act, therefore, by which anyone unites his person, which was free before, to any commonwealth, he unites to it his possessions too, which were free before. Both of them, person and possession, become subject to the government and dominion of that commonwealth for as long as it exists. From then on, therefore, whoever enjoys any part of the land so annexed to and under the government of that commonwealth — by inheritance, purchase, permission or otherwise — must take it with the condition it is under: that is, of submitting to the government of the commonwealth under whose jurisdiction it lies, as fully as any subject of it.

But the government has direct jurisdiction only over the land, and it reaches the possessor of the land (before he has actually incorporated himself into the society) only as he lives on it and enjoys it. So the obligation anyone is under to submit to the government by virtue of such enjoyment begins and ends with the enjoyment. Whenever the owner, who has given nothing but such a tacit consent to the government, gives up that possession by gift, sale or otherwise, he is at liberty to go and incorporate himself into any other commonwealth, or to agree with others to begin a new one, in vacuis locis — in any part of the world they can find free and unoccupied. By contrast, whoever has once given his consent to be of any commonwealth by actual agreement and some express declaration is perpetually and indispensably obliged to be, and to remain, unalterably its subject. He can never again be in the liberty of the state of nature — unless some calamity dissolves the government he was under, or else some public act cuts him off from being a member of it any longer.

But submitting to the laws of a country, living quietly and enjoying privileges and protection under them, does not make a man a member of that society. This is only the local protection and homage that is due to and from all those who, not being in a state of war, come within the territories belonging to any government, to every part of which the force of its laws extends. But this no more makes a man a member of that society, a perpetual subject of that commonwealth, than it would make a man a subject of someone in whose family he found it convenient to stay for some time — though while he stayed there he was obliged to comply with the laws and submit to the government he found there. And so we see that foreigners who live all their lives under another government and enjoy its privileges and protection are bound, even in conscience, to submit to its administration as fully as any denizen; yet they do not by that become subjects or members of that commonwealth. Nothing can make any man so except actually entering into it by positive engagement and by express promise and compact. This is what I think concerning the beginning of political societies, and the consent that makes anyone a member of any commonwealth.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 — Of the Ends of Political Society and Government
paragraphs: If man in the state of nature is as free as has been said — if he is absolute lord of his own person and possessions, equal to the greatest, and subject to nobody — why will he part with his freedom? Why will he give up this empire and subject himself to the dominion and control of any other power? The obvious answer is that, though in the state of nature he has such a right, the enjoyment of it is very uncertain and constantly exposed to invasion by others. For since all are kings as much as he is, every man his equal, and the greater part of them no strict observers of fairness and justice, his enjoyment of the property he has in this state is very unsafe, very insecure. This makes him willing to leave a condition which, however free, is full of fears and continual dangers. And it is not without reason that he seeks out, and is willing to join in society with, others who are already united, or have a mind to unite, for the mutual preservation of their lives, liberties and estates, which I call by the general name, property.

The great and chief end, therefore, of men’s uniting into commonwealths and putting themselves under government is the preservation of their property. For that purpose many things are lacking in the state of nature.

First, there is lacking an established, settled, known law, received and accepted by common consent as the standard of right and wrong and the common measure for deciding all disputes between them. For though the law of nature is plain and intelligible to all rational creatures, men are biased by their interest, as well as ignorant of it for lack of studying it. So they are not inclined to accept it as a law binding on them when it comes to applying it to their own particular cases.

Secondly, in the state of nature there is lacking a known and impartial judge, with authority to settle all differences according to the established law. For everyone in that state is both judge and executioner of the law of nature. And since men are partial to themselves, passion and revenge are very apt to carry them too far, and with too much heat, in their own cases, just as negligence and lack of concern are apt to make them too slack in other men’s.

Thirdly, in the state of nature there is often lacking the power to back and support a sentence when it is right, and to carry it out properly. Those who have offended by some injustice will seldom fail, where they are able, to make good their injustice by force. Such resistance often makes the punishment dangerous, and frequently destructive, to those who attempt it.

So mankind, despite all the privileges of the state of nature, are in a poor condition while they remain in it, and are quickly driven into society. That is why we seldom find any number of men living together for any length of time in this state. The inconveniences they are exposed to in it, through the irregular and uncertain exercise of the power every man has of punishing the transgressions of others, make them take refuge under the established laws of government, and seek the preservation of their property there. It is this that makes them so willing each to give up his single power of punishing, to be exercised only by those who shall be appointed to it among them, and by such rules as the community, or those authorized by it for that purpose, shall agree on. And here we have the original right and rise of both the legislative and the executive power, as well as of governments and societies themselves.
For in the state of nature, leaving aside his liberty to enjoy innocent pleasures, a man has two powers.

The first is to do whatever he thinks fit for the preservation of himself and others, within the permission of the law of nature. By this law, which is common to them all, he and all the rest of mankind are one community and make up one society, distinct from all other creatures. And were it not for the corruption and viciousness of degenerate men, there would be no need of any other society — no necessity for men to separate from this great and natural community and combine by positive agreements into smaller and divided associations.

The other power a man has in the state of nature is the power to punish the crimes committed against that law. He gives up both of these when he joins a private — if I may call it that — or particular political society, and incorporates into any commonwealth separate from the rest of mankind.

The first power, namely of doing whatever he thought fit for the preservation of himself and the rest of mankind, he gives up to be regulated by laws made by the society, as far as the preservation of himself and the rest of that society shall require. And these laws of the society in many things restrict the liberty he had by the law of nature.

Secondly, he gives up the power of punishing entirely. He commits his natural force — which before he could use as he thought fit, by his own single authority, in executing the law of nature — to assist the executive power of the society, as its law shall require. For he is now in a new state, in which he is to enjoy many advantages from the labour, help and company of others in the same community, as well as protection from its whole strength. So he must also part with as much of his natural liberty in providing for himself as the good, prosperity and safety of the society shall require. This is not only necessary but just, since the other members of the society do the same.

But when men enter into society, they give up the equality, liberty and executive power they had in the state of nature into the hands of the society, to be disposed of by the legislative as far as the good of the society shall require. Yet each of them does this only with the intention of better preserving himself, his liberty and property — for no rational creature can be supposed to change his condition intending to be worse off. So the power of the society, or of the legislative constituted by them, can never be supposed to extend further than the common good. It is obliged to secure everyone’s property by providing against the three defects mentioned above, which made the state of nature so unsafe and uneasy. And so whoever has the legislative or supreme power of any commonwealth is bound to govern by established standing laws, promulgated and known to the people, and not by improvised decrees; by impartial and upright judges, who are to decide disputes by those laws; and to use the force of the community at home only in the execution of such laws, or abroad to prevent or redress foreign injuries and to secure the community from raids and invasion. And all this is to be directed to no other end than the peace, safety and public good of the people.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 — Of the Forms of a Commonwealth
