paragraphs: The majority, as has been shown, have the whole power of the community naturally in them when men first unite into society. They may use all that power in making laws for the community from time to time, and in executing those laws through officers of their own appointing; and then the form of the government is a perfect democracy. Or else they may put the power of making laws into the hands of a few select men and their heirs or successors; and then it is an oligarchy. Or else they may put it into the hands of one man; and then it is a monarchy. If to him and his heirs, it is a hereditary monarchy. If to him only for life, with only the power of nominating a successor returning to them at his death, it is an elective monarchy. And accordingly, out of these forms the community may make compound and mixed forms of government, as they think good. And if the majority at first give the legislative power to one or more persons only for their lives, or for some limited time, after which the supreme power is to revert to them again, then once it has reverted the community may dispose of it anew into whatever hands they please, and so constitute a new form of government. For the form of government depends on where the supreme power, which is the legislative, is placed. It is impossible to conceive that an inferior power should give orders to a superior one, or that any but the supreme power should make laws. So the form of the commonwealth is whatever the placing of the power of making laws makes it.

By “commonwealth” I must be understood all along to mean not a democracy, or any form of government, but any independent community — what the Latins signified by the word civitas. The word in our language that best answers to it is “commonwealth,” which most properly expresses such a society of men; “community” or “city” in English does not. For there may be subordinate communities within a government, and “city” among us has a quite different meaning from “commonwealth.” And therefore, to avoid ambiguity, I ask leave to use the word “commonwealth” in the sense in which I find it used by King James the First, which I take to be its genuine meaning. If anybody dislikes it, I agree with him to change it for a better one.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 — Of the Extent of the Legislative Power
paragraphs: The great end of men’s entering into society is the enjoyment of their properties in peace and safety, and the great instrument and means of that is the laws established in that society. So the first and fundamental positive law of all commonwealths is the establishing of the legislative power — just as the first and fundamental natural law, which is to govern even the legislative itself, is the preservation of the society and (as far as is consistent with the public good) of every person in it. This legislative is not only the supreme power of the commonwealth, but sacred and unalterable in the hands where the community have once placed it. Nor can any edict of anyone else, in whatever form it is conceived or by whatever power it is backed, have the force and obligation of a law, if it does not have its sanction from the legislative which the public has chosen and appointed. For without this the law could not have what is absolutely necessary to its being a law:* the consent of the society, over which nobody can have a power to make laws except by their own consent and by authority received from them. And therefore all the obedience that anyone can be obliged to pay, even by the most solemn ties, ultimately ends in this supreme power and is directed by the laws it enacts. Nor can any oaths to any foreign power whatever, or to any subordinate power at home, release any member of the society from his obedience to the legislative when it acts in accordance with its trust; nor can they oblige him to any obedience contrary to the laws so enacted, or beyond what those laws allow. For it is ridiculous to imagine that anyone can be bound ultimately to obey any power in the society which is not the supreme.

(*“The lawful power of making laws to command whole political societies of men belongs so properly to those same entire societies that for any prince or potentate of any kind whatever on earth to exercise it by himself — and not by express commission immediately and personally received from God, or else by authority derived at first from the consent of those on whose persons they impose laws — is no better than mere tyranny. Therefore laws which public approval has not made so are not laws.” Hooker, Ecclesiastical Polity, book I, section 10.

“On this point, therefore, we are to note that since men naturally have no full and perfect power to command whole political multitudes of men, it follows that utterly without our consent we could not in that way be at the command of any man living. And we do consent to be commanded when the society of which we are a part has at any time before consented, without afterwards revoking it by a like universal agreement. Human laws, therefore, of whatever kind, are valid by consent.” Ibid.)
Though the legislative — whether it is placed in one person or in more, and whether it is always in being or only at intervals — is the supreme power in every commonwealth, yet:

First, it is not, and cannot possibly be, absolutely arbitrary over the lives and fortunes of the people. For it is only the joint power of every member of the society, given up to the person or assembly that is legislator, and so it can be no more than those persons had in a state of nature before they entered into society and gave it up to the community. Nobody can transfer to another more power than he has in himself; and nobody has an absolute arbitrary power over himself, or over any other, to destroy his own life or to take away the life or property of another. A man, as has been proved, cannot subject himself to the arbitrary power of another. And since in the state of nature he has no arbitrary power over the life, liberty or possessions of another, but only as much as the law of nature gave him for the preservation of himself and the rest of mankind, this is all he does or can give up to the commonwealth, and through it to the legislative power. So the legislative can have no more than this. Their power, at its utmost bounds, is limited to the public good of the society. It is a power that has no other end but preservation, and therefore it can never have a right to destroy, enslave, or deliberately impoverish the subjects.* The obligations of the law of nature do not cease in society; in many cases they are only drawn closer, and human laws attach known penalties to them to enforce their observance. So the law of nature stands as an eternal rule to all men, legislators as well as others. The rules they make for other men’s actions must, like their own actions and other men’s, conform to the law of nature — that is, to the will of God, of which it is a declaration. And since the fundamental law of nature is the preservation of mankind, no human sanction can be good or valid against it.

(*“There are two foundations which bear up public societies: the one, a natural inclination, by which all men desire a sociable life and fellowship; the other, an order, expressly or secretly agreed on, concerning the manner of their union in living together. The latter is what we call the law of a commonwealth, the very soul of a political body, whose parts are given life by law, held together, and set to work in such actions as the common good requires. Political laws, ordained for outward order and government among men, are never framed as they should be unless they presume that the will of man is inwardly obstinate, rebellious, and averse to all obedience to the sacred laws of his nature. In a word, unless they presume that man, in respect of his depraved mind, is little better than a wild beast, and nevertheless provide accordingly to frame his outward actions so that they are no hindrance to the common good for which societies are instituted — unless they do this, they are not perfect.” Hooker, Ecclesiastical Polity, book I, section 10.)

Secondly, the legislative, or supreme authority, cannot take to itself a power to rule by improvised, arbitrary decrees. It is bound to dispense justice and decide the rights of the subject by promulgated standing laws and known, authorized judges.* For the law of nature is unwritten, and so is nowhere to be found except in the minds of men. So those who, through passion or interest, misquote or misapply it cannot so easily be convinced of their mistake where there is no established judge. In that case it does not serve, as it ought, to determine the rights and fence in the properties of those who live under it — especially where everyone is judge, interpreter and executioner of it too, and that in his own case. And he who has right on his side ordinarily has only his own single strength, and so does not have force enough to defend himself from injuries or to punish offenders. To avoid these inconveniences, which disorder men’s properties in the state of nature, men unite into societies, so that they may have the united strength of the whole society to secure and defend their properties, and may have standing rules to set its bounds, by which everyone may know what is his. It is for this purpose that men give up all their natural power to the society they enter, and that the community puts the legislative power into such hands as they think fit — with this trust, that they shall be governed by declared laws. Otherwise their peace, quiet and property will still be as uncertain as they were in the state of nature.

(*“Human laws are measures in respect of men whose actions they must direct; yet they are such measures as also have their higher rules to be measured by. These rules are two: the law of God and the law of nature. So human laws must be made according to the general laws of nature, and without contradicting any positive law of Scripture; otherwise they are badly made.” Hooker, Ecclesiastical Polity, book III, section 9.
“To force men to do anything inconvenient does seem unreasonable.” Ibid., book I, section 10.)

Absolute arbitrary power, and governing without settled standing laws, are neither of them consistent with the ends of society and government. Men would not give up the freedom of the state of nature for these ends, and bind themselves under government, were it not to preserve their lives, liberties and fortunes, and to secure their peace and quiet by stated rules of right and property. It cannot be supposed that they would intend, even if they had the power to do so, to give anyone, one or more, an absolute arbitrary power over their persons and estates, and to put a force into the magistrate’s hand to carry out his unlimited will arbitrarily upon them. That would be to put themselves into a worse condition than the state of nature, in which they had a liberty to defend their right against the injuries of others, and were on equal terms of force to maintain it, whether it was invaded by a single man or by many in combination. Whereas, if we suppose they have given themselves up to the absolute arbitrary power and will of a legislator, they have disarmed themselves and armed him, to make a prey of them whenever he pleases. For a man who is exposed to the arbitrary power of one man who commands 100,000 is in a much worse condition than one who is exposed to the arbitrary power of 100,000 separate men. Nobody can be sure that the will of the man who has such command is better than that of other men, though his force is 100,000 times stronger. And therefore, whatever form the commonwealth is under, the ruling power ought to govern by declared and received laws, and not by improvised dictates and undetermined resolutions. For mankind will be in a far worse condition than in the state of nature if they have armed one man, or a few, with the joint power of a multitude, to force them to obey at pleasure the exorbitant and unlimited decrees of their sudden thoughts, or their unrestrained and, until that moment, unknown wills, without any measures set down which may guide and justify their actions. For all the power the government has is only for the good of the society. So, just as it ought not to be arbitrary and at pleasure, it ought to be exercised by established and promulgated laws. In that way the people may know their duty and be safe and secure within the limits of the law; and the rulers too may be kept within their bounds, and not be tempted, by the power they have in their hands, to use it for such purposes, and by such measures, as they would not have known and would not willingly own.

Thirdly, the supreme power cannot take from any man any part of his property without his own consent. For the preservation of property is the end of government, and that for which men enter into society. This necessarily supposes and requires that the people should have property; otherwise they must be supposed to lose, by entering into society, the very thing that was the end for which they entered into it — too gross an absurdity for any man to accept. Men in society, therefore, having property, have such a right to the goods which by the law of the community are theirs that nobody has a right to take their substance, or any part of it, from them without their own consent. Without this they have no property at all. For I truly have no property in what another can by right take from me whenever he pleases, against my consent. So it is a mistake to think that the supreme or legislative power of any commonwealth can do what it will, and dispose of the estates of the subject arbitrarily, or take any part of them at pleasure. This is not much to be feared in governments where the legislative consists, wholly or in part, of assemblies which change, whose members, when the assembly is dissolved, are subjects under the common laws of their country, equally with the rest. But in governments where the legislative is one lasting assembly always in being, or one man, as in absolute monarchies, there is still a danger that they will think they have an interest distinct from the rest of the community, and so will be inclined to increase their own riches and power by taking what they think fit from the people. For a man’s property is not at all secure, even though there are good and fair laws to set its bounds between him and his fellow subjects, if the one who commands those subjects has power to take from any private man whatever part of his property he pleases, and to use and dispose of it as he thinks good.

But government, into whatever hands it is put, is entrusted, as I have shown before, on this condition and for this end: that men might have and secure their properties. So the prince or senate, however much power it may have to make laws for regulating property among the subjects, can never have a power to take to itself the whole, or any part, of the subjects’ property without their own consent; for this would in effect leave them no property at all. And to see that even absolute power, where it is necessary, is not arbitrary just because it is absolute, but is still limited by the reason, and confined to the ends, that required it to be absolute in some cases, we need look no further than the common practice of military discipline. The preservation of the army, and through it of the whole commonwealth, requires absolute obedience to the command of every superior officer, and it is justly death to disobey or dispute even the most dangerous or unreasonable of their commands. Yet we see that the sergeant, who could command a soldier to march up to the mouth of a cannon, or to stand in a breach where he is almost sure to die, cannot command that soldier to give him one penny of his money. Nor can the general, who can condemn him to death for deserting his post or for not obeying the most desperate orders, dispose of one farthing of that soldier’s estate, or seize one jot of his goods, with all his absolute power of life and death — though he can command him to do anything, and hang him for the least disobedience. For such blind obedience is necessary to the end for which the commander has his power, namely the preservation of the rest; but disposing of the soldier’s goods has nothing to do with that end.

It is true that governments cannot be supported without great expense, and it is right that everyone who enjoys his share of the protection should pay his proportion toward its maintenance out of his estate. But it must still be with his own consent — that is, the consent of the majority, given either by themselves or by representatives they have chosen. For if anyone claims a power to lay and levy taxes on the people by his own authority, and without such consent of the people, he thereby invades the fundamental law of property and subverts the end of government. For what property have I in something that another may by right take for himself whenever he pleases?

Fourthly, the legislative cannot transfer the power of making laws to any other hands. For since it is only a power delegated from the people, those who have it cannot pass it over to others. The people alone can appoint the form of the commonwealth, which they do by constituting the legislative and appointing in whose hands it shall be. And when the people have said, “We will submit to rules and be governed by laws made by such men, and in such forms,” nobody else can say that other men shall make laws for them. Nor can the people be bound by any laws except those enacted by the men they have chosen and authorized to make laws for them. The power of the legislative is derived from the people by a positive, voluntary grant and institution, and so it can be no other than what that positive grant conveyed. That grant was only to make laws, not to make legislators. So the legislative can have no power to transfer its authority of making laws and place it in other hands.

These, then, are the bounds that the trust placed in them by the society, together with the law of God and of nature, have set to the legislative power of every commonwealth, under all forms of government.

First, they are to govern by promulgated, established laws, which are not to be varied in particular cases, but are to have one rule for rich and poor, for the favourite at court and the countryman at the plough.
Secondly, these laws ought also to be designed, ultimately, for no other end than the good of the people.

Thirdly, they must not raise taxes on the property of the people without the consent of the people, given by themselves or by their deputies. And strictly speaking, this concerns only governments where the legislative is always in being, or at least where the people have not reserved any part of the legislative to deputies whom they themselves choose from time to time.
Fourthly, the legislative neither must nor can transfer the power of making laws to anybody else, or place it anywhere but where the people have placed it.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 — Of the Legislative, Executive, and Federative Power of the Commonwealth
paragraphs: The legislative power is the power that has a right to direct how the force of the commonwealth is to be used for preserving the community and its members. But the laws that are to be constantly executed, and whose force is to continue permanently, can be made in a short time. So there is no need for the legislative to be always in being, since it does not always have business to do. There is a further reason. It may be too great a temptation to human frailty, which is apt to grasp at power, for the same persons who have the power of making laws also to have in their hands the power of executing them. They could then exempt themselves from obedience to the laws they make, and shape the law, both in making it and in executing it, to their own private advantage. In that way they would come to have an interest distinct from that of the rest of the community, which is contrary to the end of society and government. Therefore, in well-ordered commonwealths, where the good of the whole is given the consideration it ought to have, the legislative power is put into the hands of a number of different persons. When duly assembled, they have, by themselves or jointly with others, a power to make laws; and once they have made them, they separate again and are themselves subject to the laws they have made. This is a new and close tie on them to take care that they make those laws for the public good.

But the laws that are made at once, and in a short time, have a constant and lasting force, and they need to be executed perpetually, or attended to. So it is necessary that there should be a power always in being to see to the execution of the laws that have been made and remain in force. And that is how the legislative and executive power often come to be separated.

There is another power in every commonwealth, which one might call natural, because it corresponds to the power every man naturally had before he entered into society. In a commonwealth the members are still distinct persons in relation to one another, and as such they are governed by the laws of the society. But in relation to the rest of mankind they make up one body, and that body is still in the state of nature with the rest of mankind, just as each of its members was before. That is why controversies that arise between any member of the society and those outside it are handled by the public, and why an injury done to one member of their body engages the whole body in obtaining reparation for it. So, seen in this light, the whole community is one body in the state of nature with respect to all other states or persons outside it.

This power, then, contains the power of war and peace, of leagues and alliances, and of all dealings with persons and communities outside the commonwealth. It may be called federative, if anyone likes. As long as the thing itself is understood, I do not mind what name it goes by.

These two powers, executive and federative, are really distinct in themselves. The one covers the execution of the society’s municipal laws within itself, upon all who are part of it; the other covers the management of the security and interest of the public abroad, in dealings with all those from whom it may receive benefit or damage. Yet they are almost always united. The federative power, well or badly managed, is of great importance to the commonwealth. Even so, it is much less capable than the executive of being directed by antecedent, standing, positive laws, and so it must necessarily be left to the prudence and wisdom of those in whose hands it lies, to be managed for the public good. The reason is this. The laws that concern subjects in their dealings with one another are meant to direct their actions, and so they can well enough come before those actions. But what is to be done in relation to foreigners depends a great deal on what they do, and on shifts in their designs and interests. So it must be left in great part to the prudence of those to whom this power has been committed, to be managed as skilfully as they can for the advantage of the commonwealth.

Though, as I said, the executive and federative power of every community are really distinct in themselves, they can hardly be separated and placed at the same time in the hands of different persons. Both of them require the force of the society to be exercised, and it is almost impracticable to place the force of the commonwealth in separate hands that are not subordinate to one another, or to put the executive and federative power in persons who might act separately. In that case the force of the public would be under different commands, which would be likely, sooner or later, to cause disorder and ruin.

chapters.title: Chapter 13 — Of the Subordination of the Powers of the Commonwealth
paragraphs: In a constituted commonwealth, standing on its own basis and acting according to its own nature, that is, acting for the preservation of the community, there can be only one supreme power. That is the legislative, to which all the rest are and must be subordinate. Yet the legislative is only a fiduciary power to act for certain ends. So there still remains in the people a supreme power to remove or alter the legislative when they find it acting contrary to the trust placed in it. For all power given in trust for achieving an end is limited by that end. Whenever that end is plainly neglected or opposed, the trust must necessarily be forfeited, and the power returns into the hands of those who gave it, who may place it anew wherever they think best for their safety and security. In this way the community perpetually keeps a supreme power of saving itself from the attempts and designs of anybody, even of its own legislators, whenever they are so foolish or so wicked as to form and carry out designs against the liberties and properties of the subject. No man or society of men has a power to hand over their own preservation, or consequently the means of it, to the absolute will and arbitrary dominion of another. So whenever anyone sets out to bring them into such a slavish condition, they will always have a right to preserve what they have no power to part with, and to rid themselves of those who invade this fundamental, sacred, and unalterable law of self-preservation, for the sake of which they entered into society. In this respect, then, the community may be said to be always the supreme power, but not when it is considered under any form of government, because this power of the people can never come into play until the government is dissolved.

In all cases, while the government lasts, the legislative is the supreme power. Whatever can give laws to another must necessarily be superior to him. And the legislative is the legislative of the society only because of the right it has to make laws for all its parts and for every one of its members, prescribing rules for their actions and giving power to execute those rules where they are broken. So the legislative must necessarily be the supreme power, and all other powers, in any members or parts of the society, are derived from it and subordinate to it.

In some commonwealths the legislative is not always in being, and the executive is vested in a single person who also has a share in the legislative. There that single person may, in a quite tolerable sense, also be called supreme. This is not because he has in himself all the supreme power, which is the power of making laws. It is because he holds the supreme execution, from which all inferior magistrates derive their various subordinate powers, or at least most of them. He also has no legislative superior to him, since no law can be made without his consent, and he cannot be expected ever to consent to one that would subject him to the other part of the legislative. So in this sense he is properly enough called supreme. But it should still be noted that, although oaths of allegiance and fealty are taken to him, they are taken to him not as supreme legislator but as supreme executor of the law, a law made by him jointly with others. Allegiance is nothing but obedience according to law. So when he violates the law, he has no right to obedience, and he cannot claim it except as the public person vested with the power of the law. He is therefore to be considered as the image, phantom, or representative of the commonwealth, moved by the will of the society as declared in its laws; and so he has no will and no power but that of the law. But when he abandons this representation, this public will, and acts by his own private will, he degrades himself. He is then only a single private person, without power and without any will that has a right to obedience, since the members owe obedience only to the public will of the society.

The executive power, when it is placed anywhere other than in a person who also has a share in the legislative, is plainly subordinate and accountable to the legislative, and may be changed and displaced at its pleasure. So it is not the supreme executive power as such that is exempt from subordination. It is the supreme executive power vested in one person who, having a share in the legislative, has no distinct superior legislative to be subordinate and accountable to, except as far as he himself chooses to join and consent. He is therefore no more subordinate than he himself thinks fit, which, one may safely conclude, will be very little indeed. Of the other ministerial and subordinate powers in a commonwealth we need not speak. They are multiplied in endless variety by the different customs and constitutions of different commonwealths, so it is impossible to give a detailed account of them all. We need only note this much about them, which is necessary for our present purpose: none of them has any kind of authority beyond what has been delegated to it by positive grant and commission, and all of them are accountable to some other power in the commonwealth.

It is not necessary, and not even convenient, for the legislative to be always in being. But it is absolutely necessary for the executive power to be, because there is not always a need for new laws to be made, but there is always a need for the laws already made to be executed. When the legislative has put the execution of the laws they make into other hands, they still have the power to take it back out of those hands when they find cause, and to punish any maladministration against the laws. The same holds for the federative power, since it and the executive are both ministerial and subordinate to the legislative, which, as has been shown, is supreme in a constituted commonwealth. In this case the legislative is also supposed to consist of several persons. (If it is a single person, it cannot help being always in being, and so, as supreme, will naturally have the supreme executive power together with the legislative.) These persons may assemble and exercise their legislative power at the times appointed either by their original constitution or by their own adjournment; or, if neither of these has appointed any time and no other way of convening them has been prescribed, whenever they please. For the supreme power was placed in them by the people, so it is always in them, and they may exercise it when they please, unless their original constitution limits them to certain seasons, or they have adjourned to a certain time by an act of their supreme power; and when that time comes, they have a right to assemble and act again.

Suppose the legislative, or any part of it, is made up of representatives chosen for that time by the people, who afterwards return to the ordinary condition of subjects and have no share in the legislative unless they are chosen again. Then this power of choosing must also be exercised by the people, either at certain appointed times or else when they are summoned to it. In the latter case the power of convening the legislative is ordinarily placed in the executive, and it is subject to one of two limitations as regards time. Either the original constitution requires the legislative to assemble and act at certain intervals, and then the executive power does nothing but issue directions, in a purely ministerial way, for their election and assembly according to the proper forms. Or else it is left to his prudence to call them by new elections when the occasions or emergencies of the public require old laws to be amended or new ones made, or require the remedy or prevention of any inconveniences that burden or threaten the people.

It may be asked here: what if the executive power, having possession of the force of the commonwealth, uses that force to hinder the meeting and acting of the legislative when the original constitution or the public emergencies require it? I say that using force on the people without authority, and contrary to the trust placed in whoever does so, is a state of war with the people, and they have a right to restore their legislative to the exercise of its power. They set up a legislative intending it to exercise the power of making laws, either at certain fixed times or when there is need of it. So when it is hindered by any force from doing what is so necessary to the society, and on which the safety and preservation of the people depend, the people have a right to remove that force by force. In all states and conditions, the true remedy for force without authority is to oppose force to it. The use of force without authority always puts the one who uses it into a state of war, as the aggressor, and makes him liable to be treated accordingly.

The power of assembling and dismissing the legislative, when it is placed in the executive, does not give the executive a superiority over the legislative. It is a fiduciary trust placed in him for the safety of the people, in a case where the uncertainty and changeableness of human affairs could not bear a steady, fixed rule. The first framers of the government could not, by any foresight, be such masters of future events as to fix in advance periods for the return and duration of the legislative’s assemblies so exactly that they would meet all the needs of the commonwealth in all times to come. So the best remedy that could be found for this defect was to entrust the matter to the prudence of someone who was always to be present and whose business it was to watch over the public good. Constant, frequent meetings of the legislative, and long continuations of their assemblies without necessary occasion, could only be burdensome to the people, and in time would necessarily produce more dangerous inconveniences. And yet the quick turn of affairs might sometimes be such as to need their immediate help. Any delay in their convening might endanger the public; and sometimes, too, their business might be so great that the limited time of their sitting would be too short for their work, and would rob the public of the benefit that could come only from their mature deliberation. What else, then, could be done in this case to prevent the community from being exposed, sooner or later, to imminent danger on one side or the other by fixed intervals and periods set for the meeting and acting of the legislative? Only to entrust it to the prudence of some who, being present and acquainted with the state of public affairs, might make use of this prerogative for the public good. And where else could it be so well placed as in the hands of the one who was entrusted with the execution of the laws for the same end? So, supposing the regulation of times for the assembling and sitting of the legislative was not settled by the original constitution, it naturally fell into the hands of the executive. It did so not as an arbitrary power depending on his good pleasure, but with this trust: that it should always be exercised only for the public good, as the occurrences of the times and changes of affairs might require. Whether settled periods for their convening, or a liberty left to the prince to convene the legislative, or perhaps a mixture of both, carries the fewest inconveniences with it is not my business to inquire here. I only want to show that, although the executive power may have the prerogative of convening and dissolving such meetings of the legislative, it is not thereby superior to it.

The things of this world are in such constant flux that nothing stays long in the same state. So population, riches, trade, and power shift from place to place. Mighty, flourishing cities fall into ruin and in time become neglected, desolate corners, while other places that nobody used to visit grow into populous regions, filled with wealth and inhabitants. But things do not always change evenly, and private interest often keeps customs and privileges alive after the reasons for them have ceased. So it often happens that in governments where part of the legislative consists of representatives chosen by the people, this representation becomes, in the course of time, very unequal and out of proportion to the reasons on which it was first established. We can see how gross the absurdities are to which following custom may lead, once reason has left it, when we see the mere name of a town, of which not even the ruins remain, where there is scarcely so much housing as a sheepfold, or more inhabitants than a shepherd, sending as many representatives to the great assembly of lawmakers as a whole county, numerous in people and powerful in riches. Strangers are amazed at this, and everyone must admit that it needs a remedy. Yet most people think a remedy hard to find. The constitution of the legislative is the original and supreme act of the society, prior to all positive laws in it, and it depends wholly on the people, so no inferior power can alter it. And in the kind of government we have been speaking of, the people, once the legislative has been constituted, have no power to act as long as the government stands. So this inconvenience is thought to be beyond remedy.

Salus populi suprema lex is certainly so just and fundamental a rule that anyone who sincerely follows it cannot go dangerously wrong. So suppose the executive, who has the power of convening the legislative, attends to the true proportion of representation rather than its customary form, and regulates the number of members by true reason rather than old custom, in all places that have a right to be separately represented. No part of the people, however incorporated, can claim such a right except in proportion to the assistance it gives to the public. In that case the executive cannot be judged to have set up a new legislative. It has restored the old and true one, and corrected the disorders that the passage of time had introduced, imperceptibly as well as inevitably. For it is the interest as well as the intention of the people to have a fair and equal representative body, and whoever brings it closest to that is an undoubted friend of the government and one who establishes it, and cannot fail to have the consent and approval of the community. Prerogative is nothing but a power in the hands of the prince to provide for the public good in cases that depend on unforeseen and uncertain occurrences, which fixed and unalterable laws could not safely direct. So whatever is done plainly for the good of the people, and for establishing the government on its true foundations, is, and always will be, just prerogative. The power of creating new corporations, and with them new representatives, carries with it the assumption that the measures of representation might change over time: that places which had no right to be represented before may come to have a just right to it, and, by the same reasoning, that places which had it before may cease to have a right to it and become too insignificant for such a privilege. What makes an inroad on the government is not a change from the present state of things, which corruption or decay has perhaps introduced, but a change’s tendency to injure or oppress the people, and to set up one part or party with a distinction from the rest, and an unequal subjection of the rest. Whatever cannot but be acknowledged to benefit the society and the people in general, on just and lasting measures, will always justify itself once it is done. And whenever the people choose their representatives on just and undeniably equal measures, suited to the original frame of the government, it cannot be doubted that this is the will and act of the society, whoever permitted or caused them to do so.

chapters.title: Chapter 14 — Of Prerogative
paragraphs: Where the legislative and executive power are in different hands (as they are in all moderated monarchies and well-framed governments), the good of the society requires that various things be left to the discretion of the one who has the executive power. The legislators are not able to foresee everything that may be useful to the community and provide for it by laws. So the executor of the laws, having the power in his hands, has a right by the common law of nature to use it for the good of the society in many cases where the municipal law has given no direction, until the legislative can conveniently be assembled to provide for it. There are many things which the law can in no way provide for, and those must necessarily be left to the discretion of whoever has the executive power in his hands, to be ordered by him as the public good and advantage require. Indeed, it is fitting that the laws themselves should in some cases give way to the executive power, or rather to this fundamental law of nature and government: namely, that as far as possible all the members of the society are to be preserved. For many accidents may happen in which a strict and rigid observance of the laws may do harm (for example, refusing to pull down an innocent man’s house to stop a fire when the house next to it is burning). And a man may sometimes come within the reach of the law, which makes no distinction between persons, through an action that may deserve reward and pardon. So it is fitting that the ruler should have a power, in many cases, to soften the severity of the law and to pardon some offenders. For since the end of government is the preservation of all, as far as possible, even the guilty are to be spared where this can do no harm to the innocent.

This power to act according to discretion, for the public good, without the prescription of the law, and sometimes even against it, is what is called prerogative. In some governments the lawmaking power is not always in being, and it is usually too numerous, and so too slow, for the speed that execution requires. It is also impossible to foresee, and so to provide for by laws, all the accidents and necessities that may concern the public, or to make laws that will do no harm if they are executed with inflexible rigour on all occasions and upon all persons who may come in their way. For these reasons a latitude is left to the executive power to do many things by its own choice which the laws do not prescribe.

As long as this power is employed for the benefit of the community, and in keeping with the trust and ends of the government, it is undoubted prerogative and is never questioned. The people are very seldom, if ever, scrupulous or fussy on this point. They are far from examining prerogative as long as it is employed to any tolerable degree for the use it was meant for, that is, for the good of the people, and not plainly against it. But if a dispute arises between the executive power and the people about something claimed as a prerogative, the question will easily be decided by whether the exercise of that prerogative tends to the good or the harm of the people.

It is easy to imagine that in the infancy of governments, when commonwealths differed little from families in the number of their people, they also differed little from them in the number of their laws. The governors were like fathers to them, watching over them for their good, and so the government was almost all prerogative. A few established laws served the purpose, and the discretion and care of the ruler supplied the rest. But when error or flattery persuaded weak princes to use this power for private ends of their own, and not for the public good, the people were obliged to have prerogative defined by express laws on those points where they found it working to their disadvantage. So the people found it necessary to declare limits on prerogative in cases which they and their ancestors had left, with the widest latitude, to the wisdom of those princes who made nothing but a right use of it, that is, who used it for the good of their people.

So those who say that the people have encroached on the prerogative when they have had any part of it defined by positive laws have a very wrong notion of government. In doing so the people have not taken from the prince anything that rightly belonged to him. They have only declared that the power they left indefinitely in his hands, or his ancestors’, to be exercised for their good, was not something they intended him to have when he used it otherwise. For since the end of government is the good of the community, whatever alterations are made in it that tend toward that end cannot be an encroachment on anybody, because nobody in government can have a right that tends toward any other end. The only encroachments are those that harm or hinder the public good. Those who say otherwise speak as if the prince had an interest distinct and separate from the good of the community, and was not made for it. That is the root and source from which almost all the evils and disorders that happen in kingly governments spring. And indeed, if that is so, the people under his government are not a society of rational creatures who have entered into a community for their mutual good. They are not people who have set rulers over themselves to guard and promote that good. Instead they are to be regarded as a herd of inferior creatures under the dominion of a master, who keeps them and works them for his own pleasure or profit. If men were so devoid of reason, and so brutish, as to enter into society on such terms, prerogative might indeed be what some men would like it to be: an arbitrary power to do things harmful to the people.

But a rational creature cannot be supposed, when he is free, to put himself into subjection to another for his own harm (although, where he finds a good and wise ruler, he may not perhaps think it either necessary or useful to set precise limits to his power in all things). So prerogative can be nothing but the people’s permitting their rulers to do various things by their own free choice, where the law was silent, and sometimes even against the direct letter of the law, for the public good, together with the people’s acceptance of it when it has been done. A good prince, who is mindful of the trust placed in his hands and careful of the good of his people, cannot have too much prerogative, that is, too much power to do good. But a weak and bad prince may claim the power his predecessors exercised without the direction of the law as a prerogative belonging to him by right of his office, which he may exercise as he pleases to create or promote an interest distinct from that of the public. Such a prince gives the people occasion to claim their right and to limit that power, which they were content to allow tacitly as long as it was exercised for their good.

So anyone who looks into the history of England will find that prerogative was always largest in the hands of our wisest and best princes. The people saw that the whole tendency of their actions was the public good, and so did not contest what was done without law to that end. Or, if some human frailty or mistake appeared in small deviations from that end (for princes are only men, made like others), it was still plain that the main course of their conduct aimed at nothing but the care of the public. The people therefore, finding reason to be satisfied with these princes, accepted what they did whenever they acted without the letter of the law or contrary to it, and, without the least complaint, let them enlarge their prerogative as they pleased. They judged rightly that in this the princes did nothing to harm their laws, since they acted in accordance with the foundation and end of all laws, the public good.

Such god-like princes did indeed have some title to arbitrary power, by the argument that would prove absolute monarchy the best government, as the one by which God himself governs the universe: because such kings share in his wisdom and goodness. On this is founded the saying that the reigns of good princes have always been the most dangerous to the liberties of their people. For their successors, managing the government with different ideas, would take the actions of those good rulers as precedents and make them the standard of their own prerogative, as if what had been done only for the good of the people gave them a right to do the same for the harm of the people, if they so pleased. This has often caused conflict, and sometimes public disorder, before the people could recover their original right and have it declared that this was not prerogative, as it truly never was. For it is impossible that anybody in the society should ever have a right to do the people harm, although it is quite possible, and reasonable, that the people should not try to set any limits to the prerogative of those kings or rulers who did not themselves overstep the bounds of the public good. For prerogative is nothing but the power of doing public good without a rule.

The power of calling parliaments in England, as to their exact time, place, and duration, is certainly a prerogative of the king, but still with this trust: that it is to be used for the good of the nation, as the needs of the times and the variety of occasions require. It is impossible to foresee which place will always be the fittest for them to assemble in, and what the best season will be, so the choice of these was left with the executive power, to be made in the way that might best serve the public good and best suit the ends of parliaments.

In this matter of prerogative the old question will be asked: but who shall be judge of when this power is being used rightly? I answer: between an executive power in being with such a prerogative, and a legislative that depends on his will for its convening, there can be no judge on earth. Nor can there be one between the legislative and the people, should either the executive or the legislative, once they have the power in their hands, plan or set about enslaving or destroying them. In this case, as in all other cases where they have no judge on earth, the people have no other remedy but to appeal to heaven. For the rulers, in such attempts, are exercising a power the people never put into their hands (since the people can never be supposed to consent that anybody should rule over them for their harm), and so they are doing what they have no right to do. And where the body of the people, or any single man, is deprived of their right, or is subjected to the exercise of a power without right, and has no appeal on earth, they have a liberty to appeal to heaven whenever they judge the cause to be of sufficient importance. Therefore, although the people cannot be judge in the sense of having, by the constitution of that society, any superior power to decide the case and pass an effective sentence, they have nevertheless, by a law prior and superior to all the positive laws of men, reserved to themselves that ultimate decision which belongs to all mankind where there is no appeal on earth: namely, to judge whether they have just cause to make their appeal to heaven. And they cannot part with this judgment, because it is beyond a man’s power to submit himself to another so far as to give him a liberty to destroy him. God and nature never allow a man to abandon himself so far as to neglect his own preservation; and since he cannot take away his own life, neither can he give another the power to take it. Nor should anyone think that this lays a perpetual foundation for disorder. For it does not come into operation until the inconvenience is so great that the majority feel it, are weary of it, and find it necessary to have it put right. But the executive power, or wise princes, never need come into danger of this; and it is the thing, above all others, that they most need to avoid, as the most perilous of all.

chapters.title: Chapter 15 — Of Paternal, Political, and Despotical Power, Considered Together
paragraphs: Although I have had occasion to speak of these powers separately before, the great mistakes made lately about government have, I suppose, arisen from confusing these distinct powers with one another. So it may not, perhaps, be out of place to consider them here together.

First, then, paternal or parental power is nothing but the power parents have over their children to govern them for the children’s good, until they come to the use of reason, or to a state of knowledge in which they may be supposed capable of understanding the rule they are to govern themselves by, whether that is the law of nature or the municipal law of their country. Capable, I say, of knowing it as well as many others who live as free men under that law. The affection and tenderness which God has planted in the hearts of parents toward their children make it evident that this is not meant to be a harsh, arbitrary government, but only to serve the help, instruction, and preservation of their offspring. But however that may be, there is, as I have proved, no reason why it should be thought to extend at any time to life and death over their children, any more than over anybody else. Nor can there be any pretext for this parental power keeping the child, once grown to a man, in subjection to the will of his parents, any further than this: having received life and education from his parents obliges him, all his life, to respect, honour, gratitude, assistance and support toward both father and mother. And so it is true that paternal power is a natural government, but it does not extend at all to the ends and jurisdiction of political government. The power of the father does not reach at all to the property of the child, which is his alone to dispose of.

Secondly, political power is the power which every man had in the state of nature and has given up into the hands of the society, and through it to the governors whom the society has set over itself, with this express or tacit trust: that it shall be employed for their good and the preservation of their property. Now this power, which every man has in the state of nature, and which he parts with to the society in all those cases where the society can protect him, is the power to use such means for preserving his own property as he thinks good and nature allows him, and to punish breaches of the law of nature by others in the way that (according to the best of his reason) may most contribute to the preservation of himself and the rest of mankind. So the end and measure of this power, when it is in every man’s hands in the state of nature, is the preservation of all of his society, that is, of all mankind in general. Therefore it can have no other end or measure, when it is in the hands of the magistrate, than to preserve the members of that society in their lives, liberties, and possessions. And so it cannot be an absolute, arbitrary power over their lives and fortunes, which are to be preserved as far as possible. It is a power to make laws, and to attach to them such penalties as may tend to the preservation of the whole, by cutting off those parts, and those only, which are so corrupt that they threaten the sound and healthy parts; without that, no severity is lawful. And this power has its origin only in compact and agreement, and in the mutual consent of those who make up the community.

Thirdly, despotic power is an absolute, arbitrary power which one man has over another, to take away his life whenever he pleases. This is a power which nature does not give, for it has made no such distinction between one man and another; nor can compact convey it, for since a man does not have such an arbitrary power over his own life, he cannot give another man such a power over it. It is the effect only of forfeiture, which the aggressor makes of his own life when he puts himself into the state of war with another. He has abandoned reason, which God has given to be the rule between man and man and the common bond by which humankind is united into one fellowship and society. He has renounced the way of peace which reason teaches, and has used the force of war to achieve his unjust ends against another where he has no right. In this way he revolts from his own kind to that of beasts, by making force, which is theirs, his rule of right. So he makes himself liable to be destroyed by the injured person, and by the rest of mankind who will join with him in the execution of justice, like any other wild beast or noxious brute with whom mankind can have neither society nor security*. And so captives taken in a just and lawful war, and only such captives, are subject to a despotic power. As this power does not arise from compact, so neither is it capable of any; it is the state of war continued. For what compact can be made with a man who is not master of his own life? What condition can he perform? And if he is once allowed to be master of his own life, the despotic, arbitrary power of his master ceases. Whoever is master of himself and his own life has a right too to the means of preserving it. So as soon as compact enters, slavery ceases; and whoever enters into conditions with his captive to that extent gives up his absolute power and puts an end to the state of war.
(*Another copy corrected by Mr. Locke has it this way: Noxious brute that is destructive to their being.)

Nature gives the first of these, namely paternal power, to parents for the benefit of their children during their minority, to make up for their lack of ability and of understanding in managing their property. (By property I must be understood here, as in other places, to mean the property which men have in their persons as well as in their goods.) Voluntary agreement gives the second, namely political power, to governors for the benefit of their subjects, to secure them in the possession and use of their properties. And forfeiture gives the third, despotic power, to lords for their own benefit, over those who are stripped of all property.

Whoever considers the distinct origin and extent, and the different ends, of these separate powers will plainly see that paternal power falls as far short of the power of the magistrate as despotic power exceeds it. He will also see that absolute dominion, wherever it is placed, is so far from being one kind of civil society that it is as inconsistent with it as slavery is with property. Paternal power exists only where minority makes the child incapable of managing his property; political power, where men have property at their own disposal; and despotic power, over those who have no property at all.

chapters.title: Chapter 16 — Of Conquest
paragraphs: Although governments can originally have no other origin than the one described earlier, and political societies can be founded on nothing but the consent of the people, ambition has filled the world with such disorders that, in the noise of war, which makes up so great a part of the history of mankind, this consent is little noticed. So many people have mistaken the force of arms for the consent of the people, and count conquest as one of the origins of government. But conquest is as far from setting up any government as demolishing a house is from building a new one in its place. It often makes way, indeed, for a new frame of commonwealth by destroying the old one; but without the consent of the people it can never erect a new one.

All men will readily agree that the aggressor, who puts himself into the state of war with another and unjustly invades another man’s right, can never, by such an unjust war, come to have a right over the conquered. That is, all men will agree who do not think that robbers and pirates have a right of empire over whoever they have force enough to master, or that men are bound by promises which unlawful force extorts from them. Suppose a robber breaks into my house and, with a dagger at my throat, makes me seal deeds conveying my estate to him. Would this give him any title? An unjust conqueror who forces me into submission has just such a title, by his sword. The injury and the crime are the same, whether committed by the wearer of a crown or by some petty villain. The rank of the offender and the number of his followers make no difference to the offence, unless it is to aggravate it. The only difference is that great robbers punish little ones to keep them in obedience, while the great ones are rewarded with laurels and triumphs, because they are too big for the weak hands of justice in this world and have in their own possession the power that ought to punish offenders. What is my remedy against a robber who has broken into my house like that? To appeal to the law for justice. But perhaps justice is denied, or I am crippled and cannot move, or robbed and do not have the means to do it. If God has taken away every means of seeking a remedy, there is nothing left but patience. But my son, when he is able, may seek the relief of the law that is denied to me; he or his son may renew the appeal until he recovers his right. The conquered, however, or their children, have no court and no arbitrator on earth to appeal to. Then they may appeal, as Jephthah did, to heaven, and repeat their appeal until they have recovered the native right of their ancestors, which was to have such a legislative over them as the majority should approve and freely accept. If it is objected that this would cause endless trouble, I answer: no more than justice does, where she is open to all who appeal to her. Whoever troubles his neighbour without cause is punished for it by the justice of the court he appeals to. And whoever appeals to heaven must be sure he has right on his side, and a right, too, that is worth the trouble and cost of the appeal, since he will answer for it at a tribunal that cannot be deceived and will be sure to repay everyone according to the harms he has done to his fellow subjects, that is, to any part of mankind. From all this it is plain that whoever conquers in an unjust war can have no title by it to the subjection and obedience of the conquered.
But supposing victory favours the right side, let us consider a conqueror in a lawful war, and see what power he gets, and over whom.

First, it is plain that by his conquest he gets no power over those who conquered with him. Those who fought on his side cannot lose by the conquest, but must be at least as free as they were before. Most commonly they serve on terms, on condition that they share with their leader and enjoy a part of the spoils and the other advantages that come with the conquering sword; or at least that they have a part of the subdued country given to them. And the conquering people are not, I hope, to be made slaves by conquest, and to wear their laurels only to show that they are sacrifices to their leader’s triumph. Those who found absolute monarchy on the title of the sword turn their heroes, the founders of such monarchies, into out-and-out Drawcansirs, and forget that they had any officers and soldiers who fought on their side in the battles they won, or helped them to subdue, or shared in possessing, the countries they mastered. Some tell us that the English monarchy is founded on the Norman conquest, and that our princes therefore have a title to absolute dominion. Even if that were true (and the history shows otherwise), and William had a right to make war on this island, his dominion by conquest could still reach no further than the Saxons and Britons who were then the inhabitants of this country. The Normans who came with him and helped to conquer, and all who are descended from them, are free men and not subjects by conquest, whatever dominion that conquest may give. And if I, or anybody else, claim freedom as descended from them, it will be very hard to prove the contrary. It is plain, too, that the law, which has made no distinction between the one and the other, does not intend there to be any difference in their freedom or privileges.

But suppose, which seldom happens, that the conquerors and the conquered never merge into one people under the same laws and freedom. Let us see next what power a lawful conqueror has over the subdued; and that, I say, is purely despotic. He has an absolute power over the lives of those who have forfeited them by an unjust war, but not over the lives or fortunes of those who did not take part in the war, nor over the possessions even of those who were actually engaged in it.

Secondly, I say, then, that the conqueror gets power only over those who have actually assisted, concurred in, or consented to the unjust force that is used against him. The people have given their governors no power to do an unjust thing, such as making an unjust war, for they never had such a power in themselves. So they ought not to be charged as guilty of the violence and injustice committed in an unjust war, any further than they actually abet it, any more than they are to be thought guilty of any violence or oppression their governors might use on the people themselves, or on any part of their fellow subjects; for they have empowered them no more to do the one than the other. Conquerors, it is true, seldom trouble themselves to make this distinction; they willingly let the confusion of war sweep everyone together. But that does not alter the right. The conqueror’s power over the lives of the conquered exists only because they have used force to commit or maintain an injustice, so he can have that power only over those who have concurred in that force. All the rest are innocent. He has no more title over the people of that country who have done him no injury, and so have made no forfeiture of their lives, than he has over anyone else who, without any injuries or provocations, has lived on fair terms with him.

Thirdly, the power a conqueror gets over those he overcomes in a just war is perfectly despotic. He has an absolute power over the lives of those who have forfeited them by putting themselves in a state of war; but he does not thereby have a right and title to their possessions. I do not doubt that at first sight this will seem a strange doctrine, since it is so completely contrary to the practice of the world. Nothing is more familiar, when speaking of the dominion of countries, than to say that so-and-so conquered it, as if conquest, without any further ado, conveyed a right of possession. But we should consider that the practice of the strong and powerful, however universal it may be, is seldom the rule of right, even though it is one part of the subjection of the conquered not to argue against the conditions the conquering sword has cut out for them.

In all war there is usually a mixture of force and damage, and the aggressor seldom fails to harm the estate of those he makes war on when he uses force against their persons. Yet it is the use of force alone that puts a man into the state of war. Whether he begins the injury by force, or, having done the injury quietly and by fraud, refuses to make reparation and maintains it by force (which is the same as having done it by force in the first place), it is the unjust use of force that makes the war. Someone who breaks open my house and violently turns me out of doors, and someone who gets in peaceably and then keeps me out by force, in effect do the same thing. That is supposing we are in such a state that we have no common judge on earth whom I may appeal to and whom we are both obliged to submit to, for that is the case I am now speaking of. It is the unjust use of force, then, that puts a man into the state of war with another, and by it whoever is guilty of it forfeits his life. For in abandoning reason, which is the rule given between man and man, and using force, the way of beasts, he becomes liable to be destroyed by the one he uses force against, like any savage, ravenous beast that is dangerous to his existence.

But the father’s misdeeds are not the children’s faults, and they may be rational and peaceable in spite of the brutishness and injustice of the father. So the father, by his misdeeds and violence, can forfeit only his own life, and does not involve his children in his guilt or destruction. His goods, which nature, willing the preservation of all mankind as far as possible, has made to belong to the children to keep them from perishing, still continue to belong to his children. For supposing they did not join in the war, whether through infancy, absence, or choice, they have done nothing to forfeit them. Nor does the conqueror have any right to take them away merely on the ground of having subdued the man who attempted his destruction by force; though perhaps he may have some right to them to repair the damages he has suffered from the war and from the defence of his own right. How far that reaches to the possessions of the conquered we shall see shortly. So whoever has, by conquest, a right over a man’s person to destroy him if he pleases, does not thereby have a right over his estate to possess and enjoy it. For it is the brutal force the aggressor has used that gives his adversary a right to take away his life and destroy him, if he pleases, as a noxious creature; but it is damage suffered that alone gives him a title to another man’s goods. I may kill a thief who attacks me on the highway; yet I may not (which seems a lesser thing) take away his money and let him go. That would be robbery on my part. His force, and the state of war he put himself in, made him forfeit his life, but gave me no title to his goods. The right of conquest, then, extends only to the lives of those who joined in the war, and not to their estates, except in order to make reparation for the damages received and the costs of the war; and even that is subject to reserving the right of the innocent wife and children.

Let the conqueror have as much justice on his side as can be imagined; he still has no right to seize more than the vanquished could forfeit. The vanquished man’s life is at the victor’s mercy, and the victor may take his service and goods to make himself reparation. But he cannot take the goods of his wife and children. They too had a title to the goods he enjoyed, and their shares in the estate he possessed. For example, suppose that I, in the state of nature (and all commonwealths are in the state of nature with one another), have injured another man and, refusing to give satisfaction, have brought things to a state of war, in which my defending by force what I had gained unjustly makes me the aggressor. I am conquered. My life, it is true, is forfeit and at his mercy, but not the lives of my wife and children. They did not make the war, nor did they assist in it. I could not forfeit their lives; they were not mine to forfeit. My wife had a share in my estate, and I could not forfeit that either. And my children also, being born of me, had a right to be maintained out of my labour or substance. Here, then, is the case: the conqueror has a title to reparation for damages received, and the children have a title to their father’s estate for their subsistence. (As for the wife’s share, whether her own labour or a compact gave her a title to it, it is plain that her husband could not forfeit what was hers.) What must be done in this case? I answer: since the fundamental law of nature is that all, as far as possible, should be preserved, it follows that if there is not enough to satisfy both fully, namely the conqueror’s losses and the children’s maintenance, the one who has enough and to spare must give up something of his full satisfaction, and give way to the pressing and stronger title of those who are in danger of perishing without it.

But suppose the costs and damages of the war are to be made up to the conqueror to the last penny, and that the children of the vanquished, stripped of all their father’s goods, are to be left to starve and perish. Even so, satisfying what is due to the conqueror on this account will hardly give him a title to any country he conquers. For the damages of war can hardly amount to the value of any considerable tract of land in any part of the world where all the land is possessed and none lies waste. And if I have not taken away the conqueror’s land (which, since I am the one vanquished, I cannot possibly have done), hardly any other damage I have done him can amount to the value of my land, supposing mine is equally cultivated and of an extent at all close to what I had overrun of his. The destruction of a year’s produce, or two (for it seldom reaches four or five), is the most damage that can usually be done. As for money, and such riches and treasure taken away, these are not nature’s goods; they have only a fanciful, imaginary value. Nature has put no such value on them. By her standard they are worth no more than the wampompeke of the Americans to a European prince, or than the silver money of Europe would once have been to an American. And five years’ produce is not worth the perpetual inheritance of land where all is possessed and none remains waste, to be taken up by the one who has been dispossessed. This will easily be granted if one only sets aside the imaginary value of money, for the disproportion is greater than that between five and five hundred. At the same time, though, half a year’s produce is worth more than the inheritance where there is more land than the inhabitants possess and use, and anyone is at liberty to make use of the waste; but there conquerors take little trouble to possess themselves of the lands of the vanquished. So no damage that men in the state of nature (as all princes and governments are in relation to one another) suffer from one another can give a conqueror power to dispossess the descendants of the vanquished and turn them out of that inheritance, which ought to be the possession of them and their descendants to all generations. The conqueror will indeed be inclined to think himself master, and it is the very condition of the subdued not to be able to dispute their right. But if that is all, it gives no title other than what bare force gives the stronger over the weaker; and by that reasoning, whoever is strongest will have a right to whatever he pleases to seize.

Over those, then, who joined with him in the war, and over those of the subdued country who did not oppose him, and even over the descendants of those who did, the conqueror has no right of dominion by his conquest, even in a just war. They are free from any subjection to him, and if their former government is dissolved, they are at liberty to begin and set up another for themselves.

The conqueror, it is true, usually uses the force he has over them to compel them, with a sword at their breasts, to bow to his conditions and submit to whatever government he pleases to give them. But the question is, what right does he have to do so? If it is said that they submit by their own consent, then this admits that their own consent is necessary to give the conqueror a title to rule over them. It remains only to consider whether promises extorted by force, without right, can be counted as consent, and how far they bind. To this I say that they do not bind at all, because whatever another gets from me by force, I still keep the right to, and he is obliged to restore it at once. If someone takes my horse from me by force, he ought to return it at once, and I still have a right to take it back. By the same reasoning, if someone forced a promise from me, he ought to give it back at once, that is, release me from its obligation; or I may take it back myself, that is, choose whether I will keep it. For the law of nature lays obligations on me only through the rules she prescribes, so she cannot oblige me through the violation of her rules; and extorting anything from me by force is exactly such a violation. Nor does it change the case at all to say, “I gave my promise,” any more than it excuses the force and passes the right when I put my hand in my pocket and hand my purse over myself to a thief who demands it with a pistol at my chest.

From all this it follows that the government of a conqueror, imposed by force on the subdued, whether on those against whom he had no right of war, or on those who did not join in the war against him where he did have right, lays no obligation on them.

But let us suppose that all the men of that community, being all members of the same body politic, may be taken to have joined in the unjust war in which they are subdued, and so their lives are at the conqueror’s mercy.

I say this does not concern their children who are still minors. Since a father does not himself have a power over the life or liberty of his child, no act of his can possibly forfeit it. So the children, whatever may have happened to the fathers, are free men, and the absolute power of the conqueror reaches no further than the persons of the men he subdued, and dies with them. And even if he governs those men as slaves, subjected to his absolute arbitrary power, he has no such right of dominion over their children. He can have no power over the children except by their own consent, whatever he may drive them to say or do; and he has no lawful authority as long as force, and not choice, compels them to submit.

Every man is born with a double right. First, a right of freedom for his person, over which no other man has any power; the free disposal of it lies in himself. Secondly, a right, before any other man, to inherit his father’s goods together with his brothers and sisters.

By the first of these, a man is naturally free from subjection to any government, even if he is born in a place under its jurisdiction. But if he disowns the lawful government of the country he was born in, he must also give up the right that belonged to him by its laws, and the possessions there that came down to him from his ancestors, if it was a government made by their consent.

By the second, the inhabitants of any country who are descended from those who were subdued and had a government forced on them against their free consent, and who derive a title to their estates from them, keep a right to the possessions of their ancestors, even though they do not freely consent to the government whose harsh conditions were imposed by force on the owners of that country. For the first conqueror never had a title to the land of that country. So the people who are descended from, or claim under, those who were forced by constraint to submit to the yoke of a government always have a right to shake it off and free themselves from the usurpation or tyranny which the sword has brought upon them, until their rulers place them under a frame of government to which they willingly and by choice consent. Who doubts that the Grecian Christians, descendants of the ancient owners of that country, may justly throw off the Turkish yoke, under which they have groaned so long, whenever they have the opportunity? For no government can have a right to obedience from a people who have not freely consented to it. And they can never be supposed to have done so until either they are put in a full state of liberty to choose their government and governors, or at least until they have standing laws to which they have given their free consent, by themselves or their representatives, and also until they are allowed their due property. That means being owners of what they have in such a way that nobody can take away any part of it without their own consent. Without this, men under any government are not in the state of free men, but are outright slaves under the force of war.

But grant that the conqueror in a just war has a right to the estates of the conquered, as well as power over their persons; which, it is plain, he does not. Even so, no absolute power will follow from it in the continuance of the government.
