For the descendants of these people are all free men, and if he grants them estates and possessions to live on in his country (without which it would be worth nothing), then whatever he grants them, they have property in, as far as it is granted. And the nature of property is that it cannot be taken from a man without his own consent.

Their persons are free by a native right, and their properties, whether more or less, are their own and at their own disposal, not at his; otherwise it is not property. Suppose the conqueror gives one man a thousand acres, to him and his heirs for ever, and leases another man a thousand acres for his life, at a rent of £50 or £500 a year. Does the first not have a right to his thousand acres for ever, and the second a right to his during his life, as long as he pays that rent? And does the tenant for life not have a property in everything he gains over and above his rent by his labour and industry during that term, supposing it is double the rent? Can anyone say that the king, or conqueror, after his grant, may by his power as conqueror take away all or part of the land from the heirs of the one, or from the other during his life while he pays the rent? Or can he take away from either of them, at his pleasure, the goods or money they have earned on that land? If he can, then all free and voluntary contracts cease and are void in the world. Nothing is needed to dissolve them at any time but enough power, and all the grants and promises of men in power are only mockery and collusion. For can there be anything more ridiculous than to say, “I give you and yours this for ever, and in the surest and most solemn form of conveyance that can be devised,” and yet for it to be understood that I have a right, if I please, to take it away from you again tomorrow?

I will not argue now about whether princes are exempt from the laws of their country. But this I am sure of: they owe subjection to the laws of God and nature. Nobody and no power can exempt them from the obligations of that eternal law. Those obligations are so great and so strong in the case of promises that omnipotence itself can be bound by them. Grants, promises, and oaths are bonds that hold the Almighty, whatever some flatterers tell the princes of the world, who all together, with all their people joined to them, are, in comparison with the great God, only as a drop of the bucket or a dust on the balance: insignificant, nothing!

In short, the case of conquest is this. The conqueror, if he has a just cause, has a despotic right over the persons of all who actually aided and concurred in the war against him, and a right to make up his damages and costs out of their labour and estates, provided he does not injure the right of anyone else. Over the rest of the people, if there were any who did not consent to the war, and over the children of the captives themselves, or the possessions of either, he has no power. So he can have, by virtue of conquest, no lawful title to dominion over them himself, nor pass one on to his descendants. Instead he is an aggressor if he makes attempts on their properties, and thereby puts himself in a state of war against them. And neither he nor any of his successors has any better right of rule than Hingar or Hubba, the Danes, had here in England, or than Spartacus would have had if he had conquered Italy; which is to say, a right to have their yoke thrown off as soon as God gives those under their subjection the courage and opportunity to do it. So, whatever title the kings of Assyria had over Judah by the sword, God helped Hezekiah to throw off the dominion of that conquering empire. “And the Lord was with Hezekiah, and he prospered; wherefore he went forth, and he rebelled against the king of Assyria, and served him not” (2 Kings xviii. 7). From this it is plain that shaking off a power which force, and not right, has set over anyone, though it bears the name of rebellion, is no offence before God. It is something he allows and approves, even where promises and covenants obtained by force have intervened. For it is very probable, to anyone who reads the story of Ahaz and Hezekiah attentively, that the Assyrians subdued Ahaz and deposed him, and made Hezekiah king in his father’s lifetime; and that Hezekiah, by agreement, had done him homage and paid him tribute all this time.

chapters.title: Chapter 17 — Of Usurpation
paragraphs: Just as conquest may be called a foreign usurpation, so usurpation is a kind of domestic conquest. There is this difference, though: a usurper can never have right on his side, since there is no usurpation except where someone has got possession of what another has a right to. Usurpation, so far as it is only usurpation, is a change of persons alone, not of the forms and rules of the government. For if the usurper extends his power beyond what rightfully belonged to the lawful princes or governors of the commonwealth, that is tyranny added to usurpation.

In all lawful governments, the designation of the persons who are to rule is as natural and necessary a part of the government as its form, and it is something that was originally established by the people. The anarchy is much the same whether there is no form of government at all, or whether people agree that it shall be monarchical but lay down no way of designating the person who is to have the power and be the monarch. That is why all commonwealths, along with their established form of government, also have rules for appointing those who are to have any share in the public authority, and settled methods of conveying the right to them. For the anarchy is much the same whether there is no form of government at all, or whether people agree that it shall be monarchical but lay down no way of knowing or designating the person who is to have the power and be the monarch. Whoever comes to exercise any part of the power by ways other than those the laws of the community have prescribed has no right to be obeyed, even though the form of the commonwealth is still preserved. He is not the person the laws have appointed, and so he is not the person the people have consented to. Nor can such a usurper, or anyone who derives his claim from him, ever have a title until the people are both free to consent and have actually consented to allow and confirm in him the power he has until then usurped.

chapters.title: Chapter 18 — Of Tyranny
paragraphs: Just as usurpation is the exercise of power that someone else has a right to, so tyranny is the exercise of power beyond right, which nobody can have a right to. It consists in using whatever power one holds, not for the good of those who are under it, but for one’s own private, separate advantage. That is what happens when the governor, whatever his title, makes his own will the rule instead of the law, and when his commands and actions are directed not to the preservation of the properties of his people but to the satisfaction of his own ambition, revenge, greed, or any other unruly passion.

If anyone doubts that this is true, or reasonable, because it comes from the obscure hand of a subject, I hope the authority of a king will persuade him to accept it. King James the First, in his speech to Parliament in 1603, told them this:

“I will always prefer the welfare of the public, and of the whole commonwealth, in making good laws and constitutions, to any particular and private ends of my own. I will always regard the wealth and welfare of the commonwealth as my greatest good and worldly happiness. This is a point on which a lawful king directly differs from a tyrant. For I acknowledge that the special and greatest point of difference between a rightful king and a usurping tyrant is this: the proud and ambitious tyrant thinks that his kingdom and people are ordained only to satisfy his desires and unreasonable appetites, whereas the righteous and just king, on the contrary, acknowledges that he himself is ordained to procure the wealth and property of his people.” And again, in his speech to Parliament in 1609, he used these words:

“The king binds himself by a double oath to observe the fundamental laws of his kingdom. He binds himself tacitly, simply by being a king, and so being bound to protect both the people and the laws of his kingdom; and he binds himself expressly, by his oath at his coronation. So every just king in a settled kingdom is bound to observe the compact he has made with his people through his laws, framing his government in keeping with it, in accordance with the compact God made with Noah after the Flood: ‘Hereafter, seed-time and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night, shall not cease while the earth remaineth.’ And therefore a king governing in a settled kingdom ceases to be a king, and degenerates into a tyrant, as soon as he stops ruling according to his laws.” And a little later:

“Therefore all kings who are not tyrants, or perjured, will be glad to bind themselves within the limits of their laws; and those who persuade them otherwise are vipers and plagues, both to them and to the commonwealth.” So that learned king, who understood the nature of things well, makes the difference between a king and a tyrant consist in this alone: the one makes the laws the limits of his power, and the good of the public the end of his government; the other makes everything give way to his own will and appetite.

It is a mistake to think that this fault belongs only to monarchies. Other forms of government are as liable to it as monarchy is. For wherever the power that is placed in any hands for governing the people and preserving their properties is applied to other ends, and used to impoverish them, to harass them, or to subject them to the arbitrary and irregular commands of those who hold it, it at once becomes tyranny, whether those who use it in this way are one or many. So we read of the Thirty Tyrants at Athens as well as of the one at Syracuse; and the intolerable rule of the Decemviri at Rome was no better.

Wherever law ends, tyranny begins, if the law is broken to another’s harm. Whoever in authority exceeds the power the law gives him, and uses the force under his command to bring about against the subject what the law does not allow, ceases in that act to be a magistrate. Since he is acting without authority, he may be opposed like any other man who invades another’s right by force. This is acknowledged in the case of subordinate magistrates. A man who has authority to seize me in the street may be opposed as a thief and a robber if he tries to break into my house to serve a writ, even though I know he has a warrant, and legal authority, that would empower him to arrest me outside. And I would gladly be told why this should not hold for the highest magistrate as well as for the lowest. Is it reasonable that the eldest brother, because he has the largest part of his father’s estate, should for that reason have a right to take away any of his younger brothers’ portions? Or that a rich man who owned a whole region should for that reason have a right to seize the cottage and garden of his poor neighbour whenever he pleased? Rightfully possessing great power and riches, far beyond most of the sons of Adam, is so far from being an excuse, much less a reason, for plunder and oppression (which is what harming another without authority amounts to) that it makes them much worse. For exceeding the bounds of authority is no more a right in a great officer than in a petty one, and no more justifiable in a king than in a constable. It is all the worse in the king, because more trust has been placed in him, because he already has a far greater share than the rest of his brethren, and because he is supposed, from the advantages of his education, employment and counsellors, to know better the measures of right and wrong.

May the commands of a prince, then, be opposed? May he be resisted as often as anyone feels himself wronged, and merely imagines that he has not been given his due? That would unhinge and overturn every political system, and leave nothing but anarchy and confusion in place of government and order.

To this I answer that force is to be opposed to nothing but unjust and unlawful force. Whoever offers opposition in any other case brings on himself a just condemnation from both God and man. So no such danger or confusion will follow as is often suggested. For:

First, in some countries the person of the prince is sacred by law. So whatever he commands or does, his person remains free from all question or violence, and is not liable to force or to any judicial censure or condemnation. Yet opposition may still be made to the illegal acts of any inferior officer, or of anyone else commissioned by him, unless the prince himself chooses, by actually putting himself into a state of war with his people, to dissolve the government and leave them to that defence which belongs to everyone in the state of nature. For in such matters, who can tell what the end will be? A neighbouring kingdom has shown the world a strange example. In all other cases the sacredness of his person exempts him from all inconveniences, so that while the government stands he is safe from all violence and harm whatever. There could not be a wiser constitution than this. The harm he can do in his own person is not likely to happen often or to spread far; nor can he by his single strength subvert the laws or oppress the body of the people, even if some prince should be weak and ill-natured enough to want to. So the inconvenience of some particular harms, which may sometimes occur when a headstrong prince comes to the throne, is well repaid by the peace of the public and the security of the government, with the person of the chief magistrate thus set beyond the reach of danger. For it is safer for the body that a few private men should sometimes be in danger of suffering than that the head of the republic should be exposed easily and on slight occasions.

Secondly, this privilege belongs only to the king’s person. It does not prevent those who use unjust force from being questioned, opposed and resisted, even though they claim a commission from him that the law does not authorize. This is plain in the case of someone who has the king’s writ to arrest a man, which is a full commission from the king. Yet the man who holds it cannot break open a man’s house to make the arrest, nor carry out this command of the king on certain days or in certain places, even though the commission contains no such exception. These are the limitations of the law, and if anyone transgresses them, the king’s commission does not excuse him. For since the king’s authority is given him only by the law, he cannot empower anyone to act against the law, or justify him by his commission in doing so. The commission or command of any magistrate, where he has no authority, is as void and meaningless as that of any private man. The difference between the two is that the magistrate has some authority, to a certain extent and for certain ends, while the private man has none at all. For it is not the commission but the authority that gives the right to act; and against the laws there can be no authority. But in spite of such resistance, the king’s person and authority both remain secure, and so there is no danger to governor or government.

Thirdly, suppose a government in which the person of the chief magistrate is not sacred in this way. Even so, this doctrine that it is lawful to resist all unlawful exercises of his power will not endanger him, or throw the government into turmoil, on every slight occasion. For where the injured party can be relieved, and his damages repaired, by appeal to the law, there can be no pretext for force. Force is to be used only where a man is prevented from appealing to the law, because nothing is to be counted hostile force except force that leaves no remedy of such an appeal. It is such force alone that puts the one who uses it into a state of war and makes it lawful to resist him. A man with a sword in his hand demands my purse on the highway, when perhaps I do not have twelve pence in my pocket: this man I may lawfully kill. I hand another man 100 pounds to hold only while I get down from my horse. When I have got up again, he refuses to give it back, and draws his sword to defend his possession of it by force if I try to take it back. The harm this man does me is a hundred, or possibly a thousand, times greater than the other perhaps intended me (and I killed that one before he had actually done me any). Yet I might lawfully kill the one, and cannot lawfully so much as hurt the other. The reason is plain. The first was using force that threatened my life, so I could not have time to appeal to the law to secure it; and once my life was gone, it would be too late to appeal. The law could not restore life to my dead body: the loss would be beyond repair. To prevent that, the law of nature gave me a right to destroy him, since he had put himself into a state of war with me and threatened my destruction. But in the other case my life is not in danger, so I can have the benefit of appealing to the law, and get reparation for my 100 pounds that way.

Fourthly, suppose the unlawful acts done by the magistrate are upheld by the power he has acquired, and the remedy due by law is blocked by that same power. Even then, the right of resisting, even in such manifest acts of tyranny, will not disturb the government suddenly or on slight occasions. For if the matter goes no further than some private men’s cases, then, although they have a right to defend themselves and to recover by force what has been taken from them by unlawful force, that right will not easily draw them into a contest in which they are sure to perish. It is as impossible for one or a few oppressed men to disturb the government, where the body of the people do not think themselves concerned in it, as it is for a raving madman or a headstrong malcontent to overturn a well-settled state; the people are as little inclined to follow the one as the other.

But suppose either that these illegal acts have extended to the majority of the people, or that the harm and oppression have fallen on only a few, but in cases where the precedent and its consequences seem to threaten everyone. And suppose the people are persuaded in their consciences that their laws, and with them their estates, liberties and lives, and perhaps their religion too, are in danger. How they can be kept from resisting the illegal force used against them, I cannot tell. This, I admit, is an inconvenience that attends every government whatever, once the governors have brought things to the point where their people generally suspect them. That is the most dangerous state they can possibly put themselves in, and they deserve all the less pity for it because it is so easy to avoid. For it is as impossible for a governor who really intends the good of his people, and the preservation of them and their laws together, not to make them see and feel it, as it is for the father of a family not to let his children see that he loves them and takes care of them.

But suppose all the world observes pretences of one kind and actions of another: tricks used to evade the law, and the trust of prerogative (which is an arbitrary power in some things, left in the prince’s hand to do good, not harm, to the people) employed contrary to the end for which it was given. Suppose the people find that the ministers and subordinate magistrates are chosen to suit such ends, and are favoured or set aside in proportion as they promote or oppose them. Suppose they see repeated experiments made with arbitrary power, and see that the religion best suited to introduce it is secretly favoured (though publicly condemned), and that those who work for it are supported as far as possible, and, when that cannot be done, are still approved of and liked all the better. If a long train of actions shows that the counsels are all tending that way, how can a man any longer keep himself from being convinced in his own mind which way things are going, or from looking about for a way to save himself? He could no more do so than he could keep himself from believing that the captain of the ship he was in was carrying him and the rest of the company to Algiers, when he found him always steering that course, even though cross winds, leaks in his ship, and a lack of men and provisions often forced him to turn another way for a while, a course he steadily returned to as soon as the wind, the weather and other circumstances would let him.

chapters.title: Chapter 19 — Of the Dissolution of Government
paragraphs: Anyone who wants to speak with any clarity about the dissolution of government ought first to distinguish between the dissolution of the society and the dissolution of the government. What makes the community, and brings men out of the loose state of nature into one political society, is the agreement each one makes with the rest to incorporate and act as one body, and so to be one distinct commonwealth. The usual, and almost the only, way in which this union is dissolved is the inroad of a foreign force that conquers them. In that case they are no longer able to maintain and support themselves as one entire and independent body, so the union that belonged to that body, and consisted in its being such a body, must necessarily cease. So everyone returns to the state he was in before, with the liberty to shift for himself and provide for his own safety, as he thinks fit, in some other society. Whenever the society is dissolved, it is certain that the government of that society cannot remain. So conquerors’ swords often cut up governments by the roots and hack societies to pieces, cutting off the subdued or scattered multitude from the protection of, and dependence on, the society that ought to have preserved them from violence. The world is too well acquainted with this way of dissolving governments, and too ready to accept it, for anything more to be said about it. And it takes little argument to prove that where the society is dissolved, the government cannot remain. That is as impossible as for the frame of a house to stand when its materials have been scattered and dispersed by a whirlwind, or jumbled into a confused heap by an earthquake.
Besides this overturning from outside, governments are also dissolved from within.

First, when the legislative is altered. Civil society is a state of peace among those who belong to it, and the state of war is shut out of it by the umpire they have provided in their legislative for ending all disputes that may arise among any of them. So it is in their legislative that the members of a commonwealth are united and combined into one coherent living body. This is the soul that gives form, life and unity to the commonwealth; from it the different members have their mutual influence, sympathy and connection. And therefore, when the legislative is broken or dissolved, dissolution and death follow. For the essence and union of the society consist in having one will, and the legislative, once established by the majority, has the declaring and, as it were, the keeping of that will. The constitution of the legislative is the first and fundamental act of society. By it, provision is made for the continuation of their union under the direction of persons, and bonds of laws, made by persons authorized for that purpose by the consent and appointment of the people. Without this, no one man or number of men among them can have authority to make laws that will be binding on the rest. When any one or more take it upon themselves to make laws without having been appointed by the people to do so, they make laws without authority, which the people are therefore not bound to obey. In this way the people are released from subjection again, and may set up a new legislative for themselves as they think best, being fully at liberty to resist the force of those who, without authority, would impose anything on them. Everyone is at the disposal of his own will when those who had, by the delegation of the society, the declaring of the public will are excluded from it, and others usurp their place who have no such authority or delegation.

Since this is usually brought about by those in the commonwealth who misuse the power they have, it is hard to consider it properly, and to know at whose door to lay the blame, without knowing the form of government in which it happens. Let us suppose, then, that the legislative is placed in the concurrence of three distinct persons.
(1). A single hereditary person, who has the constant, supreme executive power, and with it the power of summoning and dissolving the other two within certain periods of time.
(2). An assembly of hereditary nobility.
(3). An assembly of representatives chosen, pro tempore, by the people. Supposing such a form of government, it is evident:

First, that when such a single person, or prince, sets up his own arbitrary will in place of the laws, which are the will of the society declared by the legislative, then the legislative is changed. For the legislative, in effect, is the body whose rules and laws are put into execution and required to be obeyed. So when laws other than those enacted by the legislative the society constituted are set up, and other rules are claimed and enforced, it is plain that the legislative has been changed. Whoever introduces new laws without being authorized to do so by the fundamental appointment of the society, or subverts the old ones, disowns and overturns the power by which they were made, and so sets up a new legislative.

Secondly, when the prince prevents the legislative from assembling at its proper time, or from acting freely in pursuit of the ends for which it was constituted, the legislative is altered. For the legislative does not consist in a certain number of men, no, nor in their meeting, unless they also have freedom to debate, and time to complete, what is for the good of the society. When these are taken away or altered so as to deprive the society of the due exercise of its power, the legislative is truly altered. It is not names that constitute governments, but the use and exercise of the powers that were meant to go with them. So whoever takes away the freedom of the legislative, or hinders it from acting at its proper times, in effect takes away the legislative and puts an end to the government.

Thirdly, when the electors or the methods of election are altered by the arbitrary power of the prince, without the consent of the people and contrary to their common interest, there too the legislative is altered. For if people other than those the society has authorized for the purpose do the choosing, or if they choose in a way other than the one the society has prescribed, those chosen are not the legislative appointed by the people.

Fourthly, handing the people over into subjection to a foreign power, whether by the prince or by the legislative, is certainly a change of the legislative, and so a dissolution of the government. For the end for which people entered into society was to be preserved as one entire, free, independent society, governed by its own laws; and this is lost whenever they are given up into the power of another.

Why, in a constitution like this, the dissolution of the government in these cases is to be blamed on the prince is evident. He has the force, the treasury and the offices of the state at his disposal, and he often persuades himself, or is flattered by others into believing, that as supreme magistrate he is beyond control. So he alone is in a position to make great advances toward such changes under the pretence of lawful authority, and he has it in his power to frighten or suppress those who oppose him, branding them factious, seditious and enemies of the government. By contrast, no other part of the legislative, nor the people, can by themselves attempt any alteration of the legislative without open and visible rebellion, which is conspicuous enough to be noticed and which, when it succeeds, produces effects very little different from foreign conquest. Besides, in such a form of government the prince has the power of dissolving the other parts of the legislative, and so turning them into private persons. They can therefore never alter the legislative by a law in opposition to him, or without his agreement, since his consent is needed to give any of their decrees that sanction. But still, so far as the other parts of the legislative in any way contribute to any attempt on the government, and either promote such designs or fail to hinder them as far as lies in their power, they are guilty, and they share in this crime, which is certainly the greatest crime men can commit against one another.

There is one more way in which such a government may be dissolved, and that is when he who has the supreme executive power neglects and abandons that charge, so that the laws already made can no longer be put into execution. This demonstrably reduces everything to anarchy, and so effectively dissolves the government. For laws are not made for their own sake, but to be, through their execution, the bonds of the society, keeping every part of the body politic in its proper place and function. When that execution entirely ceases, the government visibly ceases, and the people become a confused multitude, without order or connection. Where there is no longer any administration of justice to secure men’s rights, nor any power remaining within the community to direct its force or provide for the needs of the public, there is certainly no government left. Where the laws cannot be executed, it is just as if there were no laws; and a government without laws is, I suppose, a mystery in politics, beyond the grasp of human understanding and incompatible with human society.

In these and similar cases, when the government is dissolved, the people are at liberty to provide for themselves by setting up a new legislative, differing from the old one in its persons, or its form, or both, as they find best for their safety and good. For the society can never lose, through the fault of another, the native and original right it has to preserve itself, and that can be done only by a settled legislative and a fair and impartial execution of the laws it makes. But the condition of mankind is not so miserable that they cannot use this remedy until it is too late to look for any. To tell people they may provide for themselves by setting up a new legislative, once their old one is gone through oppression, trickery, or being handed over to a foreign power, is only to tell them they may expect relief when it is too late and the evil is past cure. In effect this is no more than telling them first to be slaves and then to take care of their liberty, and, when their chains are on, telling them they may act like free men. If that is all it is, it is mockery rather than relief. Men can never be secure from tyranny if there is no means of escaping it until they are completely under it. And that is why they have a right not only to get out of it, but to prevent it.
There is therefore, secondly, another way in which governments are dissolved, and that is when the legislative or the prince, either of them, acts contrary to their trust.

First, the legislative acts against the trust placed in them when they try to invade the property of the subject, and to make themselves, or any part of the community, masters or arbitrary disposers of the lives, liberties or fortunes of the people.

The reason why men enter into society is the preservation of their property; and the end for which they choose and authorize a legislative is that laws may be made, and rules set, as guards and fences to the properties of all the members of the society, to limit the power and moderate the dominion of every part and member of the society. For it can never be supposed to be the will of the society that the legislative should have a power to destroy what everyone intends to secure by entering into society, and for which the people submitted themselves to legislators of their own making. So whenever the legislators try to take away and destroy the property of the people, or to reduce them to slavery under arbitrary power, they put themselves into a state of war with the people. The people are then released from any further obedience, and are left to the common refuge that God has provided for all men against force and violence. Whenever, therefore, the legislative transgresses this fundamental rule of society, and, whether from ambition, fear, folly or corruption, tries to grasp for themselves, or to put into the hands of anyone else, an absolute power over the lives, liberties and estates of the people, then by this breach of trust they forfeit the power the people had put into their hands for quite contrary ends. That power devolves to the people, who have a right to resume their original liberty and, by establishing a new legislative (such as they think fit), to provide for their own safety and security, which is the end for which they are in society. What I have said here about the legislative in general holds true also of the supreme executor. He has a double trust placed in him, both to have a part in the legislative and to carry out the supreme execution of the law, and he acts against both when he sets about establishing his own arbitrary will as the law of the society. He also acts contrary to his trust when he uses the force, treasury and offices of the society to corrupt the representatives and win them over to his purposes; or when he openly secures the electors in advance and dictates their choice, pressing on them men whom he has won over to his designs by solicitations, threats, promises or otherwise, and uses them to bring in people who have promised beforehand how they will vote and what they will enact. To manage candidates and electors in this way, and to remodel the methods of election: what is that but to cut up the government by the roots and poison the very fountain of public security? For the people, having reserved to themselves the choice of their representatives as the fence around their properties, could have done so for no other end than that the representatives should always be freely chosen, and, once so chosen, should freely act and advise as the needs of the commonwealth and the public good should, after examination and mature debate, be judged to require. Those who give their votes before they have heard the debate and weighed the reasons on all sides are not capable of doing this. To prepare an assembly like this, and to try to set up the declared supporters of his own will as the true representatives of the people and the lawmakers of the society, is certainly as great a breach of trust, and as complete a declaration of a design to subvert the government, as can possibly be found. If one adds to this rewards and punishments visibly used for the same end, and all the tricks of perverted law employed to remove and destroy everyone who stands in the way of such a design and will not comply and consent to betray the liberties of their country, there will be no doubt about what is going on. What power those who use it in this way, contrary to the trust that went along with it at its first institution, ought to have in the society is easy to determine. And one cannot fail to see that he who has once attempted anything like this can no longer be trusted.

Perhaps it will be said to this that the people are ignorant and always discontented, so that to lay the foundation of government in the unsteady opinion and uncertain mood of the people is to expose it to certain ruin; and that no government will be able to last long if the people may set up a new legislative whenever they take offence at the old one. To this I answer: quite the contrary. People are not so easily brought out of their old forms as some are inclined to suggest. They can hardly be persuaded to correct the acknowledged faults in the framework they are used to. And if there are any original defects, or defects that have crept in over time or through corruption, it is not easy to get them changed, even when all the world sees there is an opportunity for it. In the many revolutions this kingdom has seen, in this age and earlier ones, this slowness and reluctance of the people to abandon their old constitutions has still kept us to our old legislative of king, lords and commons, or, after some interval of fruitless attempts, has still brought us back to it. And whatever provocations have caused the crown to be taken from the heads of some of our princes, they never carried the people so far as to place it in another line.
But it will be said that this hypothesis lays the ground for frequent rebellion. To this I answer:

First, no more than any other hypothesis does. For when the people are made miserable, and find themselves exposed to the ill-treatment of arbitrary power, you may cry up their governors as much as you like as sons of Jupiter; let them be sacred and divine, descended from heaven or authorized by it; present them as whoever or whatever you please; the same thing will happen. A people who are generally ill-treated, and contrary to right, will be ready on any occasion to relieve themselves of a burden that sits heavy on them. They will wish for the opportunity and look for it, and in the changes, weaknesses and accidents of human affairs it seldom takes long to present itself. He must have lived only a short while in the world who has not seen examples of this in his own time; and he must have read very little who cannot produce examples of it in every sort of government in the world.

Secondly, I answer that such revolutions do not happen at every small piece of mismanagement in public affairs. Great mistakes by those who rule, many wrong and inconvenient laws, and all the slips of human frailty will be borne by the people without mutiny or murmur. But if a long train of abuses, evasions and tricks, all tending the same way, makes the design visible to the people, so that they cannot help feeling what they are under and seeing where they are going, it is no wonder that they should then rouse themselves and try to put the rule into hands that may secure for them the ends for which government was first set up. Without those ends, ancient names and plausible forms are so far from being better than the state of nature, or pure anarchy, that they are much worse; the inconveniences are all as great and as near, but the remedy is further off and more difficult.

Thirdly, I answer that this doctrine, that the people have a power to provide for their safety anew by a new legislative when their legislators have acted contrary to their trust by invading their property, is the best fence against rebellion and the most probable means of preventing it. For rebellion is an opposition not to persons but to authority, which is founded only in the constitutions and laws of the government. So those, whoever they are, who break through these by force, and justify their violation of them by force, are truly and properly rebels. When men, by entering into society and civil government, have excluded force and introduced laws for the preservation of property, peace and unity among themselves, those who set up force again in opposition to the laws do rebellare, that is, bring back the state of war, and are properly rebels. And since those who are in power are the likeliest to do this (because of the claim they have to authority, the temptation of the force they hold in their hands, and the flattery of those around them), the best way to prevent the evil is to show its danger and injustice to those who are under the greatest temptation to fall into it.

In both the cases mentioned above, when either the legislative is changed or the legislators act contrary to the end for which they were constituted, those who are guilty are guilty of rebellion. For if anyone takes away by force the established legislative of any society, and the laws made by them in keeping with their trust, he thereby takes away the umpire that everyone had consented to for the peaceful settlement of all their disputes, and as a bar to the state of war among them. Those who remove or change the legislative take away this deciding power, which nobody can have except by the appointment and consent of the people. So, by destroying the authority that the people set up, and that nobody else can set up, and by introducing a power the people have not authorized, they actually introduce a state of war, which is force without authority. And so, by removing the legislative established by the society (in whose decisions the people acquiesced and were united, as in their own will), they untie the knot and expose the people once again to the state of war. And if those who take away the legislative by force are rebels, the legislators themselves, as has been shown, can be regarded as no less so, when they, who were set up for the protection and preservation of the people, their liberties and properties, invade these by force and try to take them away. By doing so they put themselves into a state of war with those who made them the protectors and guardians of their peace, and they are properly, and with the greatest aggravation, rebellantes, rebels.

But suppose those who say this doctrine lays a foundation for rebellion mean the following: that telling the people they are released from obedience when illegal attempts are made on their liberties or properties, and that they may oppose the unlawful violence of those who were their magistrates when these invade their properties contrary to the trust placed in them, may give rise to civil wars or internal conflicts; and that this doctrine is therefore not to be allowed, since it is so destructive to the peace of the world. Then they might as well say, on the same grounds, that honest men may not oppose robbers or pirates, because this may give rise to disorder or bloodshed. If any harm comes in such cases, it is not to be charged to the man who defends his own right, but to the one who invades his neighbour’s. If the innocent, honest man must quietly give up everything he has, for the sake of peace, to anyone who will lay violent hands on it, I would ask people to consider what kind of peace there will be in the world: a peace that consists only in violence and plunder, and that is to be maintained only for the benefit of robbers and oppressors. Who would not think it an admirable peace between the mighty and the lowly when the lamb, without resistance, yielded its throat to be torn by the imperious wolf? Polyphemus’s den gives us a perfect pattern of such a peace, and such a government, in which Ulysses and his companions had nothing to do but quietly let themselves be devoured. And no doubt Ulysses, who was a prudent man, preached passive obedience and urged them to quiet submission, by pointing out to them how important peace was to mankind, and by showing the inconveniences that might follow if they tried to resist Polyphemus, who now had power over them.

The end of government is the good of mankind. And which is better for mankind: that the people should always be exposed to the boundless will of tyranny, or that rulers should sometimes be liable to be opposed when they grow excessive in the use of their power, and employ it for the destruction, and not the preservation, of the properties of their people?

Nor let anyone say that harm can arise from this as often as it pleases some meddlesome mind or turbulent spirit to want the government changed. It is true that such men may stir whenever they please, but it will only be to their own just ruin and destruction. For until the harm has become general, and the evil designs of the rulers have become visible, or their attempts have been felt by the greater part, the people, who are more inclined to suffer than to right themselves by resistance, are not apt to stir. Examples of particular injustice, or the oppression of an unfortunate man here and there, do not move them. But if they are universally persuaded, on the basis of manifest evidence, that designs are being carried on against their liberties, and the general course and tendency of things cannot fail to give them strong suspicions of the evil intentions of their governors, who is to blame for that? Who can help it if those who could avoid it bring themselves under this suspicion? Are the people to be blamed if they have the sense of rational creatures, and can think of things only as they find and feel them? And is it not rather the fault of those who put things into such a state that they would not want them to be thought to be what they are? I grant that the pride, ambition and turbulence of private men have sometimes caused great disorders in commonwealths, and that factions have been fatal to states and kingdoms. But whether the harm has more often begun in the people’s unruliness and a desire to throw off the lawful authority of their rulers, or in the rulers’ insolence and their efforts to get and exercise an arbitrary power over their people, whether oppression or disobedience gave the first rise to the disorder, I leave to impartial history to determine. This I am sure of: whoever, whether ruler or subject, sets about invading the rights of either prince or people by force, and lays the foundation for overturning the constitution and frame of any just government, is highly guilty of the greatest crime, I think, that a man is capable of. He has to answer for all the harms of bloodshed, plunder and desolation that the breaking up of governments brings on a country. And whoever does it is justly to be regarded as the common enemy and plague of mankind, and is to be treated accordingly.

That subjects or foreigners who attempt by force on the properties of any people may be resisted with force is agreed on all sides. But that magistrates who do the same thing may be resisted has lately been denied, as if those who had the greatest privileges and advantages by the law had thereby a power to break the very laws by which alone they were set in a better place than their brethren. On the contrary, their offence is all the greater for it, both because they are ungrateful for the greater share the law gives them, and because they also break the trust that their brethren have put into their hands.

Whoever uses force without right, as everyone in society does who uses it without law, puts himself into a state of war with those against whom he uses it; and in that state all former ties are cancelled, all other rights cease, and everyone has a right to defend himself and to resist the aggressor. This is so evident that Barclay himself, that great champion of the power and sacredness of kings, is forced to admit that it is lawful for the people, in some cases, to resist their king; and that, too, in a chapter in which he claims to show that the divine law shuts the people out from every kind of rebellion. From this it is evident, even by his own doctrine, that since they may resist in some cases, not all resisting of princes is rebellion. His words are these. Quod siquis dicat, Ergone populus tyrannicae crudelitati & furori jugulum semper praebebit? Ergone multitude civitates suas fame, ferro, & flamma vastari, seque, conjuges, & liberos fortunae ludibrio & tyranni libidini exponi, inque omnia vitae pericula omnesque miserias & molestias a rege deduci patientur? Num illis quod omni animantium generi est a natura tributum, denegari debet, ut sc. vim vi repellant, seseq; ab injuria, tueantur? Huic breviter responsum sit, Populo universo negari defensionem, quae juris naturalis est, neque ultionem quae praeter naturam est adversus regem concedi debere. Quapropter si rex non in singulares tantum personas aliquot privatum odium exerceat, sed corpus etiam reipublicae, cujus ipse caput est, i.e. totum populum, vel insignem aliquam ejus partem immani & intoleranda saevitia seu tyrannide divexet; populo, quidem hoc casu resistendi ac tuendi se ab injuria potestas competit, sed tuendi se tantum, non enim in principem invadendi: & restituendae injuriae illatae, non recedendi a debita reverentia propter acceptam injuriam. Praesentem denique impetum propulsandi non vim praeteritam ulciscenti jus habet. Horum enim alterum a natura est, ut vitam scilicet corpusque tueamur. Alterum vero contra naturam, ut inferior de superiori supplicium sumat. Quod itaque populus malum, antequam factum sit, impedire potest, ne fiat, id postquam factum est, in regem authorem sceleris vindicare non potest: populus igitur hoc amplius quam privatus quispiam habet: quod huic, vel ipsis adversariis judicibus, excepto Buchanano, nullum nisi in patientia remedium superest. Cum ille si intolerabilis tyrannus est (modicum enim ferre omnino debet) resistere cum reverentia possit, Barclay contra Monarchom. 1. iii. c. 8.
In English, it reads:

“But if anyone should ask: Must the people, then, always lay themselves open to the cruelty and rage of tyranny? Must they see their cities plundered and reduced to ashes, their wives and children exposed to the tyrant’s lust and fury, and themselves and their families brought by their king to ruin and to all the miseries of poverty and oppression, and yet sit idle? Must men alone be denied the common privilege of opposing force with force, which nature allows so freely to all other creatures to preserve themselves from injury? I answer: self-defence is a part of the law of nature, and it cannot be denied to the community, even against the king himself. But they must by no means be allowed to take revenge on him, since that is not in keeping with that law. Therefore, if the king shows hatred not only to some particular persons, but sets himself against the body of the commonwealth, of which he is the head, and with intolerable ill-treatment cruelly tyrannizes over the whole people, or a considerable part of it, then in this case the people have a right to resist and to defend themselves from injury. But it must be with this caution: that they only defend themselves, and do not attack their prince. They may repair the damage they have received, but must not, whatever the provocation, go beyond the bounds of due reverence and respect. They may repel the present attempt, but must not take revenge for past violence. For it is natural for us to defend life and limb, but for an inferior to punish a superior is against nature. The harm that is planned against them, the people may prevent before it is done; but once it is done, they must not take revenge for it on the king, even though he is the author of the villainy. This, therefore, is the privilege of the people in general, over and above what any private person has: particular men, as our adversaries themselves allow (Buchanan alone excepted), have no other remedy but patience; but the body of the people may, with respect, resist intolerable tyranny; for when it is only moderate, they ought to endure it.”
That is how far that great advocate of monarchical power allows resistance.
It is true that he has attached two limitations to it, to no purpose:
First, he says, it must be done with reverence.

Secondly, it must be without retaliation or punishment; and the reason he gives is that an inferior cannot punish a superior. First, then: how to resist force without striking back, or how to strike with reverence, will take some skill to make intelligible. A man who meets an assault only with a shield to take the blows, or in some even more respectful posture, without a sword in his hand to check the confidence and force of his attacker, will soon come to the end of his resistance, and will find that such a defence only brings worse treatment on himself. This is as ridiculous a way of resisting as Juvenal thought it a way of fighting: ubi tu pulsas, ego vapulo tantum. And the outcome of the combat will inevitably be the same as he describes it there:
/*[4] -----Libertas pauperis haec est: Pulsatus rogat, et pugnis concisus, adorat, Ut liceat paucis cum dentibus inde reverti. */

This will always be the outcome of such an imaginary resistance, where men may not strike back. So he who may resist must be allowed to strike. And then let our author, or anybody else, combine a knock on the head or a cut across the face with as much reverence and respect as he thinks fit. Whoever can reconcile blows and reverence may, for all I know, deserve for his pains a civil, respectful cudgelling wherever he can come across one.

Secondly, as to his second limitation, that an inferior cannot punish a superior: that is true, generally speaking, while he remains his superior. But resisting force with force is the state of war, which levels the parties and cancels every former relation of reverence, respect and superiority. And then the only difference that remains is that the one who opposes the unjust aggressor has this superiority over him: he has a right, when he prevails, to punish the offender, both for the breach of the peace and for all the evils that followed from it. Barclay therefore, in another place, more consistently with himself, denies that it is lawful to resist a king in any case. But there he names two cases in which a king may un-king himself. His words are:

Quid ergo, nulline casus incidere possunt quibus populo sese erigere atque in regem impotentius dominantem arma capere & invadere jure suo suaque authoritate liceat? Nulli certe quamdiu rex manet. Semper enim ex divinis id obstat, Regem honorificato; & qui potestati resistit, Dei ordinationi resisit: non alias igitur in eum populo potestas est quam si id committat propter quod ipso jure rex esse desinat. Tunc enim se ipse principatu exuit atque in privatis constituit liber: hoc modo populus & superior efficitur, reverso ad eum sc. jure illo quod ante regem inauguratum in interregno habuit. At sunt paucorum generum commissa ejusmodi quae hunc effectum pariunt. At ego cum plurima animo perlustrem, duo tantum invenio, duos, inquam, casus quibus rex ipso facto ex rege non regem se facit & omni honore & dignitate regali atque in subditos potestate destituit; quorum etiam meminit Winzerus. Horum unus est, Si regnum disperdat, quemadmodum de Nerone fertur, quod is nempe senatum populumque Romanum, atque adeo urbem ipsam ferro flammaque vastare, ac novas sibi sedes quaerere decrevisset. Et de Caligula, quod palam denunciarit se neque civem neque principem senatui amplius fore, inque animo habuerit interempto utriusque ordinis electissimo quoque Alexandriam commigrare, ac ut populum uno ictu interimeret, unam ei cervicem optavit. Talia cum rex aliquis meditator & molitur serio, omnem regnandi curam & animum ilico abjicit, ac proinde imperium in subditos amittit, ut dominus servi pro derelicto habiti dominium.

Alter casus est, Si rex in alicujus clientelam se contulit, ac regnum quod liberum a majoribus & populo traditum accepit, alienae ditioni mancipavit. Nam tunc quamvis forte non ea mente id agit populo plane ut incommodet: tamen quia quod praecipuum est regiae dignitatis amifit, ut summus scilicet in regno secundum Deum sit, & solo Deo inferior, atque populum etiam totum ignorantem vel invitum, cujus libertatem sartam & tectam conservare debuit, in alterius gentis ditionem & potestatem dedidit; hac velut quadam regni ab alienatione effecit, ut nec quod ipse in regno imperium habuit retineat, nec in eum cui collatum voluit, juris quicquam transferat; atque ita eo facto liberum jam & suae potestatis populum relinquit, cujus rei exemplum unum annales Scotici suppeditant. Barclay contra Monarchom. 1. iii. c. 16.
In English, this runs as follows:

“What then? Can no case arise in which the people may, by right and on their own authority, help themselves, take up arms, and attack their king when he domineers over them imperiously? None at all, while he remains a king. ‘Honour the king’ and ‘he that resists the power resists the ordinance of God’ are divine oracles that will never permit it. So the people can never gain a power over him unless he does something that makes him cease to be a king. For then he strips himself of his crown and dignity and returns to the state of a private man, and the people become free and superior, since the power they had in the interregnum, before they crowned him king, devolves to them again. But there are only a few kinds of misconduct that bring matters to this point. After considering it carefully from every side, I can find only two. There are two cases, I say, in which a king, ipso facto, becomes no king, and loses all power and royal authority over his people; and Winzerus also takes note of them.”

“The first is if he tries to overturn the government, that is, if he has a purpose and design to ruin the kingdom and commonwealth. So it is recorded of Nero that he resolved to cut off the senate and people of Rome, lay the city waste with fire and sword, and then move to some other place. And of Caligula, that he openly declared that he would no longer be a head to the people or the senate, and that he had it in mind to cut off the worthiest men of both orders and then withdraw to Alexandria; and he wished that the people had only one neck, so that he might dispatch them all at one blow. When any king harbours such designs as these in his thoughts and seriously promotes them, he immediately gives up all care and thought of the commonwealth, and consequently forfeits the power of governing his subjects, just as a master forfeits his dominion over slaves he has abandoned.”

“The other case is when a king makes himself the dependent of another, and subjects his kingdom, which his ancestors left him and which the people placed free into his hands, to the dominion of another. For though perhaps it may not be his intention to harm the people, yet because he has thereby lost the principal part of royal dignity, namely, to be next and immediately under God, supreme in his kingdom; and also because he has betrayed or forced his people, whose liberty he ought to have carefully preserved, into the power and dominion of a foreign nation. For both these reasons, by this alienation, as it were, of his kingdom he himself loses the power he had in it before, without transferring even the least right to those on whom he would have bestowed it. And so by this act he sets the people free and leaves them at their own disposal. One example of this is to be found in the Scottish annals.”

In these cases Barclay, the great champion of absolute monarchy, is forced to allow that a king may be resisted, and that he ceases to be a king. In short, not to multiply cases: wherever he has no authority, there he is no king and may be resisted. For wherever the authority ceases, the king ceases too, and becomes like other men who have no authority. And the two cases he gives differ little from those mentioned above as destructive to governments, except that he has left out the principle from which his doctrine flows: namely, the breach of trust, in not preserving the form of government agreed on, and in not pursuing the end of government itself, which is the public good and the preservation of property. When a king has dethroned himself and put himself in a state of war with his people, what is to stop them from proceeding against him, who is no king, as they would against any other man who has put himself into a state of war with them? Barclay, and those of his opinion, would do well to tell us. I would also ask the reader to take note of this further point in Barclay. He says, “The harm that is planned against them, the people may prevent before it is done”; and by this he allows resistance when tyranny is only at the stage of design. “When any king harbours such designs as these in his thoughts and seriously promotes them,” he says, “he immediately gives up all care and thought of the commonwealth.” So, according to him, the neglect of the public good is to be taken as evidence of such a design, or at least as a sufficient cause for resistance. And he gives the reason for it all in these words: “because he has betrayed or forced his people, whose liberty he ought to have carefully preserved.” What he adds, “into the power and dominion of a foreign nation,” counts for nothing, since the fault and the forfeiture lie in the loss of their liberty, which he ought to have preserved, and not in any distinction between the persons to whose dominion they were subjected. The people’s right is equally invaded, and their liberty equally lost, whether they are made slaves to some of their own nation or to a foreign one; the injury lies in this, and it is against this alone that they have the right of defence. And instances can be found in every country which show that it is not the change of nations in the persons of their governors, but the change of government, that gives the offence. Bilson, a bishop of our church and a great stickler for the power and prerogative of princes, does, if I am not mistaken, acknowledge in his treatise of Christian subjection that princes may forfeit their power and their title to the obedience of their subjects. And if authority were needed in a case where reason is so plain, I could send my reader to Bracton, Fortescue, and the author of the Mirrour, and others, writers who cannot be suspected of being ignorant of our government or enemies to it. But I thought Hooker alone might be enough to satisfy those men who, relying on him for their ecclesiastical polity, are by a strange fate led to deny the principles on which he builds it. Whether in this they are being made the tools of craftier workmen to pull down their own building, they had better look to it. This I am sure of: their civil policy is so new, so dangerous, and so destructive to both rulers and people, that, just as former ages could never bear to have it broached, so it may be hoped that the ages to come, redeemed from the impositions of these Egyptian under-taskmasters, will abhor the memory of such servile flatterers. While it seemed to serve their turn, they reduced all government to absolute tyranny, and would have had all men born to what their mean souls fitted them for: slavery.

Here, it is likely, the common question will be raised: Who shall be judge whether the prince or the legislative acts contrary to their trust? Perhaps ill-disposed and factious men may spread this question among the people when the prince is only making use of his due prerogative. To this I reply: The people shall be judge. For who shall be judge whether his trustee or deputy acts well, and in accordance with the trust placed in him, but the one who deputes him, and who, by having deputed him, must still have a power to discard him when he fails in his trust? If this is reasonable in the particular cases of private men, why should it be otherwise in a case of the greatest importance, where the welfare of millions is concerned, and where, moreover, the evil, if not prevented, is greater, and the remedy very difficult, costly and dangerous?

But further, this question (Who shall be judge?) cannot mean that there is no judge at all. For where there is no court on earth to decide disputes among men, God in heaven is judge. He alone, it is true, is judge of the right. But every man is judge for himself, as in all other cases so in this one, whether another has put himself into a state of war with him, and whether he should appeal to the Supreme Judge, as Jephthah did.

If a dispute arises between a prince and some of the people in a matter where the law is silent or doubtful, and the thing is of great consequence, I should think the proper umpire in such a case would be the body of the people. For in cases where the prince has a trust placed in him and is exempted from the common, ordinary rules of the law, if any men find themselves wronged and think the prince is acting contrary to that trust, or beyond it, who is so fit as the body of the people (who first placed that trust in him) to judge how far they meant it to extend? But if the prince, or whoever is in the administration, refuses that way of settling it, the appeal then lies nowhere but to heaven. Force between persons who have no known superior on earth, or force that permits no appeal to a judge on earth, is properly a state of war, in which the appeal lies only to heaven; and in that state the injured party must judge for himself when he will think fit to make use of that appeal and put himself upon it.

To conclude: the power that every individual gave the society when he entered into it can never revert to the individuals again as long as the society lasts, but will always remain in the community, because without this there can be no community and no commonwealth, which is contrary to the original agreement. In the same way, when the society has placed the legislative in any assembly of men, to continue in them and their successors, with direction and authority for providing such successors, the legislative can never revert to the people while that government lasts. For having provided a legislative with power to continue for ever, they have given up their political power to the legislative and cannot resume it. But suppose they have set limits to the duration of their legislative, and made this supreme power in any person or assembly only temporary; or else it is forfeited through the misconduct of those in authority. Then, upon the forfeiture, or when the set time has expired, it reverts to the society, and the people have a right to act as supreme and to continue the legislative in themselves, or to set up a new form, or to place it in new hands under the old form, as they think good.
